COUNTY BOROUTEI OF WARR' vOTON.— MUNICIPAL BYE ELUTION 1933. TO THE BLECTOR3 OF St. JOHN'S WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEUEN, Owing to the much regretted death of Mr. Coun- Beirit a ritemiry has arimen in the representa- tion of the Wart on the Tawn Council, and I have the honour of offering my,elf, in the inferests of the general body of ratepayers and re4dents, as an indepond-int o nudists for your serf 11. ces• I AS NOT THE NOSIINE NI OF ANY PARTY, PorAtt- CkG. RELIGIOUS, OR OTHER erISE BELJEV- (NG AS I DO TH a.T TO SERVE THE BEiT INTERESTS OF THE TOWN IS THIS TRUE AND PROPIIR OBJECT TO BE AIMED AT. I WILL NOT BE CONNECTS° WITH ANY CLIQUE OR FACTION: NOR wnr, I DO THE BIDDING OF ANY BODY OF PEOPLE BUT THE BLEOTOSS TEIENNELVHS. I detnane a full end seteching INQUIRY into the accnset*ons mad- against several of the members of the Council, in the lute-eats of the accused as well as of the accusers, but especially in the interests of the ratepayers and the good reputation of our town. I object to all outside interference and dictation, and I trust to the intelligence an .1 goad sense of the ratepaye a to settle our own disputes and manage our own affairs. I am. aid always hews been a None Trader and I protested against gentlemen being elected to the Council who had as their oeject to use the position they held as councillors to their own advantage or the ads' entageof their friends.Mv views on this matter were well known by the people in g-ners.l lon before severalsoffice-seekerr thought of winning a seat by this means after all other means had failed them. I realise to pledge trysail to any party, political, religious, or atherwise, as I cannot see the advantage of introducing into the diumussion of cur Jogai con- cerns any particular set of views which may be held upon Imperial or Parliamentary politics. Neither can I see how the division of the Coencil into two hostile Carnes. on a questioe which is largely personal, will hen,fit the ratepayers, consequently I am not going to waste any time in useless denuncia- tion of this or that group of cmncillors. but will give my best attention and assistance to all projects which make for the benefit of the whole town and the good of St. John's Ward in particular. If you do me the honour to elect me as one of the representatives of your Ward, it will be my endoevour to see that you get a fair return for the rates you pay, which you do not rieseive at present. Your street peving, lighting, and eewering are any- thing but satisfactory, and many of the dwelling- houses in the Ward are amongst the worst in the town, I intend to do all I can to have the Cleansing Department's Depot removed ouC of the Ward, as it is in a most unsuitable position at pre- sent. Standing in the miss of a densely populated neighbonrho el. it is a permanent danger to the health of the inhabit Ants, and a disgrace to any up-to-date Corporation. I hope to be able to explain to you at my public meeting which will be held durine the coining week a simple means of sopping all unfair. unjust, and dishonest trading with the Corporation, either by members of the Council or their friends. I also hope to have he opportunity of proving to you the unjust means by which the rtsteable valuation of your buildings is arrived at, thereby causing the working people, and several businesses, to be forced to pay more t ar. their rightful share of tbe rates, and at the same time giving other businesses and monopolies an unjust advantage in letting them off without paying anything like their due share of the working expenses of the town. In conelusion Ladies and Gentlemen if I have ties honour of securing election for the present vacancy, thus term of which is very short. viz., 15 months, I will do all in my power to assist you in managing the affairs of our town in the Council to your own advantage and to the advantage of all the ratepayers and to put an end to the disgraceful scenes in the Council Chamber which are a serious injury to the commercial and finenciel interests of the Borough of Warrington, and are holding us up to the ridicule of all England. By voting for me you will be supporting amen whose interests are identical with your own. I am, Ladies and Gentesmen, Yours faithfully, JOHN HAGINN. Bridge street and Bylands street, Warrington.

London, 8.0. PROSPECTUS.

The Company was incorporated by an Act of Parliament which received the Royal Assent on the 17th August, 1901. The Company's powers were granted by that Act, and a sub- sequent Act, which received the Royal Assent on the 23rd of June, 1902, the two Statutes td,4ng "The Manchester and Liverpool Electric Express Railway Acts. 1901 and 1962." By these Acts it has been empowered to construct and work an Electrical Railway between Manchester and Liver- pool on Behr's Mono-rail system. The Manchester Terminus of the Railway will be on the west side of Deansgate, one of the principil thoroughfares of that city, and within a distance of about 600 yards from the Exchange and about 400 yards from the Town Hall. The Liverpool Terminus will be closely adjoining Church-street, and within a distance of about 700 yards from the Exchange and Town Hall.

These are most central and convenient situations,7and are both excellently served by the elee'ric tramways. The length of the railway will be about:74i mills, and the time occupied in the transit will be 20 minutes instead of 40 to 45 minutes, the time at present ttken by the fastest express trains running between Manchester and Liverpool. Hach train will carry two classes of passengers at fares not exceeding the ordinary tares at present charged by the other railways. It is proposed to work this new line at a speed of 110 miles an hour, the trains running every ten, minutes, or, it neces- sary, more frequently. Manchester and Liverpool are, after London the two greatest cities in Bnivand, and with their surroundings have an aggregate population of about 1,750,000. To bring these two communities, so closely related, within twenty minutes of each other, at the short intervals provided by a ten-minute service, will, in effect, be to make them parts of one community, and they will in point of time be nearer to each other than one end of Manchester now is to the other end. _

The fact that the present service between these two cities is an exct Rent one, carried out by three great Railway Com- panies, shows the magnitude of the traffic, and that Parlia- ment under these circumstances has granted to this Company the right to construct a fourth Railway, is in itself strong evidence of the merits of the proposed line and its importance for tke improvement of travelling generally. The line will be the pioneer of a system which, in the opinion of many eminent engineers and other competent judges, will create a new era in railway travelling. 1; is a matter of common knowledge that the great problems at present before the Railway Engineers are :- 1. The acquialtion et higher speed for passenger traffic. _

2. The increased frequency of such trains. 3. The separation,: of the various speeds, that Is to sny, the maintenance of separate lines to be appropriated aiad kept exclusively for high-speed express !raffle. The evidence given before Parliament goes to prove that the Mono-rail system solves these great problems, without the risk apparently inherent to g.-eat speed, and in fact,that in this system derailment is practically impossible. On the proposed Railway there will be no mature of fast and slow traffic, no coupling of cars, no crossings, no points, no shunting, so that all these fertile causes of rtelays and accidents vanish. The cars running at regular intervals and at uniform speed, the distance between trainiqwill be exactly maintained.

The foregoing statements are given as the pith of the evi- dence given before parliament by some of the greatest engin- eers and scientists of the day including Sir Frederick:Bramwell, Bert D.C.L.,L.L.D.,F,11.5..&0•;Pa5t President of the Institution of Civil Engineers ; Past Presi- dent of the Institution of Mechanioss Engineers ; Past President of the Royal Society, Sir William Preece IC.C. 8., F.R,S., Past President of the Institution of Civil Engineers.

The Council of the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce took an active part in forming a Committee of representatives of the two of cities Manchester and Liverpool for the purpose of investigating and reporting upon the feasibility of an electrical express setvice between these two cities upon the Mono-rail system. This Committee consisted of the Lord Mayors of the two cities and 40 of the best known and most representative men of the two districts
A full list of the members and a Report of their proceedings accompAny the Prospectus. . _

Ihe.Coriunittee o4t InyestigAtion, having reported most favourably upon the engineering and commercial feasibility of the setieme, the necessary steps were taken to obtain the Company's Acts of ?arliament, and, after a most minute and careful examination of the scheme, extending over in all 37 days, and after examining no fewer than 84 witnesses, Parliament has approved the principle and authorised the construation of the liailway.

Toe Legislature, while sanctioning this important under- taking, has taken care that special powers should be given to the Boar lof Tra-e for the putpose of securing the safefy of tho public, the passengers, and the servants of the Com- pany. The Board of Trade having considered the pietas and proposals submitted to them by the Bngineers have autho- rised the construction of the line to be proceeded with. Mr. S. 13. Cottrell, the Engineer and General Manager of the Liverpool Overhead Electric Railway, put in evidence before Parliament a detailed estimate of the working ex- penses of the line based upon a ten minutes' service, and also based upon the cost of product!, n of electricity, main- tenanne, dc., on the Liverpool Overhead Railway. He esti- mated that the total annual expenditure tor traction, main- tenance, and working expenses would amount to £65,554 per annum, equal to a cost per ta fan mile of about 71d. On this bat's, an average of 7i third-class passengers carried per train would therefore cover all working expenses. ess a7erage of 20 passengers per train,or,2oCo per day In each direction, woeld, it is estimated, be sufficient to pay 5 per cent. per annum upor4the capit,l of the Company, and every additional 2i passengers per train will be sufficient to pay about an additional 1 per cent. interest on the capital- The ten minutes' servieo with the mailed carriage pro- posed, provides for a traffic of abont 4t03 passengers each way per day. Should the nnmber of passengers increase,by utilising larger carriages and by inereasing the frequency of the trains, which can easily be done. the Railway will be able to carry up to 25,000 passengers per day in each direction.
The provision of more rapid and frequent communication between populous centres invites, and has resulted in a very
Vraepatus.

large increase of traffic. This is proved by the returns of existing electric Railways. Although the instances of all omnibus service are not altogether similar, increased speed in communication favourably affects traffic,and as ancillustra- tion we may quote the following figures of the Liverpool Overhead Electric Railway, which replaced a line of omni- buses carrying about 2,500,000 passengers annually. In that Railway's first full year of working the total number of passengers carried by the railway was 4,0)0,00. In 19 1, having been running about 8 year., it carried 8,000,000 passengers annually, or about 21.500 per day. Even more satisfactory results have ben shown by thej working of elec- tric tramways. The anticipation, tberefore, of such a traffia as will permit of very con,iderable dividends to the Share- holders cannot be considered unreasonable.

div.head: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY. i
div.p: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY. i

e summer sales having approached that fati*r end, we view our various purchases thereat with no doubt very mixed feelings as there is no woman, however practised a bargain-hunter she may be, who is not some- times led into the error of buying a few yards of silk or lace which she really does not re- quire, their virtue lying in their very cheap- ness. Indeed, if one escapes the deeper pit- falls of unnecessary and somewhat useless bats, coats, or gowns, there is every cause for self - congratulation; as the profusion of charming and lovely articles of dress exhi- bited at these sales is so alluring to every feminine beholder as to overcome much of

div.head: LINEN WALKING SKIRT:
div.p: A LINEN WALKING SKIRT:

their common sense and fill their souls with tib thirst for the so-called "sweeping reduc- tions." However, the wise precaution of making a list before leaving home of those things we actually do require, and rigidly refraining from taking any more money with us than we can actually afford to lay out, will go a long way to check all extravagant longings. Linen in self and pale colours is much worn this season, and is of a different and less easily crushed make than heretofore. It makes up into all sorts of very useful costumes, whether of the bolero and skirt style, or the bodice and skirt, and is suited to quite young children as Well as middle-aged people. / The skirt given in my illustration is one of the smartest styles for a linen walking or trottokskirt. It is made with stitched bands, -which hold the fulness in place till near the hem, when the pleats give a comfortable and pleasing amount of fulness. The front of the skirt is plain, and is cut in one with the part which closely fits the hips. The skirt clears the ground all round, and so allows of free- dom in walking—a quality especially welcome after the trailing skirts of last summer, which took at least one hand to keep in any sort of control. The trailing skirt is not, however, altogether banished from our midst, for it is the • most suitable style for very thin dia- phanous materials such as voile and mousse-

div.head: CHARMING TOQUE.
div.p: A CHARMING TOQUE.

line 4 The very prettiest and most chic skirts at present are made full but plain, save for a few frills at the hem, sometimes varied by scallops, which show i full plisse frill undef- neath. These skirts are generally made of some embroidered or beautifully patterned material as plenty cif •'scope is given by the cut to display the full beauty of the material.

It is strange to notice how rapidly the narrow- shaped belt has disappeared from our midst, being replaced by a wide swathed silk band, finished at the back of the waist by little tabs or tassels, while long sash ends are often to be seen on some very smart gowns. _ _

A charming toque, -sketched, is very modish and dainty. It is made of -folds of creamy tulle, arranged cunningly over a wire shape, -which is flat at the back. A handsome sweep- ing cream-coloured bird of paradise plume, caught by a pretty buckle, is the only trim- ming employed. The hat, which dips down over the face in front, rising a little at the side, and being again depressed at the back has become so generally popular that one can already foretell its demise; and I should counsel those of my readers who meditate selecting a new hat to invest in one of the many other pretty modes. There are some very lovely drawn lace hats which demand a very fine day, and are well suited to a garden fete. )These lace hats are trimmed with gar- lands of very small roses, and are exceedingly

div.head: SMART COAT.
div.p: A SMART COAT.

picturesque: More suited to stand the variety of weather peculiar to the English weather is the new plateau French sailor hat of satin straw, a wreath of foliage or flowers surrounding the very Slight crown, and flowers and leaves massed closely to- gether at-the back, filling in the space between the hat and the coiffure. Ribbon bows are much en evidence on plain straw or stitched linen hats, and these bows are much stiffer than. the floppy bows with which we are all so familiar. The loops are sometimes plisse. and a ruche or twist is much more fashion- able for trimming the crown than a plain ribbon band. The coat sketched is of cream-coloured canvas of a rather open mesh over a lining which closely resembles silk, but is not quite so stiff, and more durable. It is finished• by bands of coloured embroidery, and the double-shaped cape-like flounces at the shoulders and finishing the sleeves are. very smart. It is made loose-fitting, and of the sac style, and can therefore be easily put on over a very elaborate costume without crush- ing or injuring in any way the finery under- neath. There are many of these loose coats on view, which vary only in length, although sometmies a thin smooth-surfaced cloth or even a light silk is employed for their con- struction. There are also some very smart- looking three-quarter and full length coats of white linen, which require plentiful strap- pings to ensure their success, and sometimes ' the addition of a wide collar of • embroidery or coarse lace. The ecru linen coat is not so new as the white, although the tone of colour is certainly less trying to most complexions, and these coats do not soil so easily as the other& COQUETTBd

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

A casein one of the County Court-; in London, shows how keen must be the quest of artificial beauty. Cos- metics, paints, powders, and drugs have been the common resort of women of all ages, but now the pro- fession of" face culture " employs the most expensive electrical machinery appliances, and preparations. Nor are these establishments patronized only by women, though it has been said to bathe privilege of man to he as ugly as he likes. It makes but little difference to his prospects in life either from a business or social point of view, and is far less important to him than culture and manners, but to a woman no intellectual gifts, good- ness of heart, or purity of mind, will wholly compen- sate her for plainness of appearance. There is consequently mor e reason for women to resort to artificial aids, and indeed her desire for beauty is quite a legitimate one. But that is not to recom- mend her to the modern "beauty specialist," whose best resultsare but "skin deep." They seldom prevail, and moreover invariably have to be paid for with heavy interest later on in life. What cver one's features may be, the best and only lasting beauty to cultivate is that which comes from healthful habits, a cheerful spirit,and a healthful occupation of mind and body. ; There isa proverb in China that every man digs his grave with his own teeth, and this appeArs to be the I opinion of Dr. Yorke Davis who has been writing on ; the subject of improper dieting. Fewer wives he suggests would be widows, if they knew what food to provide, and how to cook it. Then be vet only com- plains about badly prepared food, but says that the • middle and luxurious classes eat about half as mubh again as they should do. There is no doubt, a good deal of truth in this, and that it specially applies to the hot I weather. We do not want fires, furs, or overcoats, and ; half the ailments of summer time might be avoided if we werecareful to reduce our consumption of heat forming foods at this time of the year. • As a rule the annual holiday at the seaside affords the , only opportunity which women have to indulge in bath- ing and swimming. There are not many swimming baths,even in London, but some progress is beim('. made I with the movement for making these available for women on certain days. Some of these gatherings are of a very fashionable description and the King and Queen accompanied by Princess Victoria, were present the other day at an entertainment organized by the Life ; Saving Society, at the Bath Club in Dover-street. The King presented a silver challenge cup, for international competition,, but the entertainment was of a varied des- cription, and in the life saving tests, their Majesties warmly applauded some little girls who showed them- selves exceedingly quick and clever in performing their tasks. _ . _ _

The choice of a bathing dress depends very largely upon whether it is wanted for elegance or utility. Those who try to combine the merits of both virtues, should avoid the common mistake of having their costume made of serge, which holds the water too much, and is heavy for swimming. Alpaca, dark blue linen, or Italian cloth, is lighter, and preferable in this respect. It is also more easily changed, and in every bathing costume one point on the score of utility is that it should permit of being quickly put on and taken off. As regards colours, dark blue and red are the best to stand slit water, which should be kept from the hair. For those who really go in for bathing and swimming there is othing for it but the unsightly mackintosh ,cap, but lippearances may be greatly improved by neatly , tying it round with a washable silk handkerchief. I Some daring innovations in dress may be attributed I-to the hot weather of recent summers. It gave birth to the sandal craze, the transparent-neck blouse and trans- parent sleeves. This year it is apparently going to in- troduce the American custom of dispensing with hats. During the last hot season, the fashionable American girl took to going without headgear, spending her days at the holiday resorts with only an elaborate parasol as protection against the sun. Many also appeared on promenade in elbow sleeves, and entirely dispensed with glove'. There are signs that a similar craze will be in evidence at our fashionable seaside resorts, and if only the summer is sufficiently hot, there is no knowing what eecentrioity in dress it may be responsible for. There is however,a general revulsion against extremes of demi toilette in day dress, and the blouse with the transparent neck and sleeves is now only seen amongst the commoner classes. The sandal has also gone out of fashion. It was introduced mainly for children, though some attempt was made to popularise it amongst girls in their teens and those of more sedate years. Those who took it up as semething new soon discarded it, and there is really nothing in the sandal to recommend it for children. It tends to make their feet less shapely and exposes the foot to the greater risk of cuts and bruises, and also disease germs. The ordinary canvas shoe, such as children wear at the seaside is much more convenient to the little folks, and is in every way a more suitable form of footgear. For years, the press, and humane individuals have been agitating the question of the sale of aigrettes, hich are obtained by shooting the beautiful white heron during the breeding season, and leaving the young to perish. it is therefore not a little discourag- ing to find that during the present summer these plumes are'being sold in greater quamtities than ever before. The vendors, when reference is made to the subject,generally declare that the plumes are artificial, but—whether they know it or not—this is not the case. Many of the aigrettes which have been sold as artificial, have been examined by experts, and in all cases they have been found to be the real plumes of the white heron. No one sympathises with the person with a cold. He or she, whoever the sufferer may be, is regarded as some- thing of a nuisance, and so also are those afflicted with "hay fever "—which has been very prevalent this summer. Whilst, however, one can "catch a cold" from another, one cannot take hay fever unless suscep- tibleto this distressing complaint. It is said that men are more subject to is than women, and if this is so, it shows that tobacco, as some recommend, is no remedy., or safeguard against it. All sorts of remedies are tried by sufferers, but though some say they find relief there seems to be no one specifio that can be relied upon by those who are naturally sensitive to this peculiarly dis- abling affliction. The recent debate in the House of Lords on the alleged decline in the physique of our people,has already had one excellent result in the numerous discussions that have since taken place on the up-bringing of children. That there is great need of lectures on the subject is apparent to all, and this especially applies to the work- ing classes whose ideas in the matter of feeding, in many cases leaves much to be desired. "Pat," Dr. Cheadle says, "is wanted for every tissue formed and forming. In children who are fed upon a deficient amount of fat, the bony structures are imperfect, and slow of growth." This is a point which should be im- pressed upon every mother. In cases of rickets aud wasting, doctors are now generally prescribing virol, a preparation consisting of marrow fat, malt and eggs which for infants is added to the milk or food in the feeding bottle. There is scarcely a Hospital in the British Isles in which in oases of weakly children, con- sumption' salmis, and gastric ulcer, this food is not used with the best possible results.

div.head: BY HARRIS BURLAND, AUTHOR OF DACOBRAIETC.
div.p: BY HARRIS BURLAND, AUTHOR OF DACOBRAIETC.
CHAPTER Vll.—Continued.

"Yes, you shall stay," she said quietly; "at any rate until your clothes are dried. Come here." She took candle from a Cupboard, and lighting it, led the way into the kitchen, where a fire blazed in the grate. As they entered they heard the sound of a key turning in a lock. The woman smiled. She knew that her father had locked himself in. " If you will wait here," she said, " I will get you a change of clothes. I have some of my—we have some upstairs. They will fit you, I think. They belonged to a big man," and she looked admiringly at the stalwart figure before her, as she turned to go. . When Tredegar was left to himself, he sat down on a chair and shivered. The water still trickled from his clothes to the floor. He felt taint and exhausted, and a strange cold feeling began to creep through his limbs. He pul.ted himself together, and stamped his feet to keep himself warm. Nkhen he moved closer to. the roaring fire. and Nrouched over the blaze. Every now and then he would look back over his shoulder ancillilisten. He had changed much during the past three weeks ix London. His eyes had a nervous, hunted look. His clothes were .shabby and dirty, and his face was covered with a bristly beard and moustache. He did not look at all a pleasant customer to have in a house that contained nearly £150,000 worth of gold and jewellery. In a few minutes Miss Cantrip returned with a complete outfit, and leaving the room, locked the door behind her. Tredegar smiled and looked at himself in a piece of cracked glass on the wall. He could hardly blame a woman for taking these precautions. He certainly looked as• though he were capable of making off with the clothes. But a minute later the door was unlocked and the old man entered, closing it behind him. His right hand was in his pocket.' "This is very good of you," Tredegar said. "I am really ashamed to give you and your— your daughter so much trouble. Mr. Cantrip did not answei, but seated him- self in a chair and inspected the young man critically. The latter began to undress wearily, and hang his clothes in front of the fire. He put down the old man as a madman rd paid no more attention to him. As the young fellow bared the magnificent muscles of his arms, Cantrip gazed at him approvingly and nodded his head. Your name ? " he said abruptly. "Edward Edwards." " Welsh ? " "From Monmouthshire—Newport." "Profession ?" "A sailor." "Out of work?" "Yes." The old man seemed to be turning over something in his mind. "A rogue ?" he said, abruptly. "A vaga- bond, eh? Perhaps a criminal ?"

'Sir I" said tredegar, in so menacing a tone that the old man started and moved his hand a little out of his pocket, "No offence—no offence. Ilr.—Edwards. But you look a rough lot, don't you? I should not care for you to hit me. Ever killed anyone, eh ?" It was now Tredegar's turn to start. .but he concealed his agitation with a nervous laugh. "Not that I know of," he replied. "You could though, eh? Just one blow, eh? So!- " and he thrust out his skinny little hand pugnaciously. Again Tredegar laughed. Then he finished dressing, and sank wearily into a chair. His brain spun round and round and a hundred pains shot through his aching limbs. He grasped the seat of the chair for support. There was a knock at the door. The old man opened it, and his daughter came in. She had a steaming glass of hot whisky-and-water in one hand, and in the other a plate with a huge piece of cake on it. She handed both to Tredegar, who took them with trembling hands. "This is too good of you," he murmured. "It is just the thing. Oh, lam so cold." He took a long gulp of the steaming drink, and ate the cake. He was ravenous, for he had eaten no food since the night before, but he devoured it slowly lest the others should notice his hunger. Before he had finished, the old man rose and left the room. - .

Miss Cantnp then seated -herself in a chair on the other side of the fireplace, and, produc- ing a gold case, offered Tredegar a cigarette. She lit one herself, and began to chat to him pleasantly. Her woman's curiosity was roused, and she wanted to find out who this man was—this young fellow with the rcmgh face and the gentle voice. But he only an- swered her in monosyllables, and, as she talked, his face grew whiter ard whiter, and his hands grasped the chair like a vice. He was suffering agony, and it seemed to him that the fires of hell were running through his veins in place of blood. The woman watched him with pity-on her face. Then suddenly he began to speak to her in a torrent of words, in long, incoherent sen- tences about scenes and places that she knew nothing of. About desert islands, and ship- wreck, and starvation, and police, and murder —and through all she caught the oft-repeated name of a woman. She rose to her feet ta call her father, and, as she did so, the great figure swayed, the arms of the chair snapped like twigs, and Tredegar fell forward sense- less to the floor.
CHAPTER VIII. THE UNPAID DEBT.

WHEN Tredegar came \to his senses he foune, himself in a small, plainly - furnished room. .The sunlight streamed through the window and showed Up all the shabby spots in the carpet and wall-paper. Miss Cantrip was sitting by his side with a me dicine-glass in her hand. At the foot of the bed stood a tall, keen-faced man with a straggly grey mous- tache. Tredegar regarded them both with an air of bewilderment, and then, moving his arm a little, gave a sharp cry of pain, and lay still. . .

"Where am I?" he murmumd, fitly. "What is the matter ?" "Rheumatic fever," said the man at the foot of the bed. " You , :.11 be all right. 3 never saw a more magnificent frame to a mar. But you will find it painful. This lady lipts kindly consented to nurse you. I wante.l. to send you to a hospital. She will probably be sorry before your illness is over." "This lady ?" Tredegar repeated, softly. "This lady? Ah. yes, I remember now. But I must leave here at once. Can't I go to a hospital ?'' " 1•Ir the doctor answered, decidedly. "You cannot be moved now. You might have been taken there ten hours ago, but I should not care to risk it now. And you must not talk. You have been delirious." "Delirious ?" Tredegar murmured. " Then I have talked a great deal?" And a look of apprehension crossed his face. Probably the whole story of his life was now known to these two people. He glanced uneasily at Miss Cantrip, and she smiled. "You have talked a lot of nonsense," she answered. "You quite frightened me last night, . But when the doctor did come, you relapsed into silence." Tredegar gave a sigh of relief. At any rate, the doctor had not heard much. He close() his eves. The pain in his limbs was terrible. He did not utter a sound. Only his white face and the little stream of blood trickling down from the lip he had bitten in his pain showed the agony he suffered.

For five long weeks Tredegar lay in till tittle room. Hour after hour had he counted the little brown roses on the faded wall-paper. 3nffeft oak the cracks on the ceiling, and tocated every stain and tear in the carpet, till the whole place had become a map to him,

with its own little islands and rivers and mountains and seas:- --Hour after hour h-1 ran through the history of this last year, and realised all the horrors of the past and the loneliness of the future that lay before him. Hour after hour he saw the face ot Mavanwy, and it was with him, even in his dreams—a white, tear-stained face with eyes fixed on the sea, waiting for the lover that could not come— a lover that was more lost than if he had been dead. He would never speak to Mavanviy again. He might see her. It would be possible to slink down to Garth, and catch a glimpse of her face; but it would be impossible to speak to her. The single foolish act of a drug-maddened brain had set a gulf between them. It would never be bridged until the other man was found the real murderer of Cyrus Walroyd. And yet through all these weary days his only moments of happiness came from the kindly presence of another woman. Miss Cantrip had nursed him through his long illness with such devotion and patience and skill that he was almost oppressed by the burden of gratitude she had laid Upon him. He often wondered how he could ever repay the debt. He also wondered-why this woman had taken pity on a perfect stranger, and had almost worn herself out with watching by his bedside and ministering to his every want. At first he put it down to the natural tender. ness of her womanly nature, and tried his best to think that his loneliness and helplessness had moved her heart to pity. But as the pain in his limbs died out and the fever in his body abated, his brain grew more clear and capable of observation. And it was then that he first learnt the terrible truth. He read it in her eyes, in the tender- ness of every action, in the way she moved, in the inflections of her voice, even in the sad little stories she told him of her lonely life. even, too, in the way she laid bare her faults to him. In all these the truth was made manifest to him, and he shuddered when he thought upon it. This woman loved him, and she would expect her reward. And it was impossible that he could return her love.

He did what he thought the best thing under the circumstances. He spoke often to her of the girl he loved. He did this with • clear honesty of purpose, but felt all the time that he was nothing better than a brute. It was agony to him to speak of Mavanwy, but he wished the &her woman to realise the truth. She listened patiently, and even took an apparent interest in his conversation. Ho laboriously explained that he could never marry the gal he loved, but that he would be true to her to the day of his death. Then Miss Cantrip would move away front the bedside, and do some little kindly act for him that would sting him to the quick. As a matter of fact he was, in his own clumsy way. doing the worst thing possible. He did not kitow the character of this beautiful woman. He saw nothing of its passionate strength. He did not even imagine that every word he spoke about Mavanwy strengthened her own resolution to win his love. It was inevitable that a crisis would come soon.

It came one sunny evening in July. Trede- ear was convalescent. He had been moved into a small sitting room on the same floor, end was sitting in a chair by the open window. His face was worn and thin, and his great body so shrunken that his clothes hung on his limbs like garments on a scarecrow. His beard and Moustache had -now grown to a respectable length. and he was more pleasant to look upon than when he had first entered the house. He was weak from his long illness, and so mi...era.ble that .he wished he had never recovered from it. During the last few days an additional terror had come upon him. He had began to mistrust his own strength of purpose. The strange beauty of this woman, the love in her eyes, the heavy debt he owed her, their intimacy as nurse and invalid, were all bringing terrible pressure upon the constancy of his love. On this particular evening he found himself wondering whether it was not his duty to marry .her, and whether Mavanwy would not forgive him under the unusual circumstances. For half an hour he reasoned out the whole situation with relent- less sophistry. Then his face suddenly crimsoned with shame, and he burst . into tears.

It was thus that Miss Cantrip \ found him when she entered the room. He was sobbing like a child, and his face was Liiried in his hands. He did not hear the sound of her footsteps as she moved silently across to his side.

Then all the pity of her woman's heart went out to this strong man so enfeebled by sickness. She stooped . and kissed the great lean hands that were wet with tears. She cared nothing for the .shame of the thing. She only saw that the man she loved was in digtress.

He started as though he had been stung, and flung; his hands from his, face with such violence that one of them :caught her on the cheek. Then he half-rose from his seat and stared at her with horror. What had he done ? He had struck her the woman who had nursed him ,as tenderly as a sister or a wife might have done. And ? She was cowering away from him, hnd her face was white and cold as death... He opened his lips to speak, but no words came. What could be said after such an act as this ?

He sank back into his seat and gasped for breath. The excitement had been too great a strain on his weak nerves. His hands trembled as he clutched the arms of the chait, and he closed his eyes with a look of pain. In an instant the hard look died from the woman's face, and moving swiftly to his side she knelt down and took one of his hands in hers. This time he did not move, and the hand lay cold and quivering in the warm clasp of her fingers. "Forgive me," she said, gently; "I was to blame. I know it was an accident !" and she looked pleadingly into his face. He faintly shook his head, and opening his eyes, gazed steadily at the beautiful woman by his side. She turned away, and clasped his hand a little more tightly as though she were afraid of losing him by the utterance of a single word. "Miss Cantrip," he said, after .a long pause, "I owe you more than. I can ever pos- sibly repay, and I owe you this much—that I will not lie to you. It was no accident. I did not mean to strike you. lam not so vile a cur as . that. But the movement was dic- tated by my heart. It was wrung from me in a moment of agony, but it was true. I was afraid —afraid of myself—afraid of 1-311 dear friend." The woman turned her head and looked passionately into his eyes. H. white face and auburn hair were strangely beautiful in the golden light that came. .up from the West. Then she suddenly bent down and pressed her lips, to his hand in • a long, ardent kiss. He did not stir, but he dared not look up. Even then his mind was trembling in the balance. A. look of despair 'crossed. her face. She resolved to cast the la.st die—to sink to the lowest depths of humiliation. She bent over him till her face was no more than a foot from his.

"Edward," she whispered, "I love you t There is shame in the words, but I glory in the shame! I love you !" For one moment he looked into her burning eyes. Her face drew nearer to his, and 'then —he kissed her, and the next moment hei arms were about his neck. and she was sob- bing on his breast. He lay cold and still in her embrace. He did not kiss her again. The Moment's papaion had died away: Only tha bitter shame =lf it 'remained. Then she raised-flit heid and lookEd into his white; ghastly face and read the truth. Slowly she took her arms from his neck and rose to her feet. She wished that he had struck her. A blow would have been easier to bear than this.
"Cynthia," he said, in a low, strained voice, "you must forget I We mast both forget." It was the first time he had called her by Tier Christian name, but she barely noticed the circumstance.

"You are a coward !" she said, calmly. "You dare not love I What is this other woman to you! You can • never marry her, you have said it yourself, She will not wait for you." "She will wait for me f" he replied; and then a furious passion seized him. "Oh, orb), have- you been so cruel to me! I owe you so much! You are so beautiful! I would give you everything—but this !" "I do not want to buy your love with kindness !" she answered passionately. " I am not so low as that! I can make you love me! I will wait till you are strong and your own self. I have taken a mean advantage of you. I own it; but what will a woman not do when she loves? You shall love me, and you shall forget this other woman. She will not wait for you !" "She once thought me dead," he answered, "and still she waited for me. She will wait now. And I—and I will always wait for her l"

The woman's face flushed with anger and shame. Then it grew very hard and cold, and she laughed bitterly. "Will she wait ?" she cried in a mocking voice. "Will she wait? Do you think that she will wait for you, Mr, Emrys Tredegar ?" She spnke the last three words slowly and incisively as though each word were a stab. He looked at her in silence. Yet, strange to say, the uppermost •thought in his mind was not. the - danger of being at the mercy of a woman he had repulsed, but that this woman who knew all had loved him in spite of what she knew.

"Yes, Emrys," she continued, more gently, "I have known everything since the day after you came here. I was with you in your delirium. I caught a chance word, and I took care that no one else should listen to your ravings. The next day I bought a back copy of a paper containing your photo- graph and an account of the murder of Cyrus Walroyd. Then I knew the truth, and it was for that reason that I kept you here, where no one would be likely to seek you. If you had gone to a hospital you might have been moved on to a gaol." Still he did not speak. His heart was too full for words. The burden of his debt lay still more heavy on his life. And he could pay nothing—nothing. "You are in my power, Emrys," she con- tinued, " and they .say hell has no fury like a woman scorned.'" "I was not thinking of that," he said at last, "I was only thinking of all you had done ior me. You are a noble woman, Cynthia, and for your sake I must leave here at once. He tried to rise from his chair; but finding he was too weak to stand without the support of her arm, he fell back into his seat.

I have all a woman's weakness," she replied sadly, "her vanity, her passion, her pride. You must marry me. I am rich, and we can go abroad and start a new life. You can never marry Mavanwy Morgan." He loQked her straight in the eyes. "You do not believe me guilty ?" he said, in a low voice. "I ant innocent—and my innocence will be proved! I shall wait." "I am sure you are innocent !" she cried; passionately. "But I, too, can wait, Emrys, and I shall not wait in vain. I hold all the cards in my hand. I.et this woman play against me, and she will see them." She swept out of the room without another look at him, and he lay back in his chair and tried to think quietly of all he had learnt. Only one thought came clearly to his mind— that he must look once more on the pure, sweet face of Mavanwy Morgan, and escape from the woman who had done more for. him than he could ever repay.

A fortnight afterwards he had gained a con- siderable amount of strength, and had already been out nearly a dozen times. He was chafing to leave, yet knew not how to manage it with kindness and courtesy. Miss Cantrip 'tad never again referred to what had passed between them. She attended to h;in with consistent care and sweetness, but never by word or look betrayed the love that burnt so fiercely within her. Yet he longed for the salt air and the shores of Cardigan Bay, and the little village stretching along by the sea. On this particular afternoon he was idly turning over a heap of old papers, when sud- denly he saw a flaming headline in one of those pink evening productions that do so much to add to the horrors of life. "Terrible murder. in Cardiganshire !" .

For •a moment his blood, ian cold, and he dared not read the column beneath. Was it possible. that Cynthia —Cantrip had pur- posely left this lying about ? Then he glanced quickly at the date and gave a sigh of relief. It was. dated ten days previously. Then, as he read, he trembled with excitement, fix the paragraph told in lurid language how another man, David James, had been murdered in the district of Garth. He had been found dead in the great bog of Gogerddan, literally- crushed to death. The paper spared nothing of realism, and described the broken back and limp necl:, and the hlood and torn clothing with all the fullest details. It also referred to the murder of Cyrus Walroyd, and kindly pointed out that .the two murdeis were probably the vi'ork of one hand, and that Emrys Tredegar had developed a homicidal mania, and must be hunted down like a wild beast. Tredegar qmiled. Here at last was a ray of hope. He could, at any rate, prove that he had not com- mitted this last murder._

That very night he arose quickly from his bed and stole out of the house. He left nothing behind him but a small packet ad- dressed to Miss Cantrip. It contained the half of the gold disc, the only thing of value he possessed in the world, and a letter which ran as follows

" MY DEAR FRIEND,.—I leave you this, not for its value, but as a memento of my gratitude. No money can repay vou for what you have done, though some day I shall hope to recom- pense your father for all the expense he has been put to on my account. For yourself, I will repay you all some day, nor can I marry with a clear conscience till I have repaid you all. In what way, God will point out to me. But I will repay you, Cynthia—l will I I swear it! Good-bye, dear friend." In the -morning Cynthia Cantrip opened the package, and read the letter with a face ihryt. *night have been cut out of marble, so .r.Oid and still were its features. Then she glanced at the gold disc, and stepped forward to the open window to throw it far over the wall into the river beyond. . .

But before she re-ached the casement she stopped and examined the few links of chain still hanging to the semi-circle of gold. Then she suddenly gave a cry of horror, and fell in a dead faint to the floor. Three hours later four detectives were on the track of Emrys Tredegar.
CHAPTER IX. HOW TREDEGAR SAID. GOOD-DYE.

TOWARDS the dawn of a hot day in August Frnrys Tredegar stood on the brow of Bryn Mawr, a high mountain overlooking the estuary of the Llyn. Below him the opening sweep of the river and the long marshes on the far side of it lay grey in the twilight, The air was full of the music of birds and the sounds of life awaking to another day. In the distance he could; hear the harsh cries of a shepherd calling to his dog. Behind him, over the wide ranges of hills, lay a bar of pale yellow, the first faint flush' of sunrise. He sat down on a block of granite and ate a piece of dry bread with evident relish. He drank deeply of a small stream which ran down the mountain-side, and afterwards bathed his face and hands in the running water. Then he rose to his feet and looked back along the narrow sheep track by which he had travelled. We was dressed in a blouse and overalls of blue linen. Over his shoulder hinng two long strings of onions such as the Breton peasants hawk along the shores of Wales. It is a strange irony of fate that in the land of the leek the inhabitants are chiefly dependent on France for their onions: The disguise had one advantage; for the wandering life of these onion sellers would ac•

count tor any irregularity of movement on his part. They came and went when they would. and they stayed as long as they pleased in a place, and no one questioned them.. At first sight it might appear that the ,language would have presented a difficulty. But it is well- known in Wales that these peasants of Brit- tany can make themselves understood in their own language by the people who know no tongue but Welsh.

For ten days Emrys Tredegar had been travelling from London on foot; and the fresh air and the exercise had brought back the glow of health to his face. At first he had travelled carelessly, but now, as he neared his old home, he neglected no precaution, All that night he had toiled up and down the long slopes of hills till he had reached the summit of Bryn Mawr. During the day to come he proposed to lie concealed' in the woods of I.lynglas. As the dawn grew brighter in the East, an the sky began to be flushed with crinison, tho made his way down the mountain to-a point where the estuary .was spanned by a long wooden railway bridge, built on piles. f4,-• crossed this, walking between the mbil4r:*4 and before the full light of day bust tiros mountain and marsh and sea, he was mount- ing the wooded slopes of the hills above Trethol.

He eneountered no one beyond two labourers, who nodded him a surly good. morning. By. nine o'clock he had found a small grassy dell by the banks of a water- fall, in the thickest part of the woods, and there lie extended his great limbs on ilw smooth green turf and bracken, and fell fast asleep. When he awoke it was about four p.m. It was a hot, still day and the shade of the ti. and the sound of the little cascade were grate- ful to him. He ate another large piece 11) bread, this time with the addition of a luner., of cheese. Then he took out a clay pipe frost his pocket, and collecting some small scraps of tobacco from the folds of a piece of paper, smoked quietly for twenty minutes. Then he made his way through the woods till he reached a point which overhung the house of Mavanwy Morgan. By climbing a tall pine tree he could see the roof and chimneys far below, and beneath them the wide green lawns stretching to the boundary walls. And then by the wall he saw a single figure in black —motionless, looking towards the sea. He trembled so violently that he nearly lost, his hold on the branch. He could not mis- take the figure even at that distance. It was Mavanwy.

He gazed at her for several minutes, till she turned round and walked slowly back into the house. Then he descended the tree, and sitting down on the trunk of a fallen pine, .2,pidly ran over the various wild schemes he had already formulated. He knew he must obtain an interview with her. Yet no plan seemed safe. Finally he resolved to leave it to chance. He put his hand in his trouser's pocket, and, pulling out some silver, counted it carefully. It amounted to 125. 6d. in all. He could live on that for more than a week, and bide his time till an opportunity offerer itself. Then he would leave England, till time revealed the secret of _Cyrus Walroyd's death.

When the sun had fallen below the hOrizon of the sea, he crept stealthily down the hill through the dark pines till he reached a point below the grounds of the house, Then be turned to the left, and moving cautiously along the wood, waited close to the edge, where he could see the boundary wall.
"Perhaps," he thought he himself, "she wi:l come here again after dinner. Perchance she will be alone.'
He waited an hour. The moonlight fell full on the wall above him, so that he could see everything. He hiniself was concealed in the darkest shadow.

At last he heard the faint sound of foot- steps on the gravel walk, and then the moon- light fell on the dark dress and white face of a woman. It was Mavanwy 1 He had not waited in vain. He could see her face clearly. It was pale and haggard. Her hands gripped the stone ledge of the wall, as she gazed wearily seawards. A single ring flashed ,on her finger. He knew it well. He had given it to her before he had left for Peru. Then he roused himself. There was no time to be lost. - .

" Mavani,vy 1" he said, almost in a whisper —for he knew not who else might be near. Mavanwy 1" She started. In the silence of that still summer's night the sound had come faintly to her, like the cry of some ghost. She leant over the wall and peered into the dark. " Mavanwy 1" he said again. "Do not be frightened I It Pi I, Emrys ! Are you alone?" . _ _
She swayed as though she would have fallen. Then she recovered herself, and look- ing behind her across the lawn, ncdded her head.

He came out of the darkness into the moon- light and stood beneath the wall, and, catch- ing hold of her hands, he kissed them fervently. " Emr7,-s 1." she cried, in a low voice of horror. " Emrys ! "

And then wrenching her hands from his, she bowed her head on her arms and gave a great sob of pain. "My darling ! " he murmured. " YOu do not believe me guilty ? I am innocent ! You know Lam :nnocent !" She raised her tear-stained face and looked at him.

" I know you are innocent," she said, slowly. " But Why are you here, Emyrs ? You are in anger! For God's sake, go!" "I have come to see you, Mavanwy," he answered. "I could not go longer without seeing you. I have not dared to write. You do not know how I have longed to see you. I have also come to say good-bye! I ntust leave England in a few days —perhapS for ' ever ! "
"For ever," she repeated mechanically. "Till the murderer of Cfrus Walroyd has been discovered—and that may be, never.!."
"Oh, if I had not mritten that letter ! " she cried, in piteous tones. "It was on that that the coroner's jury brought in a verdict of guilty. Without it there would have been no motive."

"I read the full account of the inquest," he said. . "The door was locked. I3oth Cyrus Walroyd and the murderer must have entered by the window. There were no marks outside, for there is only stone - paving below. But it does not matter. I stand condemned in the eyes of. the world. • And I must leave England—or else—" _ _

"Or else what-?" " I must face my trial, and trust to my innocence being proved:" "No, no! " . she cried. " Anything but that—anything but that !" "Then it is 'good-bye,' Mavanwy." " I will come with you, Emrys," she said, hurriedly. " I cannot lose you again now you have been brought back to me from death ! I will come with you. I will meet you somewhere. We can be married, and start a new life abroad." _

His lips twitched nervously. • Less than a fortnight ago those very words had been spoken by a woman he did not love. Then they had seemed a desecration of love. Here in the moonlight they seemed the sweetest words ever uttered by a woman's lips. Yet, like the other's, they offered that which he knew he could not take. For a Minute he stood in hesitation. The temptation was almost irresistible. But he conqueir his own desires.

" No, Mavanwy," he said. " No, My dearest sweetheart. It is impossible ! cannot bind you to a hunted man—to a pauper! I do not profess to b.; good, but I am ,not so bad as that. I will wait 1 Per- haps in a year or two, when I have settled, when I have made money to keep you in com- fort, when I am—safe —perhaps then : but whatever happens. I am always your lover." At that moment a door opened in the house, and a broad bar of light streamed aCross. tli3 lnwn. A da-1- against the openinv Msavanwy looked rounclJ "My father," she said. " Good-bye, Emrys 1"
(To be co; tin ,ed.)

I Alderman FRANCOMB, in proposing the toast of "Success to Peter Walker and Son," said it *as a well- known fact that , Messrs. He moved that the Town Clerk be again written to, asking for informa- 1 tion on the matter, and adding that they still adhered I to their resolution asking for public bowling greens to be provided. Mr. PLINSTON said the Town Clerk always did his best with the letters sent to him,and he would willingly second Mr. Podmore's proposition. 1 The proposition was unanimously carried.

div.head: 'HERE THE POPE CAUGHT HIS CHILLI
div.p: 'HERE THE POPE CAUGHT HIS CHILLI
TEE VATICAN GARDENS.

The accompanying sketch is made from a photograph of the garden at the Vatican, in which it is reported that the Pope caught his chill. In this garden is the famous box- wood bordering ingeniously grown in the form of the Papal mitre and keys. The ancient pleasure 'grounds of the Vatican are full of interest, with their fountains, statues, and shady avenues. In the niche of Bramante, guarded by two bronze peacocks, is the cele- brated fir-cone, eleven feet high, which was once the crowning glory of the mausoleum of Hadrian, and afterwards rested awhile at the iont of the old basilica of St. Peter's. The Vatican gardens are perhaps most beautiful when the groves are carpeted with sweet- smelling violets and anemones of many hues. In reference to the Pope's successor, a New York correspondent now says that Cardinal Gibbons's early departure for the conclave was urged by the Washington Administration, which fears that Cardinal Gotti may be the new Pope. This would Tint be desired owing to the complicated question of the friars in the Philippines, Cardinal "Gotti being a monk. It -is hoped in America that Cardinal Rampolla or Cardinal Vannutelli may be chosen.

Victoria: The proceedings were organiesed by that admirable body, the Life-Saving Society, tof which His Majesty is Patron, the president being the Prince of Wales. The association, which was established in 1891, fulfils a number of useful aims, chief among them being the pro- motion of technical training in life-saving and resuscitation and also to stimulate public opinion

in favour of the general adoption of natation and life-saving as a branch of instruction in schools, colleges, and other institutions, and to encourage floating, diving, plunging, and other of the swimming arts. The King has throughout displayed a warm interest in this work, as he does in others of a sporting character. The race for the King's Cup was keenly fought, and, as was generally an- ticipated, the *result vvas in favour of Eng- lond. In addition to Billington, who swam for England, there were great swimmers from Canada, Sweden, Hungary, France, and Italy. Though the cluli bath is somewhat limited for a race of this description, the competitors having to swim 18 lengths to .complete the course, they swam exceptionally well.

div.head: FAMOUS SHOOTING FRIEL.
div.p: THE FAMOUS SHOOTING FRIEL.

In view of the amount of interest taken in the international match at Bisley for the Palma Trophy not merely here and in Amer- ica, but upon the Continent and in South Africa and Australia, it is in a sense surpris- ing how little is known of its early history: It is known, how- 'ever, that the Na- tional Rifle Asso- ciation of America was inaugurated in 1873, and that the following year the trophy was com- peted for as first prize at the first international shoot- ing match, when -the Irish team that won the El ch o -Shield at Wimble- don crossed the -main, only to be beaten on the last shot, a bull's-eye fired by "Old Re- liable," Colonel John Bodine, the scores being— America 934, Ire- land 931. With respect to the trophy itself, which was fashioned 41after the style of the battle-flags of THE PALMA TROPHYd -the Roman Le- gions," at the suggestion of General Martin McMahon, chairman of the trophy committee in 1876, it is perhaps more remarkable than beautiful. Standing seven • feet six inches in height, this unique banner is composed of gold, silver, copper, steel and iron. The eagle .is one foot high, and is composed of burnished -copper, while the bar upon which it perches is of solid iron; copper edged, the word "Palma" (almost obliterated by a silver -wreath) being written in raised silver letters. ' The banner, apart from the fringe, which is of gold, the inscription, which is of silver, ;and the gold tracery, is made of solid iron, as, indeed, is the staff, which, however, boasts •copper fillets. This year's contest was one of the finest on record, one remarkable circum- stance being that every shot fired in the match by the members of the British and American teams reached the target. This is phenomenal in so large a number of rounds -shot at such long ranges. In the end America won with 1,570 points, Great Britain running nip with 1'555.

div.head: PITT:NOMENAL FR.
div.p: THE PITT:NOMENAL FR.

For several years in the front rank ox ..cricket, Mr. Fry has this season left all rivals hopelessly in the rear. He has scored 1,732 runs in twenty completed innings, and has an average of something over 86 for each visit to the wicket. Thus does he show how capable he is at example as well as precept, for, unlike many who wield the bat, and the pen in the cause of the hat, he is excellent both as cricketer and wri teron cricket. In his Univer- sity days he was a luminous illustration of the truth that mind and mus- cle may both be cultivated to the highest degree without either suffering frcm the atten- tion given to the other. But,

after all, such proficiency as Mr. Fry's is somewhat to be deplored, inasmuch as it depreciates cricket. When we have reduced a game of ;kill and chance to a sort of mathematical excercise in which, to quote a famous bowler, speaking :of Dr. Grace, "I puts the ball where I likes and he puts it where he likes" we have taken from if` the charm of uncertainty and surprise. It is with runs as with strawberries. The cheaper they are the less we regard them. The famous Oxonian is said to have excelled himself re- cently by reason of his increased variety of stroke. He has 'developed the-cut considerably of late, and many of his boundaries off the Hampshire bowling were obtained by means of this fascinatin z stroke. His on-drives were beautifully timed, and his led hits well placed. Others just now also worthy of mention when sdealing with cricket prowess are Vine, Reif, •and Brann. A singular feature is that the two latter and Fry each obtained his so in sixty-five minutes.

div.head: DOUGAL CASE AND THE PRESS.
div.p: THE DOUGAL CASE AND THE PRESS.

The Dougal case .has created quite a flutter in newspaper dovecotes, a number of actions having resulted from too trenchant comment and enterprise. The London "Sun," for instance, had what is technically termed a "scoop" on Dougal's "confession," repro- ducing the man- uscript full size, and thereby giv- ing its circula- tion one of those momentary in- creases for which it lives. The Daily Express,' however, also gave a repro- duction of the manuscript, a feature that re- sulted in the startling state- ment by the " Sun " that the "confession" had been stolen from the "Sun" office. The cul- mination at pre- sent is that MR. ERNEST PARKE, J ewichustice EDITOR OF THE "STAR." Kek, in the Chancery Division, has granted an interim injunctioi. pf a week against the "Sun," refraining the latter from repeating its charge of theft. By far the most interesting case, however, is that in which Mr. Ernest Parke, the editor of the "Star," has been figuring for several weeks. Mr. Parke has been called upon to show why he should not be committed for contempt of :ourt for having in March wrongfully published statements purporting to give a history of Dougal's career, .and alluding to a charge of forgery against him. This case has resolved itself into a point of law, the defence intend- ing that, as the contempt was committed against the assize court, the King's Bench Division (in which.the rule is now being dealt with) has no jurisdiction. Certainly, as the Lord Chief Justice said, it is a point which must have time for consideration.

div.head: ANOTHER OLD LONDON LANDMARK GONE.
div.p: ANOTHER OLD LONDON LANDMARK GONE.

King's Way, and Aldwych, the 'London County Council's new avenue from Holborn to the Strand, will undoubtedly be of the utmost service to London traffic at an impor- tant point, but its construction is leaving a great deal of wreckage in its wake. Its ruthless line of march is being carried on regardless of antiquity and tradition, and everything has to bow down beforc this great modern Juggernaut. Clifford's Inn and many other old landmarks have already gone; and now New Inn, new only in name and by comparison with older structures, is in course of demolition. It stood just off Wych Street, which used to be the narrowest street in
BEEN DEMOLISHED.

London, and in the widening it had to go. On Saturday night, another well-known land- mark practically ceased to exist owing to the same cause. This is the old Gaiety Theatre which is so full of traditions. Built in 1868, it has had one long record of success, and many famous names are connected with its. history; those include Henry. Irving, Mrs. Kendal, John Toole, Lionel Brough, Charles Matthews, Samuel Phelps, Fred Leslie, Nellie Farren, Kate Vaughan, Connie Gilchrist. Sylvia Grey, Letty Lind, and a host of 'others. For many years it was the home of burlesque, for the last decade it has been devoted to musical comedy. Saturday night was a very special night, and a souvenir history of ,the theatre by John Hollingshead was given away to those who were lucky enough to get /1.4at34

div.head: MESSRS. WALKER'S EXCURSION.
div.p: MESSRS. WALKER'S EXCURSION.
A Day's Rain at Blackpool.

The statement that "the English take their pleasures sadly" has often been•contested but it may be said to receive soma verification in the experience of the one- day tripper on a wet day. The one thousand employes and friends who joined Messrs. Peter Walker and Son's Limited excursion on Saturday and left Bank Quay Station at the early hour of seven o'clock or breezy Blackpool can hardly be said to have derived much pleasure from the outing, for unfortunately the rain descended persistently nearly tilt whole of the day. The pity of it was that the excursionists were altogether unprepared for such an experience. Women, young maidens and children wore light airy garments in anticipation of a hot summer's day, wkilst the men- kind sported panama and straw hats, and had not even given a thought to the advisability of bringing mackintoshes and umbrellas. Judging by past experi- ence at Messrs. Walker's excursions the trippers were perhaps justified in anticipating a fine day, for on sixteen consecutive occasions they have been fortunate in experiencing fine weather on trip day. Saturday last, however, proved a notable exception and com- pletely spoiled the record for fine weather which Messrs. Walker's employees have prided themselves upon. The arrangements made for the outing were complete in every respect, and Mr. J. Fulton Smith and his able lieutenant Mr. A. F. G. Potter, are to be congratulated upon their excellent work in this respect. Two railway tickets were presented by the directors to each workman, and they were available, as often as desired during the day, for admission to the North Pier Promenade and Pavilion, also to the Blackpool Tower and its enter- tainments. A small allowance of money was also made towards defraying the expenses of the day. The excursionists departed in two trains, the first moving out promptly at seven o'clock to the strains of the Brewery Band. Seldom has so large a company left Warrington in such high spirits and been doomed to such keen disappointment. Shortly after their arrival at the northern seaport, a drizzling rain commenced. Many of the eecursionists made use of their tickets for the Naith Pier and had the pleasure of listening to Professor Speelman's excellent orchestra in the Pavilion. Towards noon; the rain ceased and the hopes of the excursionists for finer weather revived. Still the misty clouds which hung round the Tower and obscured a portion of it fromt view looked ominous and about two o'clock a heavy downpour of rain commenced and continued without intermission until shortly before ten o'clock, when the excursionists were wending their way to the station, wet and tired and anxious to get home again. It is fortunate that Blackpool is able to offer so much indoor amusement, or the thousands of excursionists who visited it on Saturday would have had a much worse time of it. Something like GO excursion trains unloaded their human freights of one-day excursioaists on Sat- urday but somehow or other they all seemed to find accommodation indoors. The interior of the Tower with its dense masses of people:in every part, presented a scene of animation, such as is, perhaps, not to be seen anywhere else. Wherever one moved in this vast house of entertainment,there was a surging crowd of spectators In the menagerie, in the aquarium, in the covered gar- dens and in the Old English village, the excursionists passed along in a steady and what seemed an endless stream. In the concert roomlthe three galleries were packed and the corridors leading to them were impassible. Many were content to find a seat on the 'staircases and quite miserable some of them looked. Sitting in their damp clothes, a few of the women were to be seen stickling their children, whilst others were feasting on tonntoes and other edibles. The youngsters gaveexpression to their sense of the uncongenial condi- tions by pouting and screaming vigorously. Bat the orchestra played on, and as several hours were whiled away indoors, whilst the rain fell copiously outside, the excursionists seemed pleased and accepted all the drawbacks glod-humouredly. After tea, the places otainuseittent were again resorted to. It was nearly ten o'clock before the rain ceased,and bv this time the excursionists had had enough of Bl tokpool and its weather, and had taken their places in the rail- way carriages. Few were able to say that they had enjoyed themselves, and the recollections of Saturday last will hardly be of the pleasantest kind. STAFF DINNER AT THE COUNTY AND LANE
ENDS HOTEL. A TRIBUTE TO DEPARTED EMPLOYEES.

Inaocordance with custom, the staff of Messrs. Peter Walker and Son and a few invited guests sat down to dinner at the County and Lane Ends Hotel. Mr. Menro presided, and was supported by Mr. Fulton Smith in the vice-chtur, Aldermen Francomb, Hutchinson, and Smethurst°, Counc illors Tiunion and John Roberts, Messrs. James He pherd, W. H. J. Jenkins, A. F. G. Potter, E. Parry (head brewer) and others. The usual loyal and patriotic toasts were received with musical honours. The toast of" The Na vy, Army, and Reserve Forces" was responded to by Alderman H UTCH INSON. _ _ - -

Mr. MONRO said that before proceeding with the speeches, he would like—indeed he thought it a sym- pathic duty—to remind them that they had all been personally sadly grieved of late, and the directors and management had suffered great loss through the deaths of Mr. Baird and Mr. Brooks, while another old servant Savage—had also died that week. Mr. Baird and

Mr. Savage had each been with them for 40 years, while Mr. Brooks had been 35 years in the service of the Walker family. They had each seen three generations at the head of the business. All three had entered the service at the foot of the ladder, and all had risen to be heads of the departments they were connected with. Mr. Baird was pleased to tell how he walked from Scotland to Warrington as a workingman out of a job, and Wils glad to get one in the brewery at 15s. a week. When he died they all knew that he occupied the position of head brewer at Dallam Brewery, that he was highly respected by the directors, and was followed to his grave Ly the chairman and managing directors, and the whole of their employ4s at Warrington. together with some of the aldermen and councillors, Corporation officials, and a large and repre- sentative number of the general community, who paid respect to his memory. That was a lesson which should be remembered by those who might be aspirants to higher positions in the employment of Peter Walker and Son, as ib proved that worth and honesty were appreciated by the directors, and would always be recognized and recompensed. (Applause.) They missed their faces that night and would see them no more, but John Baird's cheery way and sterling character, and Tim Brooks's rugged voice, but pleasant and honourable nature—although now only memories—would, he was sure, remain long with them. (Applause.) He asked them to pay a last parting tribute to them by drinking to their memory in solemn silence.

_ This course was adopted.. • Mr. J. FuvroN SMITH proposed the toast of "The Corporation, town and trade of Warrington." Warring- ton, he said, was in existence before Liverpool, and long ago letters used to be addressed" Liverpool via Warring. ton." Now, Liverpool thought it had precedence, but Warrington would never give in to that. (Laughter.) When anybody said they came from Warringion he Was received with open arms, because Warrington men were men to be trusted—(hear, hear)—and men of honour. The Corporation was composed of the cream of Warrington, and the town was, so far as he could judge from the municipal work of the country, one of the best governed towns in England, and they would have to go a long way to find a better set of men than the alder- men and councillors of the Warrington Corpora- tion. They knew a few juniors had gone in lately whom they did not know much about—(laughter)—and they hopedeich'would improve as time improved good wine,and when they toned down and became men of experience they would keep up the credit and renown of Warrington. It was very difficult to please everybody, and War- rington people were very critical in their ways, but when they saw a good man they honoured him. So far as the town itself was concerned, he thought there was no more flourishing place in Lancashire at the present time. They led the way in many of the industries which were peculiar to the town, and he did not know another in the country which possessed so many trades. He was quite within the mark in saying they numbered 50, each of which had a name in the market of theworld. There was Warrington wire, Warrington leather— A VorcE : "And Warrington beer." (Laughter and applause.) Mr. SMITH: Modesty kept me from saying that, (Renewed laughter.) He Might say that the history of Warrington beer went back to the time when Noah left the ark. (Laughter.) He would couple with the toast the name of Alderman Smethurst, who was one of their most worthy men, and a tower of strength in the town.

Alderman SMETHURST, in • reply., said he had never regretted coming to Warrington. If Warrington would use the Ship Canal he thought it would prove of great advantage. People had their goods taken on to Manchester, only to be brought back in barges to Howley Quay. They had in War- rington a lay-bye where the ships could be unloaded, but it seemed to pay people better to take the goods on to Manchaster and bring them back again. There was no one who wished the town success more than he did. They had the iron and leather trades, they
