div.head: DANGERS OF ROAD ROLLERS. Sequel to a Trap Accident at Stockton Heath.
div.p: THE DANGERS OF ROAD ROLLERS. Sequel to a Trap Accident at Stockton Heath.
SUCCESSFUL CLAIM AGAINST THE COUNTY COUNCIL.

His Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, K.C., was engaged for the greater Part of Thursday at the Warrington County Court in hearing an action brought by Herbert iiovrardi Whitehead and Walter Stead Dutton, of Grappenhall-road, Stockton Heath against the Cheshire County Council, in which they claimed £5O each for damages alleged to have been sustained through their horse taking fright at a steam roller on Easter Mon- day. F. Cuthbert Smith (instructed by Mr. A. J. Willett) represented the plaintiffs and Mr. T. Colt Williams (instructed by Mr. Potts), defended. It was decid..d te hear Mr. Whitehead's claim first.- _ _ _ _ _ _

Mr. Cnthbert Smith, in opening the case said it, was founded upon a case o f Jeff ,ies v. the St. Pancras Vestry, in which itwas held that the owners of a steam roller were liable to damages if it was proved to be andisance to the highway. His Honour asked if a steam roller was subject to the regulations which appliel to locomotives generally. Mr. Smith: I should think so. If a man uses a steam roller on the road he should use it with the same care. A man driving a steam roller on the highway continued Mr. Smith, must use reasonable diligence and observe the ;ordinary rules of the road. The plaintiff Whitehead had for many years acted as traveller for Messrs. Webb and Sons, seed merchants, Stourbridge, and for the purpose of his business had to use a trap to enable him to drive about the country to call upon farmers to ask them to purchase seeds. The plaintiff had driven the mare for live or six years, and she had proved to be steady in harness. On gister Monday, the 1 plaintiff in company with Mr. Dutton was going to ' Crowley. Mr. Maitehead lived in Grappenhall-road, I near the spot where the accident occurred. At the time the road was being repaired by the Cheshire County Council by means of a steam roller. The men were repairing about two-thirds of the width. As Whitehead got near the engine he noticed that the animal became restive, and he did what a careful driver should do, for he held up his hand as a warning to the engine driver to stop. The latter took no notice of the warning, however, and seeing that the animal was becoming uncontrollable, Dutton also held up his hand. Still no notice was taken, and then both men called to the driver to stop. He did not do so' and as the horse neared the engine it dashed on to the footpath and the wheel of the trap caught an iron standard which enclosed a tree. The occupants were thrown out, and they suffered serious injuries. The trap was smashed and the mare went up the road towards Sandy-lane and was stopped opposite the house of a Mr. Lionel Hughes. The accident was witnessed by five or six people, and all were perfectly clear that due warning was given to the driver, but that no notice was taken of it.

In ans fver to His Honour, Mr. Williams said he was not going to contend that if the County Council was negligent that they were not liable for damages,because incumbent upon were fulfilling a public duty which was upon them. Mr. Smith: Mr. Williams admits, with his usual fairness, that the County Council take full responsibility for the roller. We shall have no technical difficulties; and the matter will be thrashed out on its merits.

div.head: EVIDENCE IN SUPPORT OF THE PLAINTIFF'S CASE.
div.p: EVIDENCE IN SUPPORT OF THE PLAINTIFF'S CASE.
Samuel Mackey, surveyor, stated that they had ;re- pared the measurementa of the plans now produced, showing the distances from Mr. Whitehead's house to the place of the accident. __

Herbert Howard Whitehead, the plaintiff, said he had driven this mare for a number of years and had had no trouble with her,!prior to this accident. The engine was about 40 or 50 yards away when he held up his hand to the driver of the engine as a signal to stop. Mr. Dutton did the same but they were ignored altogether. Witness then shouted to the driver but still no notice was taken. The horse plunged on to the footpath and collided with an iron standard mind a tree on the path He received no assistance from the driver of the engine or the roadmen. He was rendered unconscious, his head coming in contact with a stone He had been confined to the house for seven weeks and he had lost about £l5 in commission The trapilutd cost him £lB for repairs. He was attended by Dr. Parker and Dr. Joseph, and a special nurse was engaged.—Cross- examined : He was prepared to swear that he was not tucking in the rug when he started the horse. He had his mare under proper control when he started. Re-examined: He did nothing to make the horse more restive.

Dr. Joseph stated that he had been attending the plaintiff since the accident. He had been very ill, and was suffering from bruises on various parts of the body, and shock. He had been unable to follow his employ- ment for about seven weeks.
His Honour asked Mr. Smith if he intended to call Dr. Parker.

Mr. Smith: I shall, perhaps, ask yourllonour to take a certain course with regard to Dr. Parker. He has been served with a sabpcena and warned, but has abso- lutely refused to attend. Dr. Anderson, /cicala tante»: for Dr. Parker, then stepped forward, but His Honour said he could not hear a medical man who had not attended the plaintiff. Miss Kate Hatton, Heatherdene, Grappenhall-road, Stockton Heath, said that on Easter Monday she was looking through the bedroom window and saw the plaintiffs driving up in the trap. They shouted to the driver of the engine to stop. The mare was plunging and kicking. The driver did not accede to the request, and the trap went on the footpath. The engine did not stop until after the accident had oceured. Witness had had some experience of horses and she was of the opinion that if the engine, had stopped there wonld have been no accident.

Mrs. Pierpoint, Heatherdene, said Miss Hatton gave her an account of the accident soon after it happened, and it exactly corresponded with her evidence that day. Clareece Wright, nine years of age, Hilton House, Grappenhall-road, also described the accident, and said the etPine did not stop until after the trap had run against tree. He did not hear the plaintiffs shout. Mrs. Wright, mother of the last witness, said the evidence given by her son was exactly the same story that he told soon after the accident.
Frank Marsh, who was standing opposite Dr. Parker's house, said the engine did not stop when the occupants of the trap held up their hands.
William' Powell, landscape gardener, Warrington, said he saw the accident. The driver of the trap held up his hand, but the engine did not stop, and continued to move until after the accident.

Mrs. Dutton, wife of one of the plaintiffs, was called, and corroborated the evidence already submitted. Walter S. Dutton, one of the plaintiffs, gave evidence and said the last thing he remembered before he became unconscious was seeing a man try to pull the engine driver's coat to get him to stop. The engine was mov- ing when he was thrown.ont of the trap. Lionel Hughes, carter, who left the roller to bring a load of stones shortly before the accident happened, said the engine was then stopped and he did not hear it resume work whilst, he was in the road. It was stated that witness's father did carting for the County Council.
George Bowdon, cab proprietor, said the mare was stabled on his premises. He had never had a quicter animal in the stable.
Edward Burrows, horse-keeper and shoeing smith, Warrington. gave similar evidence. -

Richa-,rd Sictuim coach builder, said the cost of repair- ing the trap would be £lB. For the defence Mr. Colt Williams asked his Honour whether he considered there was any evidence of negli- ge_nce,_ _ _ _

- His Honour replied in the affirmative. Mr. Williams said his case was that the engine was not moving when Mr. Whitehead left the house, and it. was still at a standstill when the accident happened. It had beea stopped by the orders of the man in charge of the road,. because there were not sufficient stones. Evidence would also be submitted that Messrs. White- head and Dutton did not shout or giiTe any signal, and there was no reason for them to do sb. It was perfect] incredible that the driver would deliberately keep driv- ing on when he saw a terrible accident happening close hy the engine. The probability was that the mare took fright at the engine standing by the roadside, and Mr. Whitehead became nervous and pulled her across the road.

John Rutter, roadman in the employ of the County Council, who was superintending the repairs in Grappen- hall-road, said the engine was stopped before Mr. Whitehead left his house. Witness did not see the accident.

George Antwiss, driver of the steam roller, said he stopped the roller sometime before the accident occurred. The engine was not emitting steam or smoke when it was at a standstill. The plaintiffs did not hold up their hands or shout to him. Witness could not have done anything to prevent the accident even if a signal had been given. By his Honour: There might have been a little steam and smoke but not any large quantity. Fred Smith, attendant on the steam roller, said he was standing by the engine when the accident happened and corroborated the last witness's evidence.
Thomas Whitlow John Mills, Frederick Owen, and George Haddock, also gave_ evidence.

Mr: Cuthbert, Smith addressed his Honour who summed up. He was of the opinion that the horse was frightened by the roller which was in motion, making a noise and emitting steam at the time. He gave judg- ment for the plaintiff for £5O and costs. With regard to Mr. Dutton's claim the defendant's counsel, agreed t 6 pay 40 guineas and costs. Judgment forthat amount was entered.

He would awaken with a start whenever he triad to obtain sleep. The food he took, instead of being digested, decayed in the organs and set up ulcemtron of the stomach. For months he lingered between life and death, his friends considering his case hopeless. Then one day Chas. Forde's bile beans were introduced to the patient. He began straightway to improve. His nerves were strengthened, he could soon digest his food properly again, and to-day he is as strong and well as ever. div.head: ALLEGED ROBBERY FROM A FORGE. More Arrests.
div.p: ALLEGED ROBBERY FROM A FORGE. More Arrests.
Further Police Proceedings.

At the Warrington Police court on Saturday before Mr. T. Birchall and other magistrate., Charles Naylor. joiner, 24 Eldon street, Robert Martin, general dealer, Long lane, Orford, and Henry Chorley, son-in-law of Martin, were charged with stealing and also with re- ceiving knowing them to have been stolen lcwt, 41bs of bronze steps of thevalue of £8 6s 8d the property of Messrs Pearson and Knowles, Ltd between June 30th and July lst—Naylor and Martin were before the court on the previous Thursday and the magistrates remanded them in custody. Chorley was arrested early on Saturday morning. Mr. H. Taylor (Messrs Greenall alai Co) ap- peared to prosecute and Mr. T. S. Steel defended. Mr. Taylor asked for a remand until Friday in order that the case might be fully gone into. Mr. Steel applied for bail and said the prisoners Martin and Naylor had given every information to the police to enable them to trace the stolen property and to arrest men who were implicated. He understood that two other man were suspected and if the prisoners were allowed bail they would assist the police in apprehending the men. Mr. Taylor and Superintendent Monaghan opposed the application on the ground that the interests of justice might be seriously affected if bail were allowed. The superintendent denied that prisoners had given full information. Some of the bronze was found concealed on Martin's premises although Martin denied that it was there. Chorley refused to give any information. After further discussion it was decided to remand the prisoners in custody until Wednesday.

div.head: PRISONERS SENTENCED.
div.p: THE PRISONERS SENTENCED.

Another man named Alfred France, of 21, Back Crossley-street, was arrested early in the week and remanded until Wednesday, when all the prisoners appeared before the magistrates. They were charged with stealing, between June 30th and July let, 2cwt. lqr. 101 b, of bronze steps,valued £lO 18s 4d the property of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, Limited. They were also charged, in the alternative, with receiving the bronze steps, knowing them to have been stolen. Mr. Steel, who defended Martin, Naylor, and Chorley, pleaded guilty to the second charge. Mr. Taylor prosecuted and stated that on the night of the 30th June, the bronze was placed in a store room of Messrs Pearson and Knowles, forge and after the room was locked np the keys were taken to the lodge. Next morning it was found that the store had been broken into, and that the bronze had been removed. Informa- tion was given to the police, and evidence was sub- sequently obtained which warranted the arrest of the four prisoners. It was discovered that on July Ist France, Naylor, and Chorley had been seen in Langshaw's lane, and had removed three heavy Lags in a cart. They had taken them to the house of Martin,who was a metal broker carrying on business in Lang lane. Superintendent Aionaghan made inquiries and foundsome of the bronze buried on Martin's premises, Martin admitted that he had received it and knew it was" wrong." Mr. Steel made a strong appeal for leniency and even wentso far as to ask the magistrates to strain the First Offenders' Act. He said Naylor and France found the bronze and persuaded Martin to buy it, although the latter did not at first wish to do so.
The magistrates decided to send Martin to gaol for four months, Naylor and France for two months and Claorley for one month.

France was then charged with stealing from the works of the Whitecross Company 2cwts. 141 b. of bronze steps, of the value of.£B Bs. 7d. It was stated that bronze had been missed for some time and on May 22nd prisoner and another man went to Mr. Slee, brass founder, Earlestown, and soldhim:the stolen bronze for £5 10s. The other man stated that he was a broker.— The case was adjourned until France is released from gaol. A young man named Samuel Cleary was fined 10s. and costs for stealing from the fitting shop at Dalian' forge, two rules the property of Francis Puilin.

LIVERPOOL RACES.—In connection with these races on Thursday and Friday next, the Great Central Rail- way Company will issue cheap day excursion tickets from St. Helens, Haydock, Ashton-in-Makerlield, Golbome, Lowton St. Mary's and Culcheth. The fare to Liverpool will be is. 3d. from St. Helens and 2s. from the other places mentioned. div.head: VATICAN GA:
div.p: THE VATICAN GA:
Interesting Business.
Mr. J. Edwardson presided over the monthly meeting of this Council which was held in Bold-street Wesleyan Schools on Thursday evening. There was a fair attend- ance of delegates.
THE CONCILIATION BOARD AND THE WIREWEAVERS'
DISPUTE.

Mr. PLINSTON desired to mention a matter which affected him personal ly. He referred to the statements made at the last meeting, which he was unable to attend with reference to the fact that the Conciliation Board had not intervened in the wireworkers' dispute. He felt it was ratheo out of place that such strong com- ment should have been made when members of the Coun- cil appeared not to know tile rules of the Conciliation Board, and the individual concerned was not present. The rules of the Board were not as inter- preted by several speakers, the procedure being that when a dispute arose the society or the employers con- cerned should show a desire for the Board to takeaction The Board could then be called togetherand a course of action agreed upon. By the very same post that Mr. Stott wrote to him informing him of the feeling of the Council, he had communicated with the secretary of the Wireweavers' Association asking if the men were de- sirous that the Board should intervene in the dispute. He received a replyexpressing the men's willingness that this step should be taken. He also wrote to Messrs. Greening's I but the firm had not even sent a reply. As far as:he(Mr. Plinston)was concerned he had not neglected his duties as secretary of the Board. The SECRETARY said that at the last meeting he was under the impression that it was the duty of the Secre- tary of the Board to take action immediately it was known that a dispute was pending. He had now found that he was mistaken, and he wrote to Mr. Plinston apologising.

iII.:ZiKLEY, who presided at the last meeting, wished to apologise to Mr. Plinston, and said the impression of the Council in regard to the rules was entirely wrong. Mr. PLINSTON said his desire was not to obtain the apologies of the member; but to show that, the inter- pretation placed on the rules was incorrect.

div.head: SHOPS BILLS.
div.p: THE SHOPS BILLS.

- The SECRETA RY reported that in reply to a resolution of the Council Mr. R. Pierpoint M.P. wrote stating that he should reserve his judgment in regard to Lord Avebury's and Sir Charles Dilke's Shops Bills until they came up for consideration. In a postscript Mr. Pier- point said that on referring to the list he found that Sir Charles Dilke's Bill had been withdrawn. From further correspondence with Mr. Pierpoint and Mr. McPherson, secretary to the Shop Assistants' Union, it appeared that the Bill was temporarily withdrawn in order that a resolution might be introduced. It had now been read for the first time in the house.
LABOUR REPRESENTATION COMMITTEE. MR. STOTT AND ORFORD WARD.

Mr. BUCKLEY informed the Council that at a meeting of this committee Mr. Plinston was elected President. The Independent L abour Party wrote stating that they had invited Mr. F Stott to contest Orford Ward in November, and the committee endorsed his candidature. A sub-committee was appointed to draw up 41, pro- gramme for the committee. The question of obtaining a labour candidate for the Parliamentary election was discussed and the Secretary was instructed to write to the National Committee asking for their advice and in- quiring whether there was any likelihood of a candidate being found for Warrington. The local committee would be able to provide most of his expenses. The SECRETARY said the Independent Labour Party had for some time been desirous of contesting a Ward —in fact it had been part of their policy for a number of years—but they had not been able to secure a candi- date who could devotesufficient time to the work.He had been prevailed upon to contest Orford Ward and provi- sion had been made whereby he would be at liberty to stand as a candidate. The Independent Labour Party would be responsible for the funds which he expected would be raised by voluntary effort. As Secretary of that Council he hoped and expected to receive the sup- port of the delegates and he thought his record as a trade unionist ought to be sufficient recommendation for that support and in fact for the support of every trade unionist in Warrington. Mr. POOK moved a resolution that the Council heartily approved of the selection of Mr. Stott to con- test Orford Ward and pledged itself to render all possible assistance in his candidature.. He referred to Mr. Stott's services in the cause of labour and said he had always been willing to assist at meetings organised by any of the branches.

-The CHAIRMAN thought that if any labour man came forward he would receive the support of the Council. They had not been as successful as they ought to have been in the past, and they had not contested as many elections as they ought to have done. If Mr. .Stott had come out for St. John's Ward he would have had a glorious chance of success. Mr. WARD moved that the matter be deferred until the next meeting.

The SECRETAIIY said it was impossible for him to contest St. John's Ward as he would not be on the burgess roll until the new list was published. The resolution supporting Mr. Stott's candidature was carriel.

CORPORATION CONTRACTS. The SECRETARY reported that he had receivei further information regarding the Corporation clothing con- tract but he suggested that the matter should be left in the hands of the Executive Committee until further de- tails were forthcoming. He had heard nothing further about the printing contract and this might also be re- ferred to the Executive Committee for consideration. This suggestionwas agreed to. THE WOOLWICH EXPLOSION. In response Ito a letter from the Lincoln Trades Council, the meeting passed the following resolution, which it was decided to forward to Mr. Pierpoint : "That this meeting is of opinion that owing to the recent explosion at Woolwich arsenal, and the conse- quent loss of life, H.M. Government is responsible for tha maintenance of widows and children—and for the proper training andvlacinmb of children left fatherless by this deplorable accident.
THE BARNARD CASTLE ELECTION. It was agreed to send a telegram of encouragement to Mr. Henderson,the Labour Candidate in this election. THE PROPOSED SECONDARY SCHOOL.

div.head: SIXPENNY FEE ADVOCATED.
div.p: A SIXPENNY FEE ADVOCATED.

Mr. PLINSTON, the representative; --of the-Council on the Education Committee, said that at the last meeting of the committee the question of a, secondary school for Warrington was discussed. The point, was raised as to what the fee should be. It was thought by some, amongst them himself', that a fee of sixpence was sufficient, seeing that Manchester and Widnes charged that sum. A suggestion was thrown out by the Chair- man of the School Management Committee that the fee should be a shilling, and they heard now that it was likely that ninepence would be proposed. He, person- ally, maintained that sixpence was quite sufficient, and did not see why Warrington people should pay 3d. more than was charged at Manchester and Widnes. It, was for the Council to inform him, as their representative, whether theysupported his view, and would authorize him to move or support an amendment that the fee be 6d. if a larger sum were proposed. Mr. STOTT moved that Mr. Plinston support a charge of sixpence. He (the Secretary) was one of those who thought that both primary and secondary education ought to be entirely free, but at the present time he did not think there was any possibility of secondary edu- ce tion being free in Warrington. Therefore they ought to support the lowest figure. It was his intention at the last meeting to move a resolution thanking Mr. Plinston for the strong stand he took on the question of Mr. Murray's salary. He deserved their thanks for the way he spoke against-the dodge of certain members of the Committee with reference to the salary. He re- gretted that Mr. Bibby, the friendly society represen- tative, voted in favour of the increase. He (Mr. Stott) could not imagine why he should have done so. Mr. PODMORE seconded the proposition, and endorsed all the Secretary had said with reference to Mr. Piing- ton's worthy action. With reference to the fee, they found that a high fee often excluded people who could not afford to pay. It was quite possible for a labourer to have a child possessing genius, and, seeing that, he might ho desirous of having it educated in'aseconda.ry school and so give it a chance which he had probably never had. The fee was a considerable item to men in receipt of small wages. Therefore, from that point of view, if they could not get free education they should have the fee as low as possible. The resolution was carried.

Mr. PLINSTON said that when he was appointed a member of the committee he pledged himself to sup- port what was right and just to tin Trade Unionists and ratepayers of the town. He took his staind on that. It was his intention in the near future to test the feel- ing of the Education Committee on the question of =king elementary education free. Parents were telling theiSchoolAttendance Committee that th4rents were being continually raised and still they hzd to pay school fees. He thought the time liad come when•the question should be considered. The Education Committee had the power to give free education and he maintained that they ough t to do so.

div.head: 3ICNICIPAL BOWLING GREENS.
div.p: 3ICNICIPAL BOWLING GREENS.

Mr. PODMORE said tEei-a-IiVCOW-the--hiStory of the bowling green question. It hatl been discussed in the Council Chamber and referred to a committee of stick- in-the-muds. (Laughter.) So far as he could learn the committee had not moved at all in the matter. It seemed to him that it was "flouting" the public opinion of Warrington direatly in the face when a committee of the Council-who ought to be servants of the rate- payers would not move in a matter of public interest like that. He had sounded many people on the matter, and in no case had it been said that greens should not be provided. He heard it had been said by some of theirs "House of Lords"—he referred to the alder- men, who did not come out for election every three years—that:there were only two or three"making a noise" about the matter, but that certainly was not so. He wanted the matter brought forward again. (Hear, hear.) Warrington was a big bowling town and many matches were organized. The scheme of bowling greens in New- castle was a great success, and he wanted to know why it could not be a success in Warrington. Their Town Council seemed so fond of discussing £3,000 staircases

MR. BA.LFOUR S stirring prelu le in the pro. POSITION. , ceedings of the House of Commons on Wednesday. It may have extended over a matter of ten =mites or a quirter of an hon.., during wici tim3 the Prime Minister presented a,spectacle truly pitiable. Sir MICHAEL HICKS-BEACH wished to know whether

before the session closes an opportunity will be given for a full dtscussio o t'na Cal mat Secre- tary's prop esed chang es in the fiscal policy of the country, and whether to this eal facilities will be provided for the discussion of the motion which has been placed on the papor by Mr, H ENRY HOB HOUSE. Now it is to be bonze in mind that Mr. Houirouse's motion is of a wholly non-contentious character. It is a milk-and- water motion. It is intended merely to form a basis for the discussion of matters which the Colonial Secretary has invited the EIOII3B to dis- cuss. Nobody ever dreamt that the Prime Minister would decline to provide facilities for its consideration when he was raga esz,ed to do so from his own side, 'sod by s p rwarfal a rn)inber of his party as Sir IVlrcua.sr. HICKi•BRAC LI. But Mr. BALFOUR is evidently capable of anything in the fix in which he now fin is himself. He is determinal to prevent disenision of the CHAMBER- LAIN policy unless he can get it on his own terms, which are that a vote of censure shall be moved by the leader of the 0?oo ;Won. 11) endeavoured to draw Sir H. CA.MPB ELL-BA NNERMAN, but there is a great deal of Sc itti4li shrewd iess in " The liberal loader knows quite well what is the advantage that Mr. BALFOUR hopes to obtain. A. vote of censure on the Government would unite the Ministerial forces. The Irish party would either vote against it, or abstain from voting altogether. Tile motion to c mare woald be defeated by a majority such as some of those obtained on last year's Education Bill; and it would then appear to all those who are not familiar with the procedure of Parliament, which means the bulk of the nation, that the Tory party had voted solid for CHAMBERLAIN. This ap- parently is the sort of deception that Mr. BALFOUR desires to practice on the country. He is a cham- pion who declines the chi:llenges of all but one chosen knight, who, as he knows, has good and sufficient reason for not encountering him in the manner he desires. Ile would not give Mr. HOBHOUSE a day, and the refusal seems to have greatly surprised that faithful supporter of the Government. What! exclaimed Mr. HOBROUSR, did Ministers demand a vote of censure from their own friends? The Prime Minister said he was sure that his hon I friend could never contemplate such a course-

div.head: Examiner Saturday, July, 18, 1903.
div.p: The Examiner Saturday, July, 18, 1903.

Such twisting and writhing and turning on the part of a Prime Minister can seldom have been witnessed in the course of our Parliamentary history. Mr BALFOUR was reminded by LORD HUGH CECIL of the challenge which Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN has thrown down. "I should like my noble friend," he said, "to read out the terms of that invitation," ;thus expressing a doubt as to whether any such invitation had been given. Sin HENRY CAMFB ELL-BANNE RMA N was ready withlthel precise words, which are these —"lt is because it is of immense inportance that I ask the House to join eagerly in the discussion." The House is exceedingly anxious to join in eagerly ; but the Prime Minister is resolved that it shall have no opportunity of doing so. The truth is no doubt that the compact with Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN involves the denial to the House of Commons of any day for the discussion of proposals which are to be sprung upon the country in an autumn campaign, and which are certain to be less persuasive the more fully they are discussed. Mr. BALFOUR'S chief preoccupation is how to hold his Ministry together. It could scarcely , again go through the "intolerable strain" of debates in which leading Ministers make Opposite declarations on high questions of policy which involves the well-being of the whole people and the future of the Empire. But his position is not the less contemptible and pitiable because it is surrounded by embarrassments and anxieties. A Prime 'Minister who has to go fish- ing for a policy on the most important question that has been placed before the country for more than fifty years is not a creditable figure. But more to be condemnedlchan he is the Ministry that is content to cling together on a go-as-you-please principle, "Each man for himself and the devil take the hind-most," whilst one powerful colleague, professing to remain silent and inactive until he foals free to kick over the traces at the end of the session, is actually engaged through a section of the Press, in undermining the position of those members of the Government who do not share his views. Does Mr. 13anFoun ever recall his flam- boyant praises of himself and his associates in the Government of the country ? Dies he remember with any satisfaction what he said about the"corn- pulsory self-approval" of the gentlemen of the Government Front Bench? Does his more recent invitation to be called in to reconcile Liberal dissensions still remain in his memory? In that case he must now look around him with some pain and dismay, much as LUCIFER did when he lifted himself from the burning marl. But on that sad occasion LUCIFER had an advantage over Mr. BALFOUR. He was sustained by settled convictions.
On Tuesday the THE EDUCATION POLICY House of Corn- OF THE GOVERNMENT. mons found itself

once more engaged on the London E lucation Bill. That measure has been condemned by every public body in Lon- don of any importance. Even the City asks to be left outside el its provisions. Should the measure be finally carried it will be a standing example of legislation in defiance of popular opinion. Mr. BALFOUR, it is evident, has learned nothing from recent demonstrations or from the manner in which the Act of last year has been received. He had the boldness indeed to describe that measure as " one of the greatest educational reforms," —a phrase which seams to have moved the House to hearty laughter. Possibly the Prime Minister really thinks that the Act of last year is a great educational reform. Evan if it were admitted to be so, it eight not to have been forced on the people against the people's will. We have hoard a great deal of late years about a " mandate." Lard SALISBURY was using the word whilst Mr. CITAMBP.RLAIN was still talking of ransom. The Colonial Secretary new talks of a" mandate "for establishing preferential taritls by taxing the food of the people. There is in this, at least, the admission that the people have the right to be consulted. But no " mandate" was asked for in connection with the abolition of the School Boards, and for the setting up of an educational system which places denominational schools on the rates, and excludes Noncon- formist teachers from more than half the schools of the country. The Act was not the result of a mandate from the constituencies, but a bargain with the Church. It was possible to pass it because the Ministry is sup- ported by a large majority, which in this instance placed private and sectional before public interests \\That has occurred since the Act was passed should make even the most stubborn Minister pause before forcing a similar Act upon London. But Mr. BALFOUR is quite unteachable, and he has, by some strange process of logic, persuaded himself that he is doing something great for edu- cation. On Tuesday he taunte I the Opposition with having spoken for seven months on the Bill of last year ou all other subjects but education. That, he said,was a subject which they left severely alone. \Vas it the policy of the Opposition, he went on to inquire,to keep London an educational derelict, adding that "the thing, is too absurd to be entertained." A. min who can speak like this produces a feeling of mental helpless- ness and dismay. He is so obviously a man who is incapable of seeing any side but his own and believing that anybody can honestly hold views with which he does not find it possible to agree. How is London an educational derelict ? In introdming his Bill, Sir Wrr.r.wr ANSON was candid and indiscreet enough to describe it as a measure for the abolition of the London School Board. But actually in doing so he was compelled to admit that the school board is a body to which London owes a deep debt of gratitude. It has done its work nobly, unselfishly, and well. There is no public body in the country which is entitled to more praise for the manner in which it has dis- charged its duties. Education in London is far too likely to become derelict if the new Bill should be passed. Those who have the most expert knowledge say that it will not work. Those who will be entrusted with its working do not want to have anything to do with it. But there is the bargain with the Church to be considered,and so Mr. BALFOUR persists,it: spite of popular disapproval and undismayed by the very serious situation which has been created throughout the country by his former measure. His obstinacy is no doubt encouraged by the reflection that if ho can only get the Bill through there is very little likelihood that the new educational legislation can be inter- fered with under much less than a lifetime. Sir HENRY CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN has declared that it will be the duty of the Liberal party to undo the Education Act of last year. Undoubtedly that will be one of the first duties to which a Liberal Government will have to address itself. Bit the

House of Lords will present a rigid barrier to any attempts to amend the new legislation, and that we do not in the least doubt is the consideration which has induced Mr. BALFOUR to treat outside opinion as if it were of no consequence.

It may not be "in mortals to command success," but it seems within the power, of our friends, the Non-Traders, to do so. They have gained another striking victory at the polls, and it would be folly for anyone to endeavour to ignore the fact that on the general principle of trading by members of the Council with the Corporation, they have got the bulk of the electors with them. It has ba,ni alleged that the " cause" was losing ground in popular favour,but the Howley Ward election has knocked such a notion on the head. Mr. Adam Horrocks entered the field solely and simply as a Non-Trader—without any qualifying adjectives— while his opponent stood as an " independent " Conservative professing anti-trading views. Whether this profession was in the nature of a death-bed confession—as Mr. Norbury Williams styled it—we do not know but it clearly failed to convince the Howley electors. Tney voted solidly, and the return of Mr. Horrocks by a margin of S 2 votes over a Tory candidate in a Tory Ward is proof positive that the Non-Trading cause has the pull against politics. Councillor Horrocks has achieved a triumph and we hope he will signalise it by devoting his best thought and intelligence to the service of the town.

The slack contract was an important factor in determining the result of this election. No stronger plank could have been put in the Non- Trading platform. and the recent revelations of the methods of the Water Committee were made the most of. The decision of the Howley electors really amounts to a vote of censure on the Water Committee and we trust they will take the lesson to heart. There is another feature of the contest, which has its amusing aide. The Conservative cause was backed up by an overwhelming array of vehicles—horse and motor—and Mr. Sankey's friends must have carried quite two-thirds of the vo'6ers to the polls. He is a knowing bird is the workingman elector, and while gratefully accept- ing a lift from Mr. SAnkey he put his tongue in his cheek dud voted for Mr. Horrocks. Can any- one blame him ?

There should be an interesting contest in St. John's Ward a week next Thursday, when the vacancy created by the death of Councillor Baird has to be filled. At the present moment there is every indication of a close fight, for there are three prospective candidates in the field, two of whom—Messrs. Henry Thornton and J. Maginn— are to the fore with their election addresses. The third gentleman whose name is mentioned in con- nection with the contest is Mr. J. Harnblett. Four and even five aspirants for this particular seat have been mentioned, but the maximum of prob- abilities seems tl have been whittled down to three. Mr. W. J. Shaw was also expected to stand, but we believe he has abandoned the idea, and intends to come out in November under the aeyis of the Non-Traders. Tne fight should be interesting with Mr. Thornton representi•:-.g the Non-Traders, Mr. John Maginn an independent candidate, and Mr. Hatnblett a Conservative nominee. For some 'reason not explained, the " Weekly Freeman" of Dublin has developed a very sudden interest in this election and devotes about half a column to the detriment of Mr. Maginn's candidature. This outside interference appears to us particularly impertinent, and we should imagine that the St. John's Ward electors will resent it. They have managed in he past to elect their representatives without any volun- teered advice from Ireland.

Further particulars in regard to the new second- ary day school, the formation of which was sanctioned at the last meeting of the Education Committee, appear on the agenda for Monday's meeting. The School Management Committee has lost no time in pushing forward the arrange- ments, the details of which will, doubtless, be studied with interest.. We notice with some surprise that a staff of seven teachers at an aggregate salary of 980 is recommended for the teaching of the 100 scholars who are to form the new secondary school. On the face of it there seems to be a great disparity in proportion between the expenditure on salaries and the number of teachers, as compared with the number of scholars. Such a staff as is proposed ought to suffice for the teaching of a much larger school than there is any prospect of accommodat- ing at the Technical Institute, or the requirements for a secondary school are more extensive than we anticipated. For teaching alone, under the sug- gested scheme, each student will cost nearly £lO per annum. Against this we have £1450 in fees and the -.C400 which Alderman Monks puts down as the prospective earning power of the scholars in grants. There :is thus an anticipated return of overiso] per cent. but it still appears to us that the establishment expenses are going to be uncommonly high. More inf,,rnsation will doubtless be vouchsafed at the meet- ing of the Education Committee on Monday. It plainly behoves every member, however, to con- sider the scheme in all its bearings. We are very much in favour of a secondary day school, but we should like to see a much more extensive ad- vance in educational facilities for the expenditure of nearly £l,OOO in salaries alone.

The members of the Warrington Board of Guard,ar s reoeived the unwelcome intelligence on Wednesday that one of the patients admitted to the hospital had been found to be suffering from small- pox. The patient was speedily removed to the iso- lation hospital at Sankey and pro:npt and eff:ictive measures were taken to disinfect the ward and to isolate those who had coma into contact with the patient. The prospect of an outbreak of small- pixanongst the workhouse inmates is too awful ,to contemplate, and we are glad of the assurance that the measures which have been taken have ' confined the disease to the unfortunate patient who developed it shortly after admission to th,l hospital. This case makes the fourteenth which has occurred in the town since the disease was re-introduced last year. The fact that Warrington has escapel so lightly, cmnpared with many neigh- bouring towns, is largely due to the fact that our health authority has been fully prepared to deal with the plague. The smallpox hospital, it is true, waa not ready, but good use has been made of the farmhouse which was bought with the land, and here all the patients have been isolated.

Saakey Brook and its attendant nuisance have been so often written about that one almost wearies of the subject. Those who live in the vicinity of Sankey Brook are indeed a patient and long-suffering people, for with every recurring summer they are frequently reminded of the fact that the nuisance is still with us, or more correctly speaking with them, and there seems every pros- pect of it continuing in our midst to the end of time. The stench at night-time, especially during the last few weeks, has been almost unbearable, and the cli4sing, of windows and doors has not been sufficient to keep out the noisome effluvium. It almost seems a pity that some of our city fathen do not live in the neighbourhood of this open sewer for one might then hope that more active steps would be taken to abate the nuisance. The indi- vidual who could succeed in bringing about a better state of affairs would deserve to be hailed as a public benefactor. The Warrington Corporation are at last taking some steps to purify the effluent which is discharged into theßrook from the Long- ford Depot, but what, may we ask, is the St. Helens Corporation doing ? Is the new sewage system which was promised long ago in operation? We hear much of the lower rates of St. Helens in comparison with Warrington, but this cheapaess seems to be obtained at the expense of those who have to suffer from their inefficient and discredit- able sanitary system.

It is but a few weeks since the movement to provide a summer camp for poor Warring- ton children was inaugurated, but the efforts of the ladies and gentlemen who have inter- ested themselves in this commendable scheme have already borne fruit. Yesterday a band o radiautly happy youngsters journeyed to

Moreton and ere this they will have passed their first night under canvas. It cannot be said that the holiday zommenced under very encourag- ing circumstances, that is if the weather at Moreton was anything like the conditions experienced here last evening. A camp- ing ground is not the most cheerful of places when the thunder crashes and rain descends in torrents, and the lads—unless they were par- ticularly disposed to look on the bright side of things—must have felt rather depressed. Now that the storm has passed we are hoping for con- genial weather, and given this the boys will have every facility for extracting the maximum of healthful enjoyment from their short sojourn in the Wirral district.

div.head: Ellesmere Street Wesleyan Methodist Mission.
div.p: Ellesmere Street Wesleyan Methodist Mission.

The first meeting for the-second half year in counec tion with the "Charles Garrett "Temperance Union was held on Wednesday night, when there was a large number present. The ePresident (Hr. W. H. Sher- burn) conducted a devotional meeting, and led off with a quotation from one of our great poets. Mr. Ham- blett, Mr. Horton, Mr. Drinkwater, Mrs. Whitmore, and Miss Gilbert also gave quotations and remarks on each. A very helpful meeting was appreciated by all present and a desire was expressed that such meetings should be held oftener., During the meeting resolutions were unanimously passed protesting against the creation of a continuous vested interest in liquor licences. Six new members were admitted and all took the pledge. At the next meet- ing the subject of Compmsation to Publicans will be introduced by Mr. Llewellyn.
H. M. Asirros's LIFE TONIC is the KING, or TONICs.-63, SANKEY-STREET, Warri The Volunteer Encampment.

On Saturday next the members of the Ist V. 13. Prince of Wales's Volunteers Smith Lancashire Regi- ment will proceed to the Isle of Man for their annual encampment. The men will parade at the Drill Hall at 7 p.m. for medical inspection and afterwards march to the Central Station where they will entrain for Liverpool. Here they will set sail at 10 o'clock on the "Empress Queen" in company with the 2nd Cheshire Volunteers. The Warrington battalion will be allotted th, port or left side of the vessel. In the orders for the ensuing week the men are strongly recommended to wear warm clothing for the voyage. As is now generally known the camping ground is situated at Lewaigne, near Ramsey, and here the battalion will remain wail August Bth. The advance party and transport section will parade at the Drill Hall at 9.45 a.m. on Wednesday next and proceed to the camp. The heavy luggage was forwardekl yesterday. All baggage must be at the Drill Hall by 3 o'clock on Saturday afternoon. The officers' servants under the command of Second Lieutenant Connor will parade at 6 p.m. and travel by the first troop train and the Cyclists' Company in charge of Captain Haslam will also journey in this train. The battalion will parade to-morrow (Sunday), at 9.30 a.m., for the annual church parade and the Commanding Officer hopes that every man of the Churchof England will attend. Major J. M. Edelsten is at present in command of the battalion, but the official appointment of commanding officer has not yet been made.
PUBLI C BENEFIT. UNDER thlCtjr B::ir for BOOTS in LANCASHIRE.—AdVt. Death of Mr. Thomas Woods.

Mr. Thomas Woods, for many years a well-known and highly-respected tradesman, hut who has latterly lived in retirement , died unexpectedly on Thursday morning at his residence in Church-street. Mr. Woods visited the house of a friend so recently as Wednesday evening. He had been troubled by a chest affection for a few days, but this was not regarded as, serious, and none of his friends anticipated that the:encl was so near. It came as a great shock to them to learn that he suddenly expired in the early hours of Thursday morning. Mr. Woods was in his 76th year and was very active and in possession of all his faculties up to the last. His visiln was unimpared, and he was able to read and write without the aid of spectacles. For a long number of years he conducted a wholesale and retail grocery business at the large shop in Scotland- road now occupied by Mr. Banks, outfitter. From this -business he finally ;aired about three years ago. A. son and two daughters survive him, in politics he was a Conservative, but lie did not take any prominent part in public affairs, and never held any public posi- tion. He was a member of the Emmanuel Reformed Church in Bold-street. . H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE Toxrc is the KING OF TONICS.—G 3. SANKEY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt.

A Protruding Nail and the Result. Before Mr. Registrar Ridgway at the Warrington County Court on Thursday,Malcolm Garside, plumber, 17, Whitefield-road, Stockton Heath sued Messrs. J. N. Brown and Company Limited, carrying on business as the Supply Boot Stores in Horsetnarket-street, for three guineas for damage to a coat—Mr. Steel ap- peared for the plaintiff and Mr. •Crompton defended.— Plaintiff's case was that on Monday, June Ist, he was proceeding down Horsemarket-street in the direction of the Central Station, and whilst passing the defendant's shop caught his right arm against a large nail which was protruding from the front of the shop and upon which it was customary to hang boots. The coat was torn and he now claimed damages. A Mr. Massey, who carried on business as a . butcher, witnessed" the damage. On the following -evening plaintiff went to the defendant's shop and interviewed the manager who declined to give him any satisfactory information or even the address of the company.—Evidence having been given, Mr. Crompton said the 'case resolved itself into a question of damages He submitted that three guineas was an exhorbitant sum to claim as the suit cost only ;£3 12s. 6d. two years ago. He suggested that 15s. would amply repay the defendant for the loss he had • sustained.—Eventually the Registrar gave judgment for the plaintiff for two guineas and costs. You CANNOT DO BETTER! ACCIDENT AT A RUNCOILN QUARRY. Barnet Reddington, of Surrey-street,Runcorn, became entangled in a stone saw at Orme's Weston quarry, ott Friday afternoon, and had a leg completely cut off. ik) was removed to the Runcorn Hospital. AN OLD MAID'S SUICIDE. At Frodsham, on Saturday, an inquest was held by Coroner Yates on the body of Miss Louisa Grice, a. well-known tradeswoman, aged sixty-flve years, who was found drowned in the Synagogue Well on Thursday. morning. Evidence was given that deceased was wear- ing her night clothing, with one skirt thrown over them. Synagogue Well is so situated that deceased must have made a special journey to get there, and the jury returned a verdict of "Suicide whilst of unsound mind."

ELECTIC LIGHTING AT WIDNES. At a meeting of the Widnes Town Council on Wednes- day, the Mayor presiding, the Gas • and Water Commit- tee reported the receipt of a letter from the Empire Electric Lighting and Motive Power Company, Limited, intimating that the company intended to apply for a provisional order to provide electricity within the Council's area. The committee submitted names for a. special sub-comniittee to consider the question of elec- tric lighting in the borough, and all matters appertain— ing to the latter._ ,

div.head: ROBBING A LEGATEE.
div.p: ROBBING A LEGATEE.

At Ittmcorn, on Thursday, John Antrobus,an old man, and his wife Elizabeth were committed for trial at the Chester Assizes on a charge of breaking into the house of Ann Okell, widow, Nelson-street, and stealing fifteen sovereigns. Mrs. Okell had a legacy of £5O left her, and she placed it in a box in her bedroom. The box was afterwards found smashed open, and the prisoners became quite flush of cash, and hid seven - sovereigns under a stone.

- A VILLAGE HALL FOR HALTON. On Thursday evening Sir John T. Brunner, Bart, M.P. visited Halton, near Runcorn, for the purpose of formally handing over the deeds of a village hall there to the Halton Parish Council. Prior to the ceremony. Sir John entertained the members of ,the Council and others at tea in the hall.—ln replying to a vote of thanks, in which his generosity received due notice, Sir John said,he never gave anything except to fulfil what he considered his absolute duty. Many ,ears ago he made up hismind that he would devote his life rather to the prevention of evil than the cure of evil, and many of his gifts had that end in view. He thought that village hall would contribute to the self-respect and the welfare of the people of Halton. (Applause). PROPOSED EXTENSIONS OF RUNCORN. The Cheshire County Council inquiry into the pro- posed extension of Runcorn by the inclusion of the townships of Halton and Weston, was resumed in Run- corn Technical Institute on Tuesday. The case for the applicants was concluded by the evidence of Mr. Wilding, surveyor, Mr. M‘Dougall, the medical officer, and Mr. W. Handley, chairman of the General Purposes Committee. Mr. Sutton barrister, replied for the Runcorn Rural District 'Council, who opposed, and called Mr. James Diggle, C.E. of Heywood, who pro- pounded two schemes for dealing with the sewage of Halton and Weston.—Upon thenssurance of Mr. Ashton, clerk to the Rural District Council, that these schemes would be carried out, the County Council Committee gave their decision that no case foramalgamation could be made without calling upon other witnesses. THE THELWALL NUISANCE.

div.head: Payment for Professor Delepine's
div.p: The Payment for Professor Delepine's
Report,

At the monthly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Council on Monday at Dutton, Mr. Woodward in the chair, Mr. Baxter reported that the Thelwall Improve- ment Apportionment Committee met that morning, but nothing had been done owing to certain particulars not being to hand. The question of Professor Delepine's bill for his report on the Thelwall nuisance had been adjourned, and would be brought before the County Council on Friday, when he hoped the Rural Council would be able to get a large part if not the whole of the cost of the report. Admiral Jones-Parry said he did not wish to discuss the Thelwall nuisance. He would leave itto the lawyers, who when once they started the ball, would take care to keep it rolling. (Laughter.) But for the informa- tion of the ratepayers he represented and for the dignity of the Council he wished to ask—if he were not stopped —on whose authority Professor Delepine was asked to report on the question? The Professor said he had been asked to give a report by Dr. Adams. Secondly, what instructions, written or otherwise, had been given him to report on? Thirdly, was there any plan of the road in Weaste-lane before it was altered?

The Chairman: Do you ask for the production_ of the minutes dealing with the question? Ido not think we shall be justified in answering these questions unless you ask for the minutes to be produced. Admiral Jones-Parry: What's to be gained? I think Mr. Baxter for once agrees with me in asking these questions. It is a most extmording action on the part of the Chairman to refuse to let us know. I give notice to more when this claim of the Professor's comes oa that we refuse to pay and that those who ordered the report be made to pay. Mr. Linaker : I take it the point is this: He suggests that no instructions were given by this Council to any body to retain Professor Delapine and that this report was made to this Council instead of to the Cheshire County Council. This is the point Mr. Parry wishes to bring out.. _ _

TI Chairnum : Ido not think I can go into these questions. The District Council have decided to close this discussion, and I am not prepared to answer such questions. I must have chapter and verse for every- thing I give, and I cannot answer these question unless the minutes are produced. Ido not blame the clerk if he refuses to answer.
Dr. Adams: Any question addressed to me will be answ.ered on the same basis.
The matter then dropped.

div.head: SIR JOHN BRUNNER, M.P., ON EDUCATION.
div.p: SIR JOHN BRUNNER, M.P., ON EDUCATION.

Sir John T. ,3runner, M.P., distributed the prizes to the successful students at the Cheshire County Council's Agricultural and Horticultural College, at Holmes Chapel yesterday afternoon. He said that he was glad that more money Wfl,S being spent on education, not only in Cheshire but all over the country. The amount of money, which the United States spent on agricultural education put this country absolutely to shame. He hoped the day would come when England would have made up its mind that there was nothing upon which she could spend moiley with such handsome returns to themselves as to spend it upon the education of their children. •

div.p: SCHOOL CHILDREN'S PHYSIQUE. Sir John Brunner's Inquiry.

Sir William Anson, in a printed reply to a question of the medical examination of the children of their area, by a local education authority is one which the Board of Education consider must be left to that authority to decide, but the Board will of course gladly welcome any step which is likely to contribute to the improvement of the health and well-being of thechildren. The Board issued in October, 1901, a circular to the managers and teachers of schools in large towns as to the great importance of proper attention being paid to the eye- sight of the children.
THL ROYAL VISIT TO IRELAND. SEA. EXCURSION TO HOLYHEAD.

In view of the approaching visit of their Majesties the King and Queen to Ireland, the Royal yacht, with the accompanying escort of warships, will be in Holy- head harbour on Monday next, the 20th inst. The Liverpool and North Wales Steamship Company have decided to despatch their steamer St. Elvies for a special trip to Holyhead on that day,and she will leave the Prince's Landing-stage at 10 a.m., calling at Llan- dudno, and is due to arrive at Holyhead at 2.30 p.m. Passengers may remain ashore for about two and a half hours, and will thus have ample time to view the Royal yacht and the • preparations made for the Royal visit. The St. Elvies will return from Holyhead at 5 pin., nal after passing along the line of battleships will continue on for Llandudno and Liverpool, where she is due to arrive at 9.30. Those who were fortunate enough to tithe advantage of the trip made by the St. Elvies on the occasion of her late Majesty Queen Victoria's return from Ireland will view this announcement.with pleasure, and it is to be hoped that favoured with fine weather this most delightful coast trip will be as successful RS that of 21st April,l9oo.

div.p: THE BENEFITS OF SCIENCE.

It is seldom that any discovery of science is such as will benefit all classes of people. Some of the greatest discoveries of the age, while they have proved directly beneficial to thousands, have also, at least for a time, injured other thousands. div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
Minor Cases. Warrington Borough Police Court.
MONDAY.—Before Mr. F. Monks. (presiding), Alderman

Smethurst, and Messrs. Birchall and Thornton. DAMAGING A POLICEMAN'S UNIFORM.—EIijah Birkenhead, 11, Worrall's-row, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Rylands-street, and with doing damage to the amount of ss. to the uniform of P.C. Andrews on Saturday night.—The officer stated that prisoner, who was drunk, attempted to get on a train car, but was told by the inspector that he would not be allowed to travel in that condition. He became very disorderly and had to be taken into custody,where- upon he tore a large hole in witness's cape.—Prisoner was fined ss. for the drunkenness, and ordered to pay for the damage to the uniform. "BLACKLISTER IN TROUBLE.—John Wilfred Delooze' SO, Dudley-street, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket-street on July 3.—He pleaded guilty.—Superintendent Monaghan proved the case, and said the prisonerhad been before the Bench thirty times. In January last he was put on the black list.—A fine of ss. and costs was inflicted. AN OLD OFFENDER.—Jane Johnson, 63, Turner-street, was summoned for having been drunk and disorderly on the 6th inst.—P.C. Cooper proved the case.—Superin- tendent Monaghan said defendant made her 65th appear- ance.—She was fined ss.

GA.MBLING.—John Woodhall, 82, Catherine-street; Joseph Porter, 48. Pierpoint-street; James Brittle, 89, Pierpoint-street; Richard Bradley, 86,Pierpoint-street and Martin Varley, 78, Pierpoint-street,were summoned for playing " banker" in a passage at the rear of Pierpoint-street on July sth.—P.C. Newey and a boy named Reginald Delooze having given evidence a fine of ss. was inflicted.

BREACH OF TfiF. PEACE.—For committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Horsemarket-street, John Whittaker. 5, Peer's Court, and John Thornton, 9, Napier-street, were bound over and ordered to pay the costs.
MESDAY.—Before Aldermen Sutton (presiding) and Hutchinson, Dr. Fox, and Mr. J. R. Young.

ASSAULT ON THE POLlCE.—Michael Mania-an, 58, Orford-lane, was fined 10s. and costs, with the alterna- tive of 14 days' imprisonment, for having been drunk and disorderly in Winwick-strect on Monday-night and assaulting Police Constable Frank Cooper. The officer was removing some men who were standing near the Lord Rodney Inn, when prisoner came up. He became disorderly and caught hold of the officer by the throat, batted him, and kicked him. Sergeant Dean came upon the scene, and prisoner was removed to the Police Station.

DRUNK IN CHARGE OF A. ClllLD.—Benjamin Podmore, 32, Garibaldi-street, was charged with having been drunk while in charge of his child (Elizabeth Podmore) on the Town Hall lawn, at eleven o'clock on Monday night, and further with assaultinr, Horace Fear, of 17, Catherine-street.—Mr. Fear stated that when passing the park gates he heard screams. He rushed round to the lawn and found the prisoner and a young child. He asked him what the child was crying for and he replied that "it was his own brisiness.' He also said he was the best athlete in Warrington and would fight anyone. He then struck witness in the face.—Sergeant William- son stated that he, in company with Sergeant Smith, went to the park, and found the prisoner drunk, and the child was crying bitterly.—Prisoner's wife said her husband was good to the child and herself. She thought it was a bit of foolishness on his part. to take the child out when he was in drink.—A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed or 14 days'imprisonment in default of payment. Dm:sic—Ellen Turner, Lord-street, Garston, was fined ss. for having been drunk and disorderly on Bank Quay Station early that morninz.—Police Constable Gilchrist and Railway Inspector Turton (night station imastar) said the woman was drunk and shouting at the top of her voice.
Faro kv.—B3for3 Mr. H. Raborts (in the chair), Alder- nuti,.S•nethurst Councillor J.. Roberts,Messrs. Hepherd
rind Tiiorntnn.

ANOTHER CFCANCE.—A young man named Peter Taylor, residing at 5 Water-street. was charged with having been drunk and incapable in Bold-street at ten o'clock on Thursday morning and with having bean previously convictwl within the last twelve months.— P.C. Cooper proved the case and said prisoner was fined 10s. and costs on the 7th inst for having been drunk and disorderly.—Superintendent Monaghan said Taylor had been drlnking heavily all this year. During Thursday he seemed very ill and was bailed out:—Prisoner pleaded for the Bench to give him another chance and not send him to gaol. He promised to sign the pledge. —The Chairman said the magistrates would give him one more chance on the understanding that he would give up drink altogether. He would be fined 10s. UNLAWFUL REMOVAL OF Goons.—John Dunn, 18 Oliver-street. was summoned for having on June Bth removed goods from the house in his occupation at 18, Dannett-street, in order to avoid a distraint for rent.— Mr. Steel appeared for the landlord (Mr. James Gandy) and said defendant became the•tenant of the house in May. He paid one week's rent on May 11th, and had paid nothing since. He was informed that if the arrears were not paid the bailiffs would be put in the house. During the night of June Bth he removed the goods.— The magistrates made an order for the payment of £1 17s. (including costs) ht the rate of 3s. per week. WIFE ASSAULT.—..SamueI Jacksoa,l6, Margaret-street, was summoned for assaulting his wife Harriet Jackson on July 6th.—Complainant alleged that when defend- aut got up on the date named he called her bad names and struck her with a belt and also with his fist.—A fine of 10s. was imposed. • OBSCENFI LANGUAGE.—Elizabeth Ellen Fleming, Jolley's Court,was summoned by Theresa Crolla for making use of obscene language in Dial street on July llth.—Defendant apologised for the expressions used and the case was dismissed.
