A STRAYING Worral, tool maker, Higher Whitley, was fined in the costs for allowing a cow to stray, on the Warrington-road, Stretton, on June 27th.—The officer stated that he had received com- plaints about the animal straying and damaging gardens. THE REMOVAL OF SWlNE.—William Owen, farmer, Rhosybol, Anglesey, was summoned for endeavouring to obtain by means of a false pretence a licence or certifi- cate for the removal of four pigs from Anglesey into Cheshire.—Defendant pleaded not guilty.—The evidence for the prosecution was to the effect that a declaration apparently signed by James Jones, of Anglesey,was pre- sented to Sergeant Barlow, of Grappenhall, in order to obtain a licence for the removal of four pigs from Jones's premises to Whitley. It subsequently transpired that the defendant and not Jones had signed the declaration, and Jones had not sold the pigs to the defendant although he was treating with the defendant with that object in view.—Defendant said he filled the form up in mistake.—A fine of Is. and costs was imposed. C YCLISTS FINE D.—Jean Monat, was fined Is. and costs. for riding a bicycle without a light at Grappenhall on June 24.—For similar offences, Jas. Thos. Andrews, 16, Paradise-street, Northwich, Jas. Ewart Critchley, 19, Whitefield-road Stockton Heath, and Joseph Morris, 19, Dundonald-avenue, Stockton Heath, were fined in the costs.

DOGS WITHOUT COLLARS.—Ed. Maskell, of Warring- ton, and John Dobson, 13, Watkin-street, Warrington, were ordered to pay 3s. 6d. each for allowing dogs to stray without a muzzle or collar. AN OLD OFFENCE.—James Mannion, farm labourer, pleaded guilty to having been drunk and refusing to quit the Birch and Bottle Inn, Whitley, on April 29th, 1901, and was fined is. 6d. and 14s. costs.—Prisoner de- camped when, the summons was taken out, and went to work near Knutsford. On 'his re-appearance in the Whitley district he was arrested. SEQUEL TO A Cor,mstoN.--William Hayes, of Frods- ham, was summoned for having been drunk while in charge of a horse and cart at Stockton Heath on July 4th.—The evidence showed that defendant's vehicle collided with Mr. Heyl Dia's trap, the occupants of which were violently thrown out and one was seriously hurt. Defendant, who was drunk, .vas locked up, but was afterwards bailed out.—A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Baptist Church, Golborne-street.

On Sunday last the Anniversary services in connec- tion with the settlement of the Pastor, the Hey. H. litinnico, were held. Mr. Dunnico preached morning and evening and in the afternoon a sacred musical pro- gramme was given by members of the Apollo Prize Choir. Mr. Ben Few presided and spoke a few en- couraging words in connection with the success which had attended the efforts of this Church during the year of Mr. Dunnico's pastorate. Selections were given by the Choir entitled "The Crusaders," "Perfect in Christ," "The Pilgrim Chorus," and "The Hallelujah Chorus," while solos entitled "The Better Land," and "Oh! King of Love" by Miss Bridge, and "Oh! dry those Tears" 'by Miss Fairhurst were also admirably rendered. Mr. N. Balmford moved a vote of thanks to the menibers of the Choir and the Misses Bridge and Fairhurst for their voluntary services, which had been so much appreciated that afternoon. This was seconded by Mr. Clatworthy and supported by the Pastor. The church was crowded to overflowing and at the evening service there was a still larger congregation. In speaking of the success of the past year Mr. Dunnico said he believed the secret of this lay in the fact that people came and found God. He then briefly stated his creed. Facing the world in the light of modern science and taking into consider- ation those facts which had been proved to be true,he had very largely altered his conoept:ons of some religious truths and had been compelled by sheer honesty to change his views upon certain things which previously he had believed in. Upon the doctrine of evolution he had an open mind ; upon the social ques- tion he mightdiffer from some,as he was socialist to the backbone and believed the mission7of the Church was not confined exclusively to the soul, but should make provision for the body also, and that the Church would have to realize that she had her duties in the social world, not only to comfort those who were miserable but also to prevent those things which caused misery. The true wealth of the country in not lie in its hoard- ing of millions of money but n the looking after of each individual citizenand giving to every man a chance of earning a fair wage. The Pastor said he welcomed every one alike to the services at Golborne-street, it making no difference wh2ther they were rich or poor. He believed in God the Father Almighty and in His Son Jesus Christ our Lord. The great factor behind all phenomena had become vocal and revealed itself in Jesus Christ. It was not only because of what the Bible taught that we believed in that revelation, but because it was a matter of heart experience. God was was not a blind forc who neither loved nor cared and the presence of suffering did nit prove that God was not good. He urged men to trust God and find out for themselves that He was indeed good. A number of the scholars from the Sunday school sang and the anthem "Seek ye the Lord" was given by the choir, as well as" Now the day is over "at the close of the service. Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church.

On Sunday last the Rev. J. Ga,rdham Reed occupied the pulpit morning and evening, and preached two powerful sermons to large congregations. In the even- ing the choir gave a finished repetition of Mozart's Motett No. 1, "0 God, when Thou appearest." Mr. A. Spruce ably conducted, and Mr. Fred Podmare supplied the organ accompaniments.

div.head: USEFUL LITTLE PUBLICATION. The Book of Fish Sauces.
div.p: A USEFUL LITTLE PUBLICATION. The Book of Fish Sauces.

By sending a hi. stamp to Brown & Poison, Dept. Ftlo, Paisley, a new booklet entitled. "Simple Fish and Vegetable Sauces," can be obtained. It contains recipes for making White Fish Sauce. Oyster Sauce, Anchovy Sauce, Hollandaise Sauce, Caper Sance,Cardinal Sauce, Shrimp Sauce, and numerous other delicious Fish Sauces—over 39 valuable recipes in all. It is a book that ought to be in every household, forming, as it does, a reliable guide to improved dishes. It has been com- piled by the well-known Cookery expert, Ch. Herman Senn, and includes also a list of useful recipes for Vege- table Sauces and valuable hints on vegetable cooking. Mr. Senn says, "I have succeeded in producing by the aid of Brown & Poison's "Patent" Corn Flour, sauces which are superior in appearance, consistency and flavour to those made with ordinary flour." All the recipes are cheap, easy and practicable.

div.head: VOLUNTEERS. Intenstiag Manceuvres at Strattn.
div.p: THE VOLUNTEERS. Intenstiag Manceuvres at Strattn.

There was a good muster of Warrington volunteers on Saturday to participate in some interesting manceuvres at Stretton. The men, numbering about 350, paraded at the Drill Hall at four o'clock under the command of Major Edelsten, and marched to a field at Stretton, kindly lent by Mr. Lambert. Here the rnanceuvres, mainly consisting of skirmishing in com- panies, wece gone through in creditable style. The band and bugle band were in attendance, and the Mounted Infantry Company paraded under the command of Cap- tain Crosfield. The transport section was in charge of Lieutenant Ridgway. and Captain Haslam com- manded the Cyclist Company. The machine gun detachment with Maxim gun, signallers, and stretcher bearers also assembled in strong force. The officers present were Majors Edelsten and Appletor Captains Crosfield, B. Fair6lough, J. D. Fairclough, Williamson, Roberts and Haslam; Lieutenant Avery, Second Lieutenant Monks, as well as the Adjutant (Captain Leader) and Sergeant-Major Rawlinson. The men returned to tbe Drill Hall at 9.15 having marched from Stretton in the pouring rain. A "smoker" arranged by the members of E. Company was afterwards held in the bandroom and was attended by GO members and friends. The room had been very tastefully decorated for the occasion, and a prominent place was given to the Battalion Challenge Shield, at present in the custody of the company. Colour-Sergeant J. Cliffe Major Appleton, and there were also present Appleton, Captains Williamson, Smith, Roberts and Crosfleld, Lieutenant Avery. Bandmaster Richardson, Sergeant-Major Rawlinson and others. At the outset Captain Williamson proposed the health of the King, which .was enthusiastically honoured. The Chairman gave the toast of "The Battalion Officers" coupling with it the name of Captain Williamson. The toast was drunk with musical honours, and Captain Williamson responded, expressing the hopeo that the men would co-operate with him in making ' the company the pride of the battalion. (Applause) Cheer's were heartily given for the officers present,Major Edelsten, Captain Leader, (the new adjutant). Col.Sergt Cliffe, Sergeant Major Rawlinson, and E Company. Sergeant Taylor proßosed " Our Guests," which was re- sponded to by the Sergeant Major. Daring the evening songs were rendered by Captain Williainson, Lieutenant Avery, Sergeant Taylor, Pioneer Sergeant Broadhurst, Bandmaster Richardson,Corporals Payton and Coadwick, Private Knight and Mr. S. Whitfield. A number of gramophone selections, including Sousa's grand march Sir Gil'oert Greenall's Pigs. "El Capitan," were contributed by Lance Corporal At the Peterborough Agricultural Show, Sir Gilb :t Stewart. Private C. Worthington and Mr. C. Broadhurst officiated at the piano. The gathering terminated at. Greenall was awarded h in the class for the best midnight with the singing of the National Anthem. The o b f the large white breed, and the first prize in thar%s of the company are due to Quarter Master Potter the class for breeding sows of the large white breed. and Sergeant Major Rawlinson :for their assistance in H i e also received h.c. n the class for pairs of yelts of the decorations, and to Sergeant Whitfield and a willing the large white breed. The champion prize of a silver body of workers who ably looked after the wants of the cup (given by Sir Gilbert) for the best pig in any of guests. . the classes was won by the Duchess of Devonshire.

"DUMB" ANIMALS.—A small boy was pelting stones at a barking dog when a pa3Ber-by stopped and addressed him. "Little boy, don't you know you should be kind to dumb animals?" "yes, sir, I am; but he isn't dumb." NOT WHAT HE WANTED.—(Scene : Kentish Farm). tramp: "Could you give a ..00r man a little assistance or find him some employment?" —Farmer "You can have some work on the spot. I have a heap of wood yonder."—Tramp: "Hum —ha, yes—l'll send you the man directly. It's not for myself I am seeking a job, but for a friend of mine."

How IT TURNED OUT USEFUL.—" Never ,was glad for this im-iin•pediment in my speech but once," said the man from the North. "When was that?" " Fe-fe-fellow asked me h-h-how much I would take for a-a horse, and while was t-trying to tell him t-twenty p-pounds, he offered me f-tifty." BRINGING IT HOME.—" Woman," he hissed, " tvoman, do you thus spurn my heart after lead- ing me on?" "When did I lead you on, as you call it?" asked the girl. "Did you not tell me that that fortune-teller had told you that you were to wed a handsome, blonde young man, with the grace of a Greek god and the voice of an .tEo- ban harp?" LOSING No TIME —A faris shopkeeper wrote to one ot his customers as follows :—"I am able to offer you cloth like the enclosed sample at nine francs the metre. In case Ido not hear from you, I shall conclude that you wis_ to pay only eight francs. In order to lose no tiine, I accept the last- mentioned price."

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, July 18, 1903.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, July 18, 1903.

PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS. THE pessimist's only consolation is the hope that fie will be able to say, "I told you so 1" MOST of us would be all right if our actions were not so much in arrears of our intentions.

THE British Lion and American Eagle seem per- fectly %Ming to lie down together, but neither can make up his mind to lie down first. COMPARED with the amount a man wants in this world, it is surprising how little he can manage to get along with. THE first baby gets its photograph taken every three months; the other babies are lucky to geb theirs taken once in three years. "WHAT is all that racket next door?" "Well —it's the Bobbses ; they are either having a fight or holding a peace jubilee." TEACHER: " Wnat is a 'vacuum?" Bright Boy: "My pop says it's somethin' that most of the soldier boys has got inside 'em." ROCNIELLE : " How much did that cycle cost you, old man?" Parke: "I don't know; my doctor hasn't sent in his bill yet. FARMER: "Doctor, my nerve is gone." Dentist: "Oh, no, it isn't. 'Wait till I get a firm hold, and you'll find it." IT is surprising how many good things a man reads in the course of an evening that should teach a lesson to his neighbours. AMEIGIIGUS.—"Johnson wants to borrow some money of me. "Do you know anything about him ? "I know him as well as Ido you. I wouldn't let him have a farthing." SPOKE FEELINGLY.—Younger Sister (sentiment- ally): "They say that love is blind." Elder later: "And dumb, too, I think."

THE USUAL THlNG.—After all his sufferings, the poor artist died, and his soul was wafted to heaven. " Skyed again !" he exclaimed. No NEED TO Asx.—Mother : "You did not ask twice for cake when you took te% with Mrs. Prim, did you?" Glayds : "No, mamma—" Mother: "That was right." Gladys: "I helped myself." MORE MODEST.—" DO6B the professor really expect to discover the North Pole?" "No ; he merely expects to he known as the man who failed to discover it in 1898."

MEETING THE CASE.—Secretary: "This play doesn't seem to take." Manager: "Make tre- mendous success' in the advertisements twice as large as it is now." *CUSTOMER (to baker's boy) : Is your bread nice and light! Baker's boy (confidentially) : Yes ma'am; it only weighs ten ounces to the pound. Mn. SrouTzu : "An heirloom, Johnnie, is something that's handed down from father to son." Little Johnnie: " Huh I That's a funny name for pants." "THAT man Fraser doesn't borrow my lawn- mower so often nowadays." "How did you cure him of the habit?" "Every time he asked for it I sent and borrowed his bicycle." DOLLY: "Papa, do they get salt out of Salt Lake?" Papa: "Yes, dear, large quantities." Dolly: "And ink out of the Black Sea ? " Papa: "No ; now keep quiet." Dolly: "Are there any women on the Isle of Man?"
Timm fAux • OTHERS.—Grimehaw : "Pensmith, who writes so much magazine poetry, doesn't look like a poet, does he ? " Teller: No." Grim- shaw : "Well, he isn't."

"ARE the natives of the island Christianised?" asked the sombre lady. "They would be," sighed the escaped missionary, "if their diet had any effect." ILLUMINATED.—Ray. Dr. Thumper: "Does not married life seem brighter to you?" Mrs. New. : "You can imagine. My bridal gifts in- cluded twenty-five lamps." WHAT IT WAS.—" Just listen how they are pounding the floor with their feet!" said the tragedian behind the curtain. "Yes," said the leading ingenue; "that is the stamp of public approval." HURT HIS FEELlNcs.—Friend : "Is that a bright baby where you live ? " The Skye Terrier: "No ; it's a stupid little thing. It sometimes takes me for a cat and calls me 'Pussy '."

A WORD OF COMMENDATION.—" There was one moment," wrote the dramatic critic of the Cyclone County Sandbag, "when Mr. Hamfat, who played Othello, was simple, natural, and unaffected. That was when the egg struck him." COCNTERBALANCED.—SaIIy-Gay : "What do you think of Mass Bramley ?" I like her very well; for, while she is so exasperatingly clever, she is also consolingly ugly." WITH A RESERNATION.—The Proud Father: "On ! come, now! You were a boy yourself once." The Irate Neighbour "Maybe I was; but I didn't 'have an idiot or a father to encourage me to make myself an infernal nuisance!" A Suns SlGN.—Visitor : "So your poor husband has passed away, Mrs. Murphy. He died happy, I hope?" Mrs Murphy: Oi think so, mum. The last thing he did was to crack me over the head wid a medicine bottle ! " WANTED A CHANGE.—" Ido wish the weather would change," exclaimed the dyspeptic man's wife. "But it isn't nearly so disagreeable as it might be." "I know that. But it makes my husband so unhappy not to have more to complain about."

INQUISITIVE TOCrEIST : "And how do you find the crops this year, Murphy?" Murphy: "How do I find the crops, is it? Sure, your honour, 'tis by digging for 'ern, any way!" ENTIRELY SUCCESSFUL. Doctor: "Did your visit to the seaside have the desired effect, madam?" Mrs. Fullpurse "Oh, yes, doctor; both my daughters are married." SILENT.—" How do you pronounce the last syllable of that word butterme,' " asked the cus- tomer. "The last syllable is silent" stiffly replied the grocer. HIT IT THE FIRST TIME. —Mrs. Matchman : "Look how earnestly Rose and Mr. Beach are bidding each other good-night at the gate. lam sure there's something between them." Mr. Matchman : "So am I; it's the gate."

TAUGHT BY EXPERIENCE. —H'usband : "What would you say, my dear, it I were to offer you the money for a new bonnet?" Wife: "1 wouldn't say a word, darling, until I had the money in my hands, for fear you'd change your mind."

Nor ArriteitEssivE. First Boarder: "The landlady has gone to a food exhibition, but I don't think it can possibly affect as." Second Boarder: "Why should it affect us?" First Boarder: "Well, of course, if she finds any cheaper kinds of food than we are getting now, we'll have to eat them; but I don't think it's possible." APPRECIATED Jr.—" Ah, there's ,nothing like the bicycle. I've been unable to sleep for years, and—" "You rode a machine and it cured you?" "No; but a cyclist ran into me and I was insensible for several minutes." GREAT STRIDES.—" His success in a financial way has been something marvellous." " Yes ?" "Yes, sir. I've often heard him tali how, when he came here fifteen years ago, all he owed in the world was a sovereign or two, and last week he failed for ten thousand."

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

Naturalists at Frodsham. A delightful half-day in the country was spent by the Liverpool Field Naturalists on Saturday, the spot selected being Overton Hills. A charming four miles' walk by hillside paths among the gorse and bilberry, and by woodlands and pleasant lanes, led to Helsby where tea was served at the Robin Hood Hotel. Wild flowers were abundant, though chiefly of the ordinary type foxgloves, wild roses and other usual wayside species. Among the more interesting botanical finds were the handsome downy leaved wild 'rose (rosa villosa), the white climbing fumitory (corydalis clavi- culata), and the wood horse-tail (equisetum sylvaticum) There Was not much competition for prizes ; that for the' best bouquet being gained by Mr. W. A. Taylor, while the botanical enigma of the day was solved by Miss Fidler, Miss Hoffman, Mr. T. Swift, aud the hon. secretary; the plant being the foxglove (digitalis purpurea).

Parr's Bank Limited. The half-yearly meeting of this company will be held at the Bank prenttses, Winwick-street, Warring- ton, on Thursday, July 23rd, at twelve o'clock noon, for the purpose of declaring a dividend on the Ist August, and conducting the ordinary business of the company. The directors, in submitting to the shareholders the balance sheet of the bank at 30th June, 1903, certified by the auditors, report that the position and prospects of the business continue to be in every way satisfactory. Including £102,373 is. id. brought forward at 31st December, 1902, the . net balance of profits, after providing for all bad and doubtful debts, and rebating the current bills at 5 per cent is £295,067 19s. 3d. From this sum the direc- tors recommend :—The payment of ' a half-year's dividend at the rate of 19 per cent per annum, pay- able, free of income tax, on Ist August, £162,307. 10s. ; the transfer to bank premises account £20,000 ; the transfer to officers' pension and provident fund £5,000; leaving balance to be carried to next account £107,760 9s. 3d. A branch of the bank has beea opened at iigburth, Liverpool, and one will shortly be opened An Fleet street, London. Lymm Grammar School Sports. _ _ _

Old boys' race: 1, Ronald Meldium ; 2, Cecil Brown. Three-le,med race: 1, J. L. Jones and Billington; 2, Newton and Holt. Sack race: 1, Newton; 2, J. Kelsall. Bandsmen's race :1, H. Clare; 2, J. bolt; 3, H. Druce. Tug of war: 1, Wood's team; 2, D. Jones's team. The championship medal was won by H. Wood. • Presentations.

There was an interesting ceremony at Lorne House School, Froghall-lane the other evening, when a depu- tation of"old boys"and present pupils waited upon Mr. H. G. Johnstone to ask his acceptance of a token of their good wishes towards him, on the occasion of his leaving Warrington for Barnoldswick. The pre- sentation took the form of a lounge chair (supplied by Messrs. J. M. Greenhalgh and Co.). Edwin Pickles, an "old boy," made the presentation,-aud wished Mr. Johnstone every success and happiness in his new home. In accepang the presentation; Mr. Johnstone said the good feeling displayed was very grateful to him, and he would treasure the chair as evidence that his efforts to fit his pupils for their work in life, were not unappreciated. The proceedings, which bore evidence throughout of real regard between teacher and past pupils, .closed with short speeches by W. W. Winstanley, R. Moss, and J. Walsh,_ also "old boys," who expressed their gratitude to Mr. Johnstone for hi-, care and attention on their behalf.—Presentations have been made to Mrs. Johnstone by the pupils attending her school and also by past pupils. On the closing of the school the pupils presented Miss Johnstone, on behalf of Mrs. Johnstone, with a silver-mounted biscuit barrel, and Tuesday the "Old Girls" forwarded Mrs. Johnstone who has already left Warrington, a silver plated sugar basin and cream ewer, as an evidence of their esteem and regard and in recognition of the benefits they had derived from their tuition. Charge Against A Publican.

David Br-adburn, landlord of the "Chetwode Arms," Whitley, was charged at the Warrirzton Occasionfo. Court on Monday, afore Mr. F. A. Frost, with assault- ing a young woman named Elizia Haddock on the 2nd inst.—Complainant fainod after giving evidence of the alleged offence.—Mr. Browne appeared for the defendant and said he should submit that the case was one of blackmail. He ha-_,dc 1 the magistrate a letter wh:ch defendant received from the complainant before the warrant was issued, and said that in face of that communication no jury would convict.— Defendant was remanded to Daresbuty Petty Sessions, bail being allowed, himself in £lO-0 and two other sureties of £5O each.—The case again came .on for hearing before Mr. W. Long and other Magistrates et Daresbuq Petty Sessions on. Tuesday.—Mr. Browne said he understood the com- plainant did not know the purport of what she was doing when she applied for a warrant and she now wished to withdraw the charge. He thought the Police Superintendent and the Clerk would advise that in ,face of the letter which he had submitted there could not possibly be a conviction for the crime alleged against box and a inost the said shefendanwt.—ishCer to withdrawplainan t entered the case as /she had "had enough of it." She had been punished enough and she also thought defendant had. She admitted having written the letter produced.—The Bench consulted in private and on their return into court the Chairman said that in face of the complain- ant's application and the letter she had written they were willing that the charge should be withdrawn. Primrose League Fete. _

At Grappenhat Heyes on Saturday afternoon the annual fete in connection with the Grappenhall habita- tion (1573) of the Primrose League was held by per- mission of the Ruling Councillor (Mr. J. Charlton Parr.) Between six and seven hundred members of the habiMion and'friends availed themselves of the opportunity- of spending an enjoyable time in the beautiful grounds and loaunately the event was favoured with grounds, weather until the -evening when rain fell heavily. Tea was provided in a marquee and selections of music were played by the Warrington Pioneer Band under the conductorship-of Mr. R. Smith. The awards were distributed by the Dame President (Mrs. Parr), and short speeches were delivered by the Ruling Councillor (Mr. J. C. Parr), and the 1412. Allan DeTatton Egerton,:M.P.—A vote co thanks was accorded to all who had assisted in the arrangements, and to the Ruling Councillor and Dame President for their kindness in placing the grounds at the disposal of the habitation. Death of Mr. William Welsby. _ - - _

Many of our readers will regret to hear of the death of Mr. William Welsby, of Parker-street, which took place at West Kirby on Monday night. Mr. Welsby was an old servant of Messrs. Crosfield, soap rnanu- facturers, Bank Quay, having br m i their employ for over 30 years. He was, for very many years, head soapmaker to the firm, but latterly, owing to the extenSion of the business, his time wis deroted to experimenting. The flag at the works on Tuesday floated at half-mast as a mark of respect to the deceased.

div.head: ST HELENS.
div.p: ST HELENS.

FIRE AT PEA.SLEY CROSS ST&TION, ST. HELENS. Shortly after midnight on Sunday a Corporation employe, who was passing over Peasley Cross Bridge, noticed that the station buildings were on fire. He at once gave the alarm to the Broad Oak signal-box, and a message was sent to the Sutton Oak sheds. A staff of men was sent and they extinguished the fire, but not before the waiting-room was gutted and considerable damage done to the booking office. It is supposed that someone had thrown a lighted match down on Sunday night and thus caused the fire. _

div.head: BURGLARS AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: BURGLARS AT ST. HELENS.

Recently burglars have been paying visits to the resi- dences of gentlemen of St. Helens. On Tuesday night an entrance was effected at the residence of Mr. A. E. Tickle, solicitor, St. Ann's, and evidently preparations had been made fora big haul. The family were away from town, but the opportune arrival of a maid disturbed the burglar, who decamped. An attempt had also been made to enter the house of Mr. R. G. Brook adjoining.

div.head: SAD DROWNING FATALITY AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: SAD DROWNING FATALITY AT ST. HELENS.

On Wednesday at the St. Helens Town Hall, Mr. S Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest on the body of Thomas Glover,a carter, of Warrington-road,who was drowned in the canal on Sunday afternoon.—A boy named Joseph Crooks stated that on Sunday afternoon he saw deceased with a number of other boys fishing in the canal near Messrs. Quirk, Barton and Co.'s lead works. Deceased overbalanced himself and fell into the water. There were only some small boys near at the. time.—Police-constible Charlton stated that he recovered the body at 2.10. The canal was 7ft deep at the point where deceased fell in.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." JEALOUS AT EIGHTY.

A greyhaired old man, named James Houghton, of 37, Eccleston-street, St. Helens, was brought up on a warrant on Monday charged with threatening hi 4 wife. Complainant told the bench she was eighty years old, and her husband was about the same age. She had been married to him for twelve years, and durhlg that time he had not worked more than a week or two. She had had some cottages, but had to sell them, and her husband took the money to get drunk with. He was drunk beforeishe got up in the morning, and when she took money out of his pockets he threatened her and used bad language. He was also so jealous that he would nob let her keep a lodger to assist her in making a living. She wanted him to keep away from her.—The Clerk (Mr. B. Brewis) pointed out that complainant could leave her husband if she wanted.—Prisoner in- sisted that he was entitled to a third share in the property • but this complainant denied.—The bench dis- missed the case, Gdvising the old woman td`consult solicit& and act on his advice. She could go away from him and take her furniture with her. MUNICIPAL BY-ELECTION AT ST. HELENS.

On Thursday at St. Helens an election took place of a mtmber of the Town Council for the West Sutton Ward, to fill the vacancy created by the elevation of Colonel Pilkington to an aldermanic seat. Mr. Henry Houghton (Conservative), who retired from the Council only a few months ago owing to ill-health, defeated Mr J. J. Bate (Liberal) by 565 votes to 427—majority 138.

div.p: THE MONO-RAIL.
Prospectus Issued—Capital £2,100,000

On our first page will be found particulars of the prospectus of the Manchester and Liverpool Electric Express Railway Company. The capital is fixed at £2,100,000 divided into 2E0,000 shares of £lO each, for which applications are invited. The subscription list opens on Monday next and closes on Friday, the 24th inst.

The first directors of the new company are expected to be Mr. P. Lyttelton Gell, Director of the Foreign and Colonial Investment Trust Company Limited, Chairman; Sir John purcell, K.C.B. (late Registrar of Joint Stock Companies), Director of the National Bank Limited; Deputy-Chairman; Mr. J. S. Bergheim, Belsize Court, Belsize Park, London; Mr. H. A. Earle, M. Inst, C. E., Managing Director Mather and Platt Limited, Man- chester; Mr. J. H. Macmillan (Sails Schwabe and Co Limited), Manchester; Mr. J. W. McConnel (McConnel and Co Ltd.) Manchester; Mr. George Montagu, M.P., 33 Oxford Mansions London; The Honourable R. J. Stratt, Toning place, Witham Essex ; Sir Alexander Wilson, Chairman of the Mercantile Bank of India, and of Borax Consolidated Limited.

The company was incorporated by an Act of Parlia- ment which received the Royal Assent on the 17th August, 1901. The company's powers were granted by that Act, and a subsequent Act, which received the Royal Assent on the 23rd June, 1902, the two Statutes being" The Manchester and Liverpool Electric Express Railway Acts, 1901 and 1902. The Manchester terminns of the railway will be on the west side of Deansgate, one of the principal thoroughfares of that city', and within a distance of about 600 yards from the Exchange, and about 400 yards from the Town Hall. The Liver- pool terminus will be closely adjoining Church-street, and within a distance of about 700 yards from the Ex- change and the Town Hall. These are most central and convenient situations, ani are both excellently served by, the electric tramways. The length of the railway will be about 3il miles, and the time occupied in the transit will bi 20 minutes instead of 40 to 41 minutes, the time at present taken by the fastest express trains running between Manchester and Liverpool. Each train will carry two classes of passengers at fares notexceeding the ordinary fares at present charged by the other railways. It iA proposed to work this new line Ma speed of 110 miles an hour, the trains running every ten minutes, or, if necessary, more frequently,. It has been proved that the electric working of rail- ways, and mono-rail lines in particular, so far as passen- ger traitic is concerned, will be much cheaper than the present, steam-hauled trains. The workin,, expenses of the Manchester and Liverpool Mono-rail will be far lbelow those of any existing railway. The current will be supplied from a central generating station at War- rington, thus avoiding the wastefulness of numerous steam locomotives. The trains will be made up of single cars, some carrying 50 passengers and some more, and they will be run it ten minutes' interval (or less) ; the rolling stock will be less than on ordinary lines. On the double mono-rail track there will never be more than four cars at a time. The staff to work the mono-rail will be very small, for there will be no coupling of cars, no crossings, no points' no shunting, &c. The wages to be paid will be less than one-half those on the three lines now running between Manchester and Liverpool, the nurriber of porters, &c., being far less. Each car will carry but two operators, and of course there will be no stoking, no taking in of water, &c., while the up- keep and the electric machines will require far less labour and be much less expensive than that of a steam engine. It was stated before Parliament that the total annual expenditure for traction maintenance and work- ing expenses of the electric mono-rail would amount to £65,554 per annum, equal to a cost per train mile of about 71d. On this basis an average of only V,- third- bless passengers carried per train would cover all work- ing expenses. An average of 20 passengers per train, or 2,000 per day in each direction, would be sufficient to pay 5 per cent per annum on the capital of the Man- chester and Liverpool\ Electric Express Railway Com- pany. Every additional 21 passengers per train will be sufficient to pay about an additional 1 per cent upon the capital. The 10 minutes' service provides for a traffic of about 4,000 passengers each way, per day, and the mono-rail is quite capable, with lareer and more fre- quent cars, of carrying 25,000 per day in each direction. It, has been proved again and again that the supply of more rapid and frequent communication between popu- lous centres creates a great and ever-increasing traffic. There is now a very big daily traffic between Manches- ter and Liverpool. The mono-rail is expected to absorb most of this, and will create, it may safely be predicted, a new traffic which will increase in volume yearly and make the investment a profitable one.

On Wednesday evening .the bowling: enthusiasts of the Warrington Cycling Club played a in itch with Clock Face C.C. at Great Sankey. The contest was greatly enjoyed, - many of the games being very 'close. Warrington ran out winners by 16 points, the score being :—Warrington C.C. won 8 games and obtained 160 points ; Clock Face won 6 .games and obtained 144 points.

The Lovely-lane Cycling Club's fixture on Satur- day was a run to Tarporley but ton conferring with the members it was decided to visit the camp of the Welsh Fusiliers at Delamere Forest. The outing was very much enjoyed. The return journey was ma de via Kingsley, Overton, and Frodsham. When the wheelers reached Sutton Weaver ran commenced to fall and the party was well drenched for' the first time this season when Warrington was reached at 9 p.m-

Angling.

The fishing contest in aid of the Benevolent Fund of the Warrington Anglers' Association was duly de- cided in the water of the Bridgwater Canal, Stockton Heath on Saturday afternoon last. There were almost 100 entries and 93 actually competed. Only fish of standard size measurement were eligible for weighing. Sport proVed to be of a very satisfactory character. Result :-Ist, W. The visiting -team is considered to be one of the strongest in the district and the result was not to be complained of, although it would have been more satisfactory if the match could have been played to a definite conclusion. Northern's most useful wielder of the willow was W. Fraser who carried out his bat after compiling 41. The Rev. J. Burrough made a good display for his 29 and R. K. Fernie placed 25 on the score sheet.
Rugby Football.

The second eleven were thoroughly beaten by the Northern second contingent who achieved victory somewhat easily. Having put together 227 for the loss of 7 wickets the Northern eleven declared their innings and succeeded in dismissing their opponents for 131. G. W. Fraser and W. D. Lloyd rendered yeoman service for the visitors,their respective totals being 77 and 70. On the Warrington side T. Wright was the highest scorer with 37 and E. Pierpomt knocked up 30.

div.head: Cycling.
div.p: Cycling.

There is no fixture more popular with the mem- bers of the Warrington Cycling Club than " Presi- dents' Day" and the annual visit to Beeston Towers, the residence of the esteemed Presidentr Mr. John Naylor, is always looked forward to with the keenest pleasure. Himself an enthusiastic wheeler, Mr. Naylor is delighted to entertain the members of the organization in which he displays such a lively inter- est and those cyclists who take advantage of the invitation so cordially given to spend an afternoon at his charmingly situated residence may rely upon a reception which lacks nothing in heartiness. Unfor- tunately Saturdajgs weather conditions were not by any means ideal. True it was fine all afternoon although threatening clouds frequently obscured the sun, but in the evening rain fell heavily and the wheelers came in for a drenching on the return journey.

Between 60 and 70 members and friends availed themselves Of Mr. Naylor 's hospitality.Of this number over 40 rode out on cycles and enjoyed the spin through Delamere Forest. The others went by train via Chester, where a pleasant hour was spent in stiolling through the old-fashioried rows and along the Wanks of the Dee. Arrived at Beeston, the party were wel- comed by Mr. and Mrs. Naylor aad family, and also by a large house party who had been invited to meet the Warrington cyclists, prominent among them being Councillor Pedley,of Crewe,who is the president of the Crewe C.C.,, and a member of the Main Roads •Com- mittee of the Cheshire County Council, and also an enthusiastic cyclist and mozorist. Amongst the War- ringtonians were the captain (Mr. W. Taylor), the sub- captain (Mr. J. Podmore, jun.), the treasuurer (Mr. F. Garnett), Messrs. W. Bellian, W. Litton, W. Brown, F. Redfern (members of the committee), and E. Pickavanee, jun. (general hon. secretary).

An inspection of Mr. Naylor's beautiful residence, was,of course,made andafterwards tea was served on the tennis lawn, the excellent repast being heartily enjoyed After tea photographs of the guests were taken by several devotees of the camera. Adjourning to the lawn at the front of the house an impromptu concert was held, vocal and instrumental items being rendered by Miss Naylor and Mrs. Arthur Booth, and Messrs. J. Grounds, W. A. Clay; A. Fieldhouse and G. Finch. The lawn was them cleared and several dances were indulged in with great zest.

At the close of a thoroughly enjoyable time, Mr. W.` Taylor (captain) proposed a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. and Mrs. Naylor for their kind hospitality. This was seconded by Mr. E. Pickavance, jun. (hon. secretary), who' assured the worthy host and hostess of the great esteem in which they were held by the members of the club. Mr. D. Davies and Councillor Pedley supported the motion, which was carried. Mr. Naylor briefly responded, and assured the visitors that no body of ladies and gentlemen was more welcome to Beeston Towers than the members and friends of the Warrington Cycling Club.

• Hearty cheers were given for the host and hostess and the party started for home. The cyclists had only ridden about a mile when rain descended and continued for the rest of the evening. After a very unpleasant ride most of the members entrained for Warrington at Hartford. Others braved the elements for the whole of the distance home, but all accomplished the journey in safety after an outing which, but for the evening dein,* would have beeii recorded as an unqualified an ccess. •

BUTTERMILK BRIDGE. The SURVEYOR said he had seen the Borough Surveyor respecting Buttermilk Bridge, Sankey Boundary. Mr. Longdin was of the opinion that an iron or steel foot- bridge was unnecessary from the Warrington point of view. He, however promised to view the bridge and have the Corporation side repaired and to write to the Rural Council on the subject of replacing the bridge. The SURVEYOR said the Rural Council had repaired their side of the bridge as well as they could. Mr. Longdin contended that it was for the Rural Council to provide a new bridge, because the structure was not much used by the borough workpeople. The INSPECTOR said someone would be getting drowned before long if the bridge was not ' attended to. The SURVEYOR said the Corporation half was "patched up" any way. The CLERK: If anyone comes to grief this Coun- cil will have done its duty. The SURVEYOR: Unless the Corporation half pulls our half down. The whole thing is rotting away. This concluded the business.

div.head: PENKETH PARISH COUNCIL.
div.p: PENKETH PARISH COUNCIL.
Complaint Against A Visiting Football
Team.

Dr. Murray presided at the quarterly meeting of Penketh Parish Council which was held in the Wesleyan Schools on Monday evening. There were also present: —Messrs. Clarke, Snoddy, Mitiwood and Foster (clerk).
THE LIGHTING OF THE VILLAGE.

The Clerk reported that he had received another letter from the Warrington Gas Engineer respecting the quality of the gas supplied to the village. Mr. Haddock stated that a three inch main had been found near Halton's Bridge and the Corporation were going to substitute a six inch main. He therefore thought there would be no more complaints. Mr. Snoddy : Has there been any improvement inthe gas? The Chairman: It has been much better of late. I think that is probably owing to the new pipe. A suggestion by Mr. Snoddy that the Clerk should write to the gas engineer pointing out that the com- munication he had forwarded disagreed with a previous reply) did not meet with, support and the matter dropped.
ALLEGED DAMAGE BY VISITING FOOTBALL TEAMS.- . RENTING OF THE RECREATION GROUND.

The Clerk reported that in accordance with the instructions of the Council he wrote to the Secretary of the Penketh Football Club, asking him to warn visit- ing teams againstsloing wilful damage in the village. Last season one visiting club broke a lamp on the high- way. He had received no reply to the letter, but prob- ably this Was due to the fact that the committee would not meet during the summer months. _ _ _ _ _
Considerable-discussion arose on the question of the Parish Council's rights in regard to the Recreation Ground.

The Chairman said the ground belonged to the lord of the manor, and the Council simply rented the right of pasturage. The damage complained of was not done on the ground but on the highway. The Clerk: That is for the police to look after.
The Chairman suggested that the clerk should write to the Secretary of the Football club at the commence- ment of the season but no definite course was decided upon. _

At a later stage the Chairnrin read a draft of the agreement between the council and the lord of the ma or respecting therecreution ground. The Council's tenancy was a yearly one commencing on July Ist, 189 G at the rent of £1 per annum. The council had to keep the fences in good condition. _ _

Mr. Snoddysaid it was clear that they were respon- sible to the landlord for the right use of the ground. That being so it was within their powers to step in and stop any abuse. Could the Chairman say what the balance at the bank on the Recreation ground find amounted to?
The Chairman: lan afraid we have not any left. You have 12s. and there is a bill for over £5 to be mat. The Clerk was instructed to write to Mr. Pownall with respect to the cutting of the hedges. .
THE LIBRARY QUESTION.

_ Mr. Clarke informed the Council that he had inter- viewed Mr. Arnold Pickering, a member of the Knuts- ford Council, to obtain information as to what steps should be taken in applying for a grant from Mr Carnegie towards the provision of a.Free Library. Mr Pickering supplied him with full particulars and told him that one of the conditions on which grants were given was that the site should be presented to the parish free of any charge on the rates. t The Council agre d to forward a letter to Mr. Pickering thanking im for the information, and the Chairman intimated hat it had already been decided not to take immediate steps to obtain aFree Library.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS
A Case of Smallpox.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held in the Board room on Wednesday morning. Mr. A Brooks presided and there was also present: Mrs. Clay, Rev. Father Wilson, Dr. Patterson, Dr. Murray, Messrs. A. J. Jolley, A. Jolley, G. Pilling, T. H. Ashcroft, S. Davies, J. Payton, J. Clarke, R. Forshaw, T. Halton, J. Turton, Wm. Houghton. J. Backhouse, G. Mather, G. Ritchie, J. W. Knowles,J. C. Sutton (clerk) J. F. Awbery (master) and A. Wright (superintendent, Padgate schools). . -

div.head: TREAT TO THE CHILDREN.
div.p: THE TREAT TO THE CHILDREN.

The superintendent of Padgate schools reported that the children attended the Warrington Walking Day procession on July 3rd, the railway fares being paid out of the superintendent's petty cash. Mr. Robinson, one of the Guardians kindly lent a, lurry for the little ones in the procession. He had received sweets from Mr. Payton, nuts from Mr. J. W. Houghton, flowers from Mr. William Houghton. Mr. J. W, Houghton, lent a field for sports and the treat as given by the Guardians was thoroughly enjoyed. The Cheshire Lines Cricket Club gave their annual treat to the boys on July 4th.

div.head: HOUSE COMMITTEE.
div.p: HOUSE COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of the House Committee a letter was read from Mr. G. Hoult re the balance of his account. It was resolved that the acting master write Mr. Hoult informing him that they adhere to their former resolu- tion dated 13th March, 1903. Messrs. Pilling, A. J. Jolley and G. Mather were appointed a sub-committee to meet Mr. Grimsdale and make the best arrangements possible re the electric plant. It was recommended that a suitable testimonial be granted to Mr. S. H. A. Healey, the master's clerk. It was also recommended that probationer Nurses Flood and Stringer be continued in the Union service if they so desire, for a year each at the present salary of £2O with the usual emoluments; that Miss L. Seger be engaged as a probationer nurse upon the usual terms of £l2 first year, £l6 second year and £2O third year, with uniform, apartments, rations, ern.

div.head: CASE OF SMALL-PDX.
div.p: A CASE OF SMALL-PDX.

It was reported that William Green (35), was admit- ted to the hospital on Thursday week very ill, and was seen by the doctor. The illness proved to be small- pox, and the patient was speedily removed to the Small-pox Hospital at Sankey. Prompt and effective measures were immediately taken to disinfect the ward, bedding, Sm., and to isolate those who had come into contact with the patient. Some of the nurses and officers had been re-vaccinated.
Mr. P.II.LING said it was not knownat the time that it was a case of small-pox. Mr. J. BILLINGS: Where did the patient come from? Mr. A. JOLLEY : From one of the lodging-houses in Scotland-road.
Mr. PILLING: Yes. He is a Warrington man. THE NEW MASTER.

Mr. PILLING reported that the newly-appointed master (Mr. J. F, Awbery) had visited the house at each week-end following July Ist. On the first occasion he stayed from Saturday until Monday, on the second from Saturday until Tuesday, and during the last week- end he had stayed from Saturday until that day (Wed- nesday). Mr. Awbery would leave again that day and would take up his duties permanently on Saturday next. Mr. MATHER.: Is the Master's Clerk about to leave.
Mr. PILLING: He seems rather inclined to follow Mr. Gate.
THE APPOINTMENT OF NURSE IRWIN,

div.head: LONDON'S BEST.
div.p: LONDON'S BEST.
" The British Weekly," June 20th, 1903,says :

Alike among journalists, the general public, and Free Churchmen, there is much said on the growing interest and excellence of "The Daily News." It seems to im- prove day by day, and in all its splendid history, was never more vigorous and vital than it is now. Every department of the paper is being brought up to a high level. We are very glad to know that the result has been alargely increased circulation alike in. London and in the provinces. 'The Daily News "de- served support, were it only for its noble renunciation in the abandonment of betting news. But after all, no paper will succeed for negative merits, and" The Daily News "can stand safely on its quality as a great newspaper. We hope that Free Churchmen everywhere will give it their heartiest support. They may begin this support for the sake of the paper but we promise they will continue it for their own sakes.
Select The Daily News "as your morning papenatui recul it in the Train, Tram, and Bus, as a silent protest against the Betting and Gambling Evil.

div.head: POOR CHILDREN'S SUMMER CAMP. Departure of the First Contingent.
div.p: POOR CHILDREN'S SUMMER CAMP. Departure of the First Contingent.

There was Whappy scene at the Central 'Station yesterday afternoon when the first detachment of poor boys selec- ted to spend a holiday under canvas departed by the 2.50 train for Moreton, a seaside resort in no Wirral district. Naturally the youngsters were in high glee at the prospects of a week's outing, and their beaming I faces testified to their sense of appreciation of the thoughtfulness of- those who have undertaken thej organization Of the camp. It had been arranged to send7s boys yesterflay,but only 65 put in an appearance, and 10more will depart to-day. A further contingent of between 75 and 100 will journey to Moreton next Friday. The children are drawn from all the elementary schools in the town, the task of selectionl having been entrusted to the head teachers who were I requested to send in the names of the poorest scholars. The Executive Committee then decided upon the percentage of boys to be sent from each school, and the teachers made the final selection. On Wednesday afternoon the lads were examined by Dr. J. Guest Gornall at the School Attendance Offices and only three were found to be unfit to go to camp. Their places were, of course, filled by other boys. Every care been taken to ensure the comfort of the youthful holiday-makers. 'The detachment which departed yesterday will be in charge of Mr. F. J. Emson, who will have the assist- ance of Messrs. Frank Aukland, A. Malcolm, Gor- don Dawson and A. Chappell. The last-named gentle- man has served in the Army and only recently left the service after taking part in the South African cam- I paign during which he was wounded. He is now quite restored to health and has undertaken to superintend the camp as far as the maintenance of the tents is con- cerned. The lads will be taught how to deal with thej tents and will be put through drills each day by Mr.l Chappell. Inspector iTackett,N.S.P.C.C.,will accompany j the second contingent on Friday next. Every- I thing was in readiness to receive the boys yesterday and immediately on arrival tea was servel The commissariat is in charge of Mr. Thomas Macfarlane. an able ship's cook, who has had experience in the navy and merchantile marine. There will be no lack of amusements for the boys. The mem- bers of the Warrington Cricket Club have kindly sent sufacient cricket tackle to keep enthusiasts in the sport fully occupied and there will he football and other games. Bathing will also be indulged in. Some of the gentlemen in charge of theic,amp are enthusiastic anglers and 'we are informed that the "cashes" adjoining the sea shore abound with eels, flounders, fluke and other finny denizens of the deep. Given fine weather boys andadults alike should spend a highly enjoyable time. We understand that Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, the ener- getic hon. secretray, has received a letter from Lady Greenall enclosing a cheque for £2O towards the fund and promising to subscribe £lO each year. Lady Greenall considers the scheme a most excellent one and expresses her willingness to become a member of the committee.

div.head: VACANCY IN ST. JOHN'S WARD.
div.p: THE VACANCY IN ST. JOHN'S WARD.

Notices have been posted declaring a vacancy in St John's Ward. The last day on which nominations can be received is Wednesday. next, July 22nd. The Mayor will attend at the Town Hall on the following day for the purpose of hearing any objections or receiving any -withdrawals. The election will take place en Thursday, July 30th, and the polling station will be St. John's Club-room, John-street. There are no fewer than 1,802 electors in the ward, St. John's containing a larger number of electors than any other ward in the town. At the time of writing, no nominations 'have been handed in, but at present, there seems every probability of a contest. between several aspirants for the office.

_ Mr. Henry Thornton will champion the cause of the Municipal Non-trading Committee, and his address will be found in our advertising columns. Mr. Thornton states that he is strenuously opposed to all illegal and immoral trading by members of the Council with the Corporation, believing that all engaged In such trading cannot do their duty to the ratepayers. Self- interest under such conditions, he says, is bound to pre- dominate, and where that is in existence in public life the town must suffer. He pledges himself "to oppose anything and everything in the nature,of extravagance, and to work hand-in-hand with the Non-traders, who, in the Council Chamber, have been such a power for good. They have taken the ratepayers into their confidence by exposing many serious irregularities which, had it not been for them, would never have been brought before the notice of the public." Mr. John Maginn will take the field as an independent candidate. In his address, which will be found in our advertising columns, Mr. Maginn says he is not the nominee of any party, political, religious, or otherwise, believing that to serve the best interests of the town is the true and proper object to be aimed at. On the non- trading question, Mr. Maginn says: "I am, and always have been, a non-trader, and I protested against gentle- I men being elected to the Council who had as their object to use the position they held as Councillors to their own advantage or the advantage of their friends." Mr. Magina says he will endeavour to see that the ratepayers get a fair return for the rates they pay and points out that street-paving, lighting and sewering are anything but satisfactory, and many of the dwelling- houses in the ward are amongst the worst in the town. He intends to do all he can to have the intercepting depot removed out of the ward, as he thinks it is in a most nsuitable position nt present. Standing in the midst of a densely populated neighbourhood, it is. in his opinion, a permanent danger to the health of the inhabitants and a disgrace to any up-to-date Corpora- tion. Mr. Maginn intends to explain his views more fuly at a meeting he intends to hold in his word. The names of Mr. W. J. Shaw and Mr. Hamblett have also been mentioned as probable candidates. -Mr. Shaw, we understand, will not contest the ward until November next, when he will come forward as a non- trader. A meeting of the So. John's Conservative Ward Com- mittee will be heldl on Monday Droning to select a Conservative candidate.

div.head: MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S TARIFF PROPOSALS.

div.head: MR. BINDLOSS'S REPLY TO MR. PARKER
div.p: MR. BINDLOSS'S REPLY TO MR. PARKER

Mr. E. W. BINDLOSS writes:— It was not my intention to get into an interminable correspondence with Mr. Parker, and after his some- what uncourteons retort as to my "limited gifts.ainl avowed ignorance," I have less inclination than ever. A wise man should always be sensible of his deficiencies, and although, Mr. Editor, we cannot all be "Admirable Crichtons ' orpossess the ability of that famous gentle- man of Venice who was able to speak—and I suppose write—"An infinite deal of nothing," I intend out of mere fpoliteness—which one at least of the parties to a controversy should have—to make a few remarks on Mr. Parker's last letter. I am quite aware of the main features of Mr. Chamberlain's proposals so far as they have been made public, and of the object of your paper in opening up this correspondence, and it was only with the view of helping to focus the opinion of each manufacturing centre and especially of our own town, that I troubled you at all with these few letters. It is all very well to take an interest in the spiritual welfare of our fellow creatures, but I cannot help thinking that it is equally incumbent to take an interest in their tem- poral necessities. With this in view I pointed out in my letter that owing to the increasing protectivetariffs of foreign nations and the obstaeles that every Power uuder the sun was placing in the way of British mann-. factured goods,scores of thousands of pounds in the shape of wages Aere annually lost to the working men of War- rington alone, many of them owing to these very foreign tariffs being in a state of enforced idleness for nearly two days out of every week; and what this means to women and little children every one knows.—l pointed out that in one trade alone—the Iron Trade,—the exports of bar iron, had fallen off from 313,000 tons in 1882 to. 125,000 tons in 1902 thanks to Mr. Parker's Fetish of so-called Free Trade, while in the latter year we im- ported more of this kind of iron than even we exported Not sent here,in fair and honest competition, but the surplus stocks of their highly protected countries dumped at any price, the higher flguresthey get in their monopolized home markets enabling them to do this. I certainly expected Mr. Parker would make some reply to this, but beyond a semi-sarcastic allu- sion as to whether wished to protect the manufacturers of Warrington alone, like the Levite of oldhe goes to the other side of the way. Smokeless chimneys and idle furnaces are nothing to him, what- ever they are to the workingmen, as long as they in- terfere with the shibboleths of a supposed system of Free Trade that I pointed out had never really existed. He contents himself by asking what I mean by manu- factured goods, a question his superior intelligence could easily.have answered for himself. It will do no harm, however, to either of us if. I mention in my "avowed ignorance" as he so humourously calls it, some goods that I may, rightly or wrongly think, come under this heading, and by a few comparisons of our exports of same in the respective years of 1872 and 1900. show what this so-called Free Trade has done for this country.

We exported in ' Falling off in 1872. 1900. one year only Woollen Goods £32,000,000 £15,000,000 £17,000,000 Linens 8,000,000 5,000,000 3,000,000 Linen Yarns Cutlery 5,000,000 2,000,000 3,000,000 Cotton Yarns 16,000,000 7,500,000 8,500,000 Silk Goods 4,000,000 2,000.000 2,000,000 Haberdashery ... 6,500,000 1,534,000 4,966,000 How many millions lost in wages in 12 months Mr. Parker can work out for himself. His direct question: "Are pig iron and steel billets manufactured goods ? " is simply an attempt to draw a red herring across the path and it looks like, to use his own phrase "avowed ignorance "th ask such a question. As to the basic principles of Free Trade as he calls them' I have already stated such a state of things does not exist in any country under the sun and need not repeat the arguments he so persistentllignores. Mr. Parker knows perfectly well that it is by our export trade so many millions of our people exist,that this export trade is not increasing in proportion to our population while that of Germany and the United States is increasing by leapsandbounds, any such increase on the part of the former being at our expense. To stand still is retrogression and this retrogressionlwould be greater still,were it not that while our trade with foreign nations is decreasing, our trade with our colonies is rapidly increasing, one Colonial in this respect being worth as much as 20 foreigners to us.

I believe in the virtues of cheap food, but any one the least acquainted with the history of the past 50 years knows that it is more due to the marvellous reduction in freight by land and sea, the improvement in agricultural machinery and the millions and millions of acres brought under cultivation in America, Canada, Argentina, etc., than to any other cause. Canada could grow all the wheat we required in 5 years if any encouragement was given her. Why should we draw all our supplies from the United States when in case of a war with that country—which I certainly trust will never be the case--she could bring us to our knees in 6 orB weeks by stopping our food, notwithstanding our command of the seas. Mr. Parker may say such a war is impossible, the two great Anglo-Saxon nations would never do anything so fratricidal. If so, he cannot be aware of the wonderful increase in the German and Sclavonic element in that country, a state of things different to the early days when nearly all Americans traced their ancestry to the Old Country. In regard to the three pointedly marked questions which he now puts before me, and which he says I declined to answer, it passes all human ability, to reply to any question one has never seen before, and which had not hitherto left the bfatin that imagined it. contend that a moderate impost on grain, same as existed before the present Budget, would not raise the price of bread and in proof of that it did mit do so while the tax was being levied. Furthermore strange to say within the last 21 days, after the tax was taken off altogether the bakers of Liverpool and London actually advanced the price of bread. Probably Mr. Parker may say these are both conservative cities and that it was simply done to put a further card into the Colonial Secretary's hand. Besides what is the use of even cheap bread, when the time comes,that owing to our one-sided fiscal policy one has no money at all to buy bread with? Is there any man in England so devoid of common sense as to decline paying a little more for his food if he finds instead of working only 3 or 4 days a week he can find employment for sor 6 days a week? Further still I contend higher wages do not necessarily • mean increased cost of production as witness the United States where the workmen get bebter paid than any country in the world. Is it not n little nonsensical to talk of th increased cost of food doing all this harm when it could be easily and advantageously equalized by a reduction in our terrible Drink Bill? If you raise money in one way by taxation where does the harm come in, if you can reduce other ; items of taxation as I previously remarked, to a similar extent?—His third question as to a bounty on cotton goods is an evolution of his own conception and has not been seriously proposed by anybody. The present sad position of the Lancashire cotton trade could never have been brought about had the cultivation of cotton in suitable portion of the British Empire been stimulated and had the spinners sufficiently looked ahead and anticipated the day when America would use up every bale she produced. It is the old way of look- ing at things. Because certain conditions existed in the time of Cobden and Bright can such conditions be reasonably expected to last until the end of time? It is the imbecility of everlastingly looking atancl deduct- ing from the affairs of the past that has brought the trouble for labour cannot as easily remove itself as capital can to other countries, as witness the various works established by English money in Germany and the United States to the disadvantage of British and to the advantap of foreign workmen. Mr. Parker assumes to be very angry that I should doubt the ancuracy of some of his statements. Well Sir if he aspires to fill the role of" Sir Oracle "I can only say it reminds' one of the Scotch Elder's prayer "God give us a good conceit of ourselves." I thought the highly revered and deeply esteemed Head of the RomatiCatholic Church was the only person that claimed infallibility. I did not know there was another Pope nearer Home. However, while agreeing with him that the traders of this country have been, to use his own words "for long years engaged in deepening, straighten- ing buoying and lighting" the channel of business,l repeat, even if I again incur his displeasure, that the foreign traders have narrowed their channels, remora the metaphorical buoys and lighthouses he speaks of and done everything in human possibility to block up the fairway against English goods. A continuance of this would simply ruin our export trade, employment would cease, and the year 1950 see our population re- duced to one half. A man may fight for a long time if he has, one arm tied up by the acts of a Protective Tariff but if the other arm and. both legs are fastened up also what chance has he ? This is for our workmen to say and decide on. The dear loaf is simply throwing dust in their eyes. The crucial question is how to find the work that will'enable us to buy bread at all. Why should IMr. Parker and his co-thinkers be in dread of any ' enquiry. If it can be proved that our present fiscal policy is best adapted to the necessities of this country well and good, the question will be settled for a decade or so. It on the other hand some changes are inevitable and necessary for our self-protection and preservation against the havoc now being increasingly wrought by these ever augmenting tariffs, Mr. Parker is, lam sure, too good an Englishman and too patriotic a gentleman not to yield to the force of circumstances. lam obliged to you, Mr. Editor, for your courtesy and equally so to Mr. Parker. As the "-limited gifts and avowed ignorance" t think were only intended for the subject under discussion, and as he has the weaker side to defend, I give hint the ladies' privilege of the last word.

Once, the British possessions made a great effort, and sent £49j worth of picture mouldings, in one year. They never tried again. China ware, £975,748, from foreign countries (out of which Germany got £381,177. German pictures, £133,919. Maps, £256,039. Musical instruments, £1,362,083, _ _ _ _ _ _
