£1,221,487. Fancy goods and general gim-crackery £1,295,257. Silks and Satins from France (and our own silk looms
idle), over five million pounds. American boots, nearly half-a-million pounds' worth. Foreign made toys, £1,238,229. Ink and Stationery, 2288,576. _ . _

Typewriters and other mechanical contrivances (not counting steam engines, and agricultural implements) considerably over three million pounds a year, of which America gets two millions. Waste-paper Baskets, and similar articles, over £209,000

of wiiiCh Belgium gets £BO,OOO. The imports into the United Kingdom, of manufac- tured iron and steel and machinery, show an increase of two and a half millions, in 1902, as compared with the previous year, and this is co-incident with the remark- able activity of German manufacturers and merchants in British markets. While our exports of iron and steel to Germany fell from 211,5i1 tons, we actually impor- ted from Germany 763,015 tons, as compared with 421,109 tons in 1901; and, in fact, Germany is rapidly reaching a total export trade, in iron and machinery equal to our own. Last year, the iron trade had to encounter American competition. What will be the position when American Trust Goods are pouring in, on the top of increasing German supplies ? I have only touched the fringe of this big subject of imports of manufactured goods, but I hope I have said enough to set many Trade Unionists in the mood for deeply studying the great question of the hour. If I thought I could be of useful service, I would gladly attend any meeting of my fellow workingmen, in the evenings, and help to make points clear. The one-time Mr. Lister, of Bradford, now LorA Masham perhaps, next to Mr. Chamberlain, the greatest living exponent of British Protectionist theories has very kindly given me permission to utilise any of his writings; so, next week, I will embody in my letter, some of his valuable observations,—including his views as to there being no reason why the workers' cost of living should—necessarily—be increased, if we adopt a protective tariff.

div.head: MR. C. E. PARKER MADE A CONVERT TO PROTECTION BY MR. E. W. BINDLOSS AND BY THE INFLUENCE OF IRELAND.
div.p: MR. C. E. PARKER MADE A CONVERT TO PROTECTION BY MR. E. W. BINDLOSS AND BY THE INFLUENCE OF IRELAND.
MR. PARKER, writes from Lough Neagh, Ireland, as follows :

There is something in the air of this dear little, green little Island, thatassists the reason. Since I came over here, my attitude on this controversy has been strangely affected. The arguments for Protection, which in Eng- land appeared absurd and superficial, now attain all the authority of sound economic law: I have purposely put myself out of reach of the" Warrington Examiner" or any other Saxon paper so I cannot tell what further arguments Mr. Bindloss may have ad- vanced in favour of protecting our home industry, the iron of Warrington, from the invasion of the foreigners. But shure if Warrington manufacturers are being under- sold by Germans and Belgians, it is indeed high time that we revolutionized the policy of the country. If trusts and cartels get rich by selling cheaply to- England and getting high prices from their owncountry men, surely our Government should by protective tariffs fence round our local manufacturers and give them a chance to live. Why should the foreign manu- facturers getall the plums? Why not give the War- rington firms a protected area, with a notice to out- siders to this effect :—" Nothing that is cheaper than we can make shall enter here."

The object of our fiscal laws should, like those of the Germans, be to foster our own industries. What is the use 'of having a paternal Government if it does not keep off invaders both in commerce and war? If the Free Trade fetish worshippers answer that cheap materials are essential to the prosperity of the indus- tries into which they enter, if they say that cheap iron is necessary say for our shipbuilding ,industry, then I reply first, that shipbuilding does not concern Warrington, so why bother; and second that under the new conditions the shipping interest will not be of so much importance. If we can adopt a policy that will tend to isolate us from the rest of the world and make us a self-contained country and empire, if we can cut off the imports coming from foreign counkries that are ruining our manufacturers because they are so clieap,we will not require such a large mercantile marine. Why should we provide ships and sailors for carrying the produce of the world, and why should our ports be utilized as warehouses for the convenience of the pro- ducers of other countries ? The useless ships can in fu- ture be broken up for the use of the manufacturers of Warrington.

As to the wage question. If wages do not advance as Free Traders say, then let the Protection-created trusts pay a bonus out of their bank overdrafts. More difficult things have been done in this scientific age. I read the other day of a scientist, I think he was Iri3hman,an who had in hand a scheme for cv orking the village pump by an ingenious mechanism set in motion from the drippings of the pails. But I very much question if it is a desirable thing to maintain, far less to advance wages. In a peat bog opposite the window at which I write are some Irishmen, who for a ten and a half hout day, are earning ten shillings a week and appear perfectly happy. Each man cuts and lifts on to the bank about thirty tons of wet peat a day. Now in the new principle that the value of a sovereign, or ten shillings as the case may be, "depends entirely upon the ease or difficulty with which it is procured,' this ten shilliags earned by the Irish labourer may be of more value than the sovereign earned in England what- ever its purchasing power may be. This settles the wage question. Then in regard to our exports; to maintain these, let us give a bounty on all exported goods as they 40 in all sensible countries. If any inquisitive person asks where this bounty is to come from? I would at once aniwer : Pay it out of the revenue from the national debt, and if old age pensions are to be paid at all let them be paid out of the debt itself. But I very much doubt if exports are a good thing for the country. I have no"settled convictions" on the point, brit if the contention. of Free Traders is right, that exports are paid for by imports, and that their volume is paid for by imports, then since our object is to lessen imports, especially cheap imports, let us cease to export so as to check imports.

div.head: ONE-SIDED FREE-TRADE v. PROTECTION.
div.p: ONE-SIDED FREE-TRADE v. PROTECTION.
A Trade-Union Stand-point.
MR. EL P. HUGHES writes:—

in my last week's letter, I promised to enter into details as to how and why I became a Protectionist; and it will be my endeavour, in this series of letters, to weave-up the personal side of the story with some use- ful facts and figures. _ . . _ _

This week, lam taking up a Trade-Union point of view, and, in venturing to do so, I would mention that I have been°, member, since 1893, of an important Trade Union; and that, during the two years 1897-8, I had the honour of occupying the Presidential chair of the Manchester branch.

Now, let me relate, in my own way, a Trade Union incident, having a bearing upon the question before : —Well, about 12 or 14 years ago, I was a visitor at the house of a leading engineerinr, trade unionist—in fact he was one out of the two delegates chosen to represent his town (a big manufacturing centre, in Lancashire) at a then forthcoming Trade Union Congress, in London. At that period I was just as ardent a Proteztionist as I am ROW, and I thought it would be a good chance to I"awaken" my friend, so I said to him, by way of opening up my favourite topic, What would you do if a non-unionist (as I then was) like myself, started work in your shop, to-morrow ?" "Why," said he "we would knock straps off." To those who are not very familiar with machinery, I must explain that as a practical protest . against the employment, of unskilled," knob-stick," or non-union labour such as mine would then have bean, he and his mates would simply have knocked-off the driving straps from the macninery, and then marched out of the works, until I was sent away. This was just the answer I wanted, so I proceeded to explaia to him that—while his Trade Union eyes were sufficiently wide open to perceive, and not only to perceive but to resent,any interference with the fair rights of labour when such interference came froma, fellow-countryman, he had not yet reached a state of mental vision whereby he could understand the dis- turbing effect of such interference when it manifested itself in the shape of im.ported manufactured articles. As I went on with my parable, I watched my friend closely, and I think I never remember a man's features changing so remarkably. From the state of scratching his head, in doubt and hesitation, he gradually altered to the" open mind"; and then, by and by, as I steadily marshalled my facts and figures; I oould see that he was won. He candidly confessed that he had never seen the force of the Protectionist point of view before, 1 but he was now quite satisfied that it could not much longer be ignored by Trade Unionists. He said that he was attending a Trade Union Congress in London, in the following week or so, and would raise the subject at first opportunity. Some time elapsed before I had again an opportunity of a discussion with my friend. When I asked him how he had gone„along at the Congress, his reply was "the Leaders think exactly as you do ; but, they daren't tell the men." To the best of my recollection, those were my friend's exact words, and, at this critical juncture in the Empire's political history, those words deserve to form a text, not only at every Trade Union meeting but at every public meeting where Protection is dis- missed. _ -----------

The first Napoleon cynically said that the world was "governed by words," and we realise this when we endeavour to analyse the average trend of British public opinionat the present moment. "Free-trade" sounds so plausible, and so entirely fair, that not one man in twenty cares to challenge its truthfulness as an ideo- graph or word-picture, conveying (as words ought surely to do) a correct impression to the human mind, and thereby furnishing the aocurate materi 1 which, alone, can guide the mental judgment to a correct conclusion. The word "Free-trade' is so deeply rooted, that a majority of members of Parliament, a large section of the public press, and many leaders of Trade Unionism "daren't tell the men!" If the compound-word "Free- trade," had—from the beginning—been preceded by the compound-word "One-sided," I wonder how long "Free-trade" would have lasted? After more than 20 years of speaking and writing upon Protectionist questions, I have, personally-, every con- fidence in appealing to my fellow-workmen (for lam only a plain working-man myself) to look into this great question, for themselves. If a sensible question is but fairly and squarely put, before a body of working- men, you can depend upon a sensible verdict. I think I was never so much impressed with this feature of sound British workman common-seuse, as I was at Parr Hall, when Mr. Marshall Hall, KC., came to Warring- ton, a while ago. He was, in clever advocate fashion, scoring points for the Government, and detailing measures that had been passed. Rounds of applause followed most of the `wints," but when it came to the recent Beer Bill, withlti. childish, grandmotherly regu- lations, I did not hear one single hand-clap. That signi- ficant silence was the most impressive verdict I have ever noted; and though lam a Tory and an old teetotaler, I felt proud to be present at an assembly that, like the Roman Senate, could express—without words—its sentiments upon one of the questions of the moment. In the same way, I feel sure that this Pro- tectionist doubt and difficulty only wants fairly stating, and the British workingman will deal with it, at th% next general election, in the best way. To help my Trade Union friends in seeing where and why they should knock straps off, I have compiled from the " Daily Mail" a lot of figures that speak for themselves. Thei are not old and musty , statistics, but Government Blue-book figures for imports of manufactured articles for last year. In introducing these figures I will just say 'to my- working men friends that manufactured articles repre- sent, to a large extent, Wages, and, of course, it is by wages we all live. Each sovereign of wages paid to a foreigner, for work done which could equally as well and in most rases far better be dons by a Britisher, is. or ought to be a vital "first principle "question for dis- cussion by every Trade Unionist who takes a real interest in his doctrines:—
Hardware, £1,366,645. Glass, over one million pounds. House fittings. Joiners and Cabinet work, £1,095,561. Furniture Woods and Veneer5,2255;348.. -
This item we could pass as raw Material.

div.head: HAPPY FAMILY IDEA.
div.p: THE HAPPY FAMILY IDEA.

Ma. H. WHITHAII, San Frahoisco, writes:— The G.O.M. was not far wrong when he said that Mr. Chamberlain "was the first politician we have had of • the American tye, and he is destined to give a great deal of trouble." Sometimes it is good to raise trouble, ' but in delving into the real inner meaning of the words • "Wake up England" we shall find that no one man is to blame if England has fallen asleep, nor can anyone put his finger on any narrow series of circumstances to account for the fact that England is gradually taking a back seat among the industrial nations. I was very much pleased to read the invitation the ' "Examiner" gave out to the thoughtful readers it • reaches and it is to be hoped that the response will , prove that Englishmen can take up, and consider Mr. Chamberlain's Happy family idea quite apart from political party bias, and that they will show to the world that they are not worshipping Free Trade as a fetish, and that they now see " it is only one of many causes of England's prosperity." England has, hitherto,been prosperous because, in the first place, she was the first among the nations to avail herself of all the potential and latent pbwer that lay in the series of inventions and discoveriesi that developed in the latter end of the eighteenth and the beginning of the nineteenth centur- ies.- These features enabled her to become the workshop of the world. Her home markets soon became unable to consume her industrial products, and she built up an enormous export trade. She also built up a large human export business. When machinery left Lancashire, workmen to tend it went along also. The factory system with all its horrors grew up, and alongside all this there was a Corn Law in existence that made rich landowners, and the time came in due course when the cotton lords and the rich landowners had to lock horns in a fight, the prize to be who should own the peasant and the factory hand. Those familiar with the lives of Cobden and Bright will, to-day, feel the thrill of horror run through them when they think of the graphic des- scriptions of the domestic lives of those who subsisted , on the scanty earnings in the mill, mine, and factory. I have hanging just'at my right hand, as I writer, a handsome plate dedicated to Henry Hunt Esq./As chairman of the meeting assembled on St. Peter's Field Manchester on the 16th of August 1819, and to the female reformers of Manchester and the adjacent towns who were exposed to and suffered from the -wanton and furious attack made on them by that brutal armed force ' the Manchester and Cheshire Yeomanry Cavalry." Prizing this plate as I do, I am not likely to forget what I have read anent the struggle made by the people's Tribunes to obtain cheap bread for the workers. But there was something in this struggle that planted in the minds of the manufacturers the seeds of pernicious doc- • trines. It developed in the minds of the rich and ' powerful the ideas that Free Trade in business meant also Free Trade in man, woman, and child. The merest todler could scare a 'crow, and from that glide away past the school into the plough shafts an ignorant country lout whose only ambition was to havean oppor- tunity.to pull his fore-lock to squire or parson. In the towns the babe scarcely away from its mother's nursing or the "care-takers," could go into the mill and earn a ' pittance by piecing. The child grew into the parent and soon began to fill the towns of Lancashire and ' Yorkshire with deformed and sickly human beings. Then the Government had to take hofd of this monster Free Trade in God's image, and Factory Act and the thousand and one measures resulting therefrom was the ' r esult. Free Trade did mean, and has meant, right on un- bridled competition in everything animate or inanimate that could be bought and sold. Now ' where are we at? Political economists have wor- • shipped at the shrine of supply and demand, and now the Statesman comes in and says " No, we will put all you dismal science fellows on one side, and we shall from now right on ignore all the beauties of open com- petition and form a little happy family of our own to be known from now as 'The British Imperial Zollverein." John Ruskin was voted an ignoramus when he wrote "Unto this last." He is the one man to-day the British workman should turn to and read. It seems likely that Mr. Chamberlain's idea may upset the Government. Putting this and the Irish question together leads one to think that the next House of Commons will give us a great change in the make-up of political parties. This being so we should see and hope forigood results if Lord Sherburne's advice given at the time when the "leap in the dark" was taken. "Now" heZsaid, "we must educate our masters." Is the workingman educated enough to See that the Independent Labour Party is a fraud? Is his vision clear enough to see that in the make-up of a new political party there will be one that will stand for Proeress' and "Thorough "should be its motto? If he seesbthishe will determine that no Independent Labour Party 'shall gull him into tho crime :of opening the door of the House of Commons so that his most deadly enemy may walk in and do his level best to keep England asleep. So far as I understand Mr„ Chamberlain's position, it is that he asks in the first place for free discussion on the question of "Is it desirable to enter into an agree- ment, that is to enter into reciprocal arrangements, treaties, with the various 'industrial elements' making up the British Empire?" If my advice has any weight I would strongly urge upon every voter, and upon every Imaa who wishes to be a true patriot, to give this .question, which marks the parting of the ways, his Ihonest, earnest thought. The difficulty is,the workingman,and to a large extent I his employer is unable to think this question out in a logical manner. It is too abstruse. It has so many abstract features about it that it cannot be crystalized by the ordinary mind. I confess it is very much beyond ' me. I notice in Atuerica,for instance, that the ordinary street sweeper gets 10s. a day of eight hours, and the , motor man on the electric car gets 12s. This under Protection. Now what does the street sweeper in Free i Trade England get? A young lady friend of mine, an English girl, gets 125 dollars a month as stenographer. I wonder how much she would get in England? In the educational campaign Mr. Chamberlain promises to enter into, it will not be sufficient to compare the high wages paid in the states with the comparitively low wages paid in England. Nor will it help towards a solid settlemert of the tariff question to say as Mr. Courteney says "that it is mere selfishness, and a desire for isolation on the part of America that influences her • in her policy of Protection." America's protective • policy is the outcome of, first, a settled determination to develop her own wenderful natural resources, and after that a general feeling that only through protection can the American workman be saved from the evil con- sequenoes it is feared would result in an open competi- tive struggle with the pauper labour of Europe." There may be a number of fallacies in all this, that we should very likely stumble across were we to go into the questions of the growth of the Trusts and the steadily increasing number of multi-millionaires, but that's anotherstory. It may seem very like sending coals to Newcastle but in another article I will try to give an , example of America's desire to enthuse the world with
her progressive ideas as seen in the work of Mr. Stewart and Mr. Loud at Trafford Park.

Now let us look at this wage question briefly. The untravelled Englishman can have no idea of the immense magnitude of the New England cotton trade, nor of its surprising growth during the past very few years. I do not want to be a calamity howler, but I am very certain that the Lancashire cotton spinner is within measurable distance of the time when he will not be able to buy American cotton. That is a very important matter and should be kept in view during the discussions The New England manufacturer is seeking fresh wood and pastures new in which to display his talent on exploitation of the factory hand. Into the Souther States he has gone, and to read of the material develop- ment of some of those old slave States, such as Virginia and the two Carolinas is almost like reading romance. But see the result in nearly all these large factories. The same or worse conditions obtain that were to be found in Lancashire in the evil days when the cotton lord reigned supreme. Low starvation wages and ignorance; women and children in the factory, and he who ought to be the bread winner, at home wash- ing dishes. Protection does not put money in the purse of the factory hands of America. As I am merely placing points for thought I would say here that in my opinion Europe as yet has only felt in a slight degree what America can do in the way of underselling her in her own markets. She will feel and know what underselling means, when from any cause the United States receives an industrial set-back. America'a resources and their development reads like a fairy tale. Where else can you find the same conditions? Turn to Germany and you have Protection in full swing, and you have a constant struggle between the agrarian and the industrial parties. The one urging "bread usury" and the other wanting cheap bread. What party outside the land-owning class benefits from protection in Germany? Turn to Russia it is the same, In France conditions are not so bad, because she holds a somewhat unique industrial art position among the producing nations, and is therefore comparatively well- to-do, but very much of this is merely veneering. The wit of the British statesman can,l am sure, formulate a protective scheme that would help England in her need, but it must be argued on open lines, and without political bitterness. The "happy family scheme" will never work, the empire is too heterogeneous. The interests of its various members willalways follow the cry of " business is business."

div.head: PROTEST FROM THE TRADES COUNCIL.
div.p: A PROTEST FROM THE TRADES COUNCIL.

At the monthly meeting of the Warrington Trades and Labour Comcil held on Tuesday evening the Sec- retary (Mr. F. Stott) announced that at the next meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Federation of rrades and Labour Councils the question of Mr. Chamberlain's tariff proposals would be discussed. It would be advis- able for the Council to instruct their delegate (Mr. Plumb) how to vote on any resolution which might be introduced.

Mr. E. Plinston said he did not profess to be so capable as to deal with the question of preferential tariffs—at all events at the present time—but Re thought that they as trade unionists might instruct their delegate to oppose the policy at present advanced by the Colonial Secretary as being opposed to trade union principles and to the good of the country. Mr. Fargher remarked that the Colonial Secretary would forget about the matter shortly, just as he forgot about old age pensions. Mr. York seconded the motion, and advanced the opinion that a certain member of the Govern- men and a ring of his friends had for a con- siderable time been supplying a great part of the food-stuffs which came into the country and had only met with qualified success. It would suit their purposes to impose a tariff which would probably prevent foreign countries from supplying food. The present agitation, he thought, was being conducted solely with a view of endeavouring to stop a great pro- portion of the food coming in from abroad so that the "ringing" operations would be more success- ful. He thought this consideration alone was sufficient to justify them in instructing their delegate to oppose the preferential tariff proposals as strongly as lay in his power. The proposition was carried unanimously as was also the following resolution forwarded by th# Leicester Trades Council :—That this Council protest against the proposed interference with our present Free Trade policy, believing that it would tell against the best interests of the workers and the nation generally."

div.head: MARRIAGE AT HOLY TRINITY CHURCH.
div.p: MARRIAGE AT HOLY TRINITY CHURCH.
Mounfield —Henshaw.

The marriage was solemnised in Holy Trinity Church, Warrington, on Thursday, of Mr. Charles Joseph Mounfield son of Mr. George Arnold Mona- field, cabinet maker, Buttermarket-street, and •Miss Elizabeth Henshaw, of Knutsford-road, Latchford, late manageress of Chantry's shop,Horsemarket-street. i Considerable interest was taken n the happy event and a large congregation assembled to witness the ceremony. The officiating clergyman was the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton. The bride, who was given away by Mr. G. A. Mounfield (father of the bridegroom) looked exceedingly handsome in a dress of cream silk voile, trimmed with applique ornaments, and cream silk, with hat to match. She carried a beautiful bouquet of roses and lilies of the valley, the gift of the bridegroom. Two bridesmaids were in attendance, namely, Miss Mounfield (sister of the bridegroom) and Miss Law. They wore dresses of blue silk voile, trimmed with Parisian lace and black ribbon velvet, and Gainsborough hats were worn. They also carried choice bouquets composed of sweet peas, the gift of the bridegroom. The duties of best man were discharged by Mr. James A. Princep. A reception was afterwards held at the Winmar- leigh Cafe, at which a large number of guests were present. The honeymoon is being spent in the Lake district. The bride's travelling dress was a grey costume and black hat. div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

WAT,Krso DA.Y.—This red letter event took place yesterday but the severe storm in the evening militated against the success of the festival. The village was gay with flags and bunting, and fortunately the proces- sion was favoured with tine weather, much to the joy of the children who, it had been feared, would be deprived of the pleasure of parading the village in "Sunday best ' as rain fell in torrents at noon. The scholars attending St. Thomas's day and Sunday schools, to the number of 900, assembled in the church at 1.30 and a short service VMS Conducted by the Vicar (Rev. H. V, Pigot), Afterwards they formed into procession. and to the strains of the Blue Coat School band marched alone Ellesmere-road. Lawrenson's Brow,Whitefield-road, to Victoria-square. At the head of the procession walked the Vicar, andlthe Rev. C. M. Evans(curate), and the church officers. The children carried bannerettes and the procession presented a pleasing sight. A large number of infants rode in buries lent by Messrs. Green- all. Whitley and Co. At Victoria-square the procession split up into two parts, the infants proceeding to the Church Institute and the elder scholars to the National schools where they partook of a capital tea. Tea over the scholars wended their way to the Park adjoining the brewery where sports Ste., were indulged in until the evening when the storm rendered further enjoyment impossible. The arrangements were in the capable hands of Messrs. F. Rose, Starkey, Spencer and Mclntyre, and the children were in charge of Mr. A. Moss (boys), Miss Hartley (girls) and Miss Percy (infants.)
MUNICIPAL TRADING. THE PARLIAMENTARY INQUIRY. The Allegations Against Warrington.

div.head: Evidence of the Town Clerk.
div.p: Evidence of the Town Clerk.

When the Joint Committee of the two Houses of Parliament on municipal trading met on Monday morn- ing, Lord Crewe presiding, Mr. Baker, Parliamentary agent for Warrington, stated that the Town Clerk desired to be heard with reference to the allegations against Warrington which were made at the last sitting by Mr. Norbury Williams. Lord Zouche: Does he want to contradict the state- ments made? _ _
_ Mr. Baker: Certainly. Sir James Woodhouse: lam not surprised. The Chairman announced that they would hear the evidence of the Town-Clerk on Thursday.

div.head: MR. NORBURY WILLIAMS'S
div.p: MR. NORBURY WILLIAMS'S
CHARGES.
Rebutting Evidence by Mr. Henry Roberts and the Town Clerk. MUNICIPAL TRADING "MISREPRESENTED."
[Special Report.]

LONDON, THURSDAY. The Joint Committee of both 'Houses of Parliament on Municipal Trading met again to-day, the Earl of Crewe presiding. Among the witnesses called was Mr. Henry Roberts, a Justice of the Peace for Warrington. "Mr. Roberts, replying to questions put to him by the Chairman, said he had been appointed to the Commis- sion of the Peace in 1892. In November 1884 he was for the first time elected a member of the Town COUIIOI of Warrington and he continued in office until Novem- ber 1901, when he resigned. For the last fourand a half years of that period he held the office of Alderman. He was Mayor of the Borough in the years 1899, 1900 and 1901: He was managing director of Joseph Cros- field and Sons, Limited. They were soap and chemical manufacturers at Warrington. He was also Chairman of the Warrington Slate Co., Limited, builders and contractors' j merchants. The latter was originally a private concern, but for purelyfinancial reasons it was made a limited liability company in September 1882. It was not until November 1884 that he entered the Corporation of Warrington. That was nearly five and a half years after the establishment of the firm and over two years after the formation -of the Company. At the time the Company was formed he had not the remotest intention of going into municipal life. The Chairman: Then you repudiate the insinuation that the formation of the Company had anything to do with your position as a member of the municipality? The Witness : I do so most emphatically. Proceeding, witness said the statements by Norbury Williams on,ithe 9th inst were notjustifled by facts so far as his (witness's) own personal conduct was concerned, orlso far as his relation to the Corporation of Warrington, through the Warrington Slate Company was concerned. The number of shareholders on the formation of the Company in 1882 was 13. The present number of shareholders was 17, of whom five only—including himself—were members of his family. As to the capital of the company the nominal amount was £20,000, and the subscribed capital was £17,250. He and his family held of this capital £10,870 in shares. From its forma- tion to the present day the Company had been supplying i goods to the Corporation n open competition, but as a purchaser of goods from the Company, the firm had not regarded the Corporation as of much importance. For some time their sales to the Corpora- tion had only amounted to £2,000 per annum—a small matter, being only one-fiftieth of their whole business. In the year 1887 he (witness) carried in the Town Council a resolution, the effect of which was that all the committees of the Council should be re- quired in the future to procure all their requirements, whether for material to be supplied, or for labour to be done, or both, by tender, and that when- ever such material or labour involved an expenditure of £2O or upwards, the tenders should be publicly adver- tised, and that every accepted tender should be pub- lished with the minutes of the committee, together with the price and the name of the successful contractor. His solo object I in proposing that resolution was to give publicity to all purchases made by the Corporation, and so that there should be no suspicion of any kind. Since then all requirements of the Corporation of Warrington hadbeen first adver- tised, then reported on by the committee, and the i amounts had been published n the newspapers, so that the whole thing had been done in the light of day, with full knowledge on the part of all interested in the matter. The Chairman: There has not been case in which the lowest tender was not the accepted tender? The Witness: Not one. On no single occasion had he been a member of a committee which took a tender from his firm. The Chairman: Do you see any objection to the supplying of goods to a Corporation by firms, some members of which may be members of the Corporation? Witness: I, personally, do not Nee any objection. I would not object, with proper safeguards, to members of a Corporation undertaking tenders if it is not an illegal act. Continuing, there was a definite statement by Mr. Norbury Williams that the Company was a colourable one, and to this he took direct exception. Mr. Williams had no personal knowledge of Warrington, and his speech made during an agitation was full of gross mis-statements. He had accepted statements made by persons without taking the slightest trouble to verify them. The Chairman: It is only fair to Mr. Williams to say that, when giving evidence, he said he was not speaking from personal knowledge, but from information sup- plied to him. The Witness: I cannot say whether he said that. In Warrington he has not made such a qualification. He described Blackpool as the most corrupt borough in the kingdom, and said that Warrington came very near i t The witness went on to point out that in 1901 the auditors of Warrington called attention in their report to certain irregularities which had taken place. The Town Council thereupon appointed three members of the Corporation to investigate the charges, and their report was duly presented to the Corporation. They found that certain of the matters charged were not illegal and the others capable of satisfactory explanation, The sums involved were small, and in every instance the transactions had been to the advantage of the borough, The charges only concerned three members and the finding was a practical exoneration of the persons sup- posed to be concerned and the whole report was made public. The witness said that now another attempt was being made to secure a further inquiry. They had not the slightest objectionr , to t,provided it was conducted on proper lines. ' But the proposal was that the inquiry should be held by sixcommissioners and that nobody should be allowed to object to the personnel of the CommiSsioners, that no person should be allowed to appear by Counsel or solicitor, and that none of the public or the members of the press should appear and attend at the inquiry. Such an inquiry could not be a fair one. The question of trading had been greatly misrepremented.The witness said he was in favour of municipal trading, and was prepared to give the Committee figures as to the results at Warrington, but the Chairman said they did not propose to go into the details. The Chairman: Do you approve of the existing system of an elected borough auditor? -- Witness: No, and for this reason, that the gentleman selected for the position of elective auditor is not always selected specially for ability to deal with accounts, although he may have capacity for general work. And I also think that the auditor should be perfectly independent, and that his appointment and dismissal should be subject to the approval of the Local Government Board, as in the case of medical officers of health. The auditor should, in my opinion, send a report to the Local Government Board, and he would have his report published in fulV Questioned by Mr. Powell Williams, the witness said
that as mayor and a councillor it would be his duty to see that all purchases for the Corporation were made. as cheaply as possible. .......

Mr. Willianis : As a director of your company, it would be your duty to sell as dearly as you could—to. get good prices? The Witness: Yes. Mr. Williams: Did you not think the two positions were conflicting? The Witness; Not in my case, as I took no part in- directing the Corporation either as seller or as buyer. Mr. Williams: Do not you think that in the case of a member of the Corporation who is a substantial holder in a private company it would be better for the com- pany not to have any transactions with the Corpora— tion?

The Witness: I think everything would depend upon the conditions under which the business was transacted.. Mr. Williams: But would not it be better that there should be no trancmtions7as between the company and the Corporation under the circumstances I allude to? The Witness replied that with the safeguards he had referred to—advertisement and tender—he saw no objec- tion. He attached the greatest importance to the provision of these safeguards. His objection to the system of elective auditors was on the ground that other questions were often mixed up with the elections. THE TOWN CLERK'S EVIDENCE.

Mr. James Lyon Whittle, in answer to the Chairmanr said he was a solicitor and Town Clerk of Warrington, and had held the latter office for 12 or 13 years. He had read the evidence of Mr. Norbury Williams and as to the alleged refusal to show certain minutes to the ratepayers he (the witness) had never refused to show the minutes of the Town Council, although he had refused to show minutes of Committees until they had passed the Council itself- The Municipal Corporation Act of 1883 did not oblige the officials of the Corporation to show the minutes of committee meetings to any ratepayers. One rate- payer had asked for the minutes of a committee. He (the witness) being of opinion that the applicant was not entitled, refused the request. It Was' in connection with. the Gas Committee and the minute was subsequently published in the Council's proceedings. The ratepayer raised an action. for a mandamus, but the Court of Appeal refused to make the order for the production of the minutes or the committee. He (witness) was of opinion that it would be dangerous to public policy that burgesses should be allowed to inspect the minutes of the com- mittees before they had passed the Council. There was- a case within the last few months-in which somebody wanted to see how far the Corporation were likely to go in the matter of the purchase of certain propertY The TCommittees had a free hand in such matters although their decisions required confirmation by the Council as a whole. A Committee might make a pro- visional agreement for a purchase, but wheia it was onfr by public auction, the Committee might go on to rail', chase, without reference to the Council. The Council might have given them a power to fix a price up to which they might go, and it might be knocked down ta the Committee at the price' sanctioned by the Corpora- tion. His Council as a rule appointed some one ta attend a sale.

By the Earl of Crewe: Do you confine your objec- tions to ratepayers seeing the minutes of Committees solely to minutes as to the acouisition of property? , Witness: Mainly so, but I object also in reslrct °1 such questions as the extension of the boundanes of boroughs and some other matters. After hearing evidence from Stockport oor finß ac 'P the committee adjourned for the day. d l

Warrington Band of Hope Union. The quarterly meeting of the Council of the Warrington Band of Hope Union was held in the Ragged School the other evening. Mr. Thomas Dale° (chairman of the Executive Committee) presided - Considering the attractive character of the meetingr the attendance was small. After the routine business had been disposed or, an interesting address on tem" ' nerance topics generally. was given by Mr. W. B. Suttle, of Levenshulme. At the conclusion of the" , address a short discussion took place, making it clear that Mr. Suttle had impressed as well as interested his audience. The meeting was also made the occasion of an interesting presentation to Mr. Harry Woolley, the union's energetic assistant hon. secretary, on his re• cent marriage. The Chairman,after displaying his abilitr in saying the right word at the right time, presented Mr. Woolley with a handsome case of meat and game. carvers as a token of the appreciation in which 3fr, Woolley is held by the members of the Executive. Committee. The recipient, in a few well-chosen words, thanked the donors and gratified the meeting by informing them that his bride's interest in Band of Hope work was as great as his own. Votes of thanks to Mr. Suttle and to Miss Monk for her kindness in providing the refreshments brought the meeting to a close. The following resolutions were carried unani- mously :—" That this meeting protests against the creation of a continuous vested interest in liquor licences, as proposed by Mr. Butcher's Compensation Bill, and by Sir W. Hart Dyke's Bill to suspend the - discretionary power of the magistrates to refuse re- newals of licences," and "that a certified copy of the above be sent to the Right Horn A. J. Balfour, Prima Minister; to the Right Hon. A. Akers Douglas, Home Secretary; to Sir Henry Campbell-13annerman, Leader of the Opposition; to Mr. Robert Pierpofnt, M.P., aria to the newspapers.

COUNTY BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON.— MUNICIPAL BYE-ELECTION. 1903 TO THE ELMO-FORS OF Si'. JOHN'S WARD. LADIES AND GIiNTLEMEN. At the request of the Committee of the Municipal Non-Trading tAll9oeiatiOn, I have decided to offer myself as a Candidate for the vacancy occasioned by the death of the late Mr. Councillor Baird. I leave taken a very deep interest in the Non-- Trading Movement from its commencement, and should you do me the honour of returning me as your representative. I would do my utmost to help on the good work which 39 being accomplished under the Non Trading-banner. I am strenuously opposed to .11 illegal and Immoral trading by members of the Council with the Corporation, believing as I do that all engaged in such trailing cannot do their duty to the ratepayers. Self-interest under such conditions is bound to pre- dominate. and where that is in existence in public life the town must suffer. I should carefully watch all expenditure. with a view to bringiag about a reductiiin in rates, which have now reached such a figure as to be almost ruinous. Unless all extravagant expenditure is speedily checked, the rates must of necessity be increased. and that would in all probability cause higher rents, which would materially affect the working classes. I pledge myself to oppose auytking and every- thing ia the nature of extravagance. ant to work hand-in-hand with the Non- fraders, who, in the Council Chamber, have been such a power for good. They have taken the ratepayers iuto their confidence by exnosing many serious irregularities which, had it not. been for them, would never have been brougtA before the notice of the public. I appeal with every confiience for your quoport, and should you enable me to become your representa- tive, I promise to .10 my duty to the Ward and to the town as a whole. Trusting to receive your votes, I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant. HENRY THORNTON. The Laurels, Fearnhead.

THE BROOK AT BURTONWOOD. The INSPECTOR informed the Council that the brook at Burtonwood was again in a very bad state. Mr. For- sham had put down extensive sewage plant at the Brewery but for some reason or other it was not work- ing satisfactorily. Mr. FORSHAW thought the pollution was due to the yeast which was washed down with other sewage matter, The brook was an open sewer and was used by a great many people. Dr. SEPIITON asked if it were not possible to separate the yeast from the other sewage. Mr. FORSFLAW said it would be a very difficult matter to do so. Webb (14) for the visitors. AMERICA ANNEXING ISLANDS. A Press Association telegram says a report reached the Parliamentary lobby on Wednesday night that some vessels of the United States Navy have taken possession of about twenty small islands off the coast of Borneo, which are understood to belong to this country. .It is probable that a question on the subject will shortly be put in the House of Commons. The Premier, in acknowledging receipt of a resolution from the Court Duke of Devonshire of the A.0.F., at Barrow, in reference to the Outdoor Relief Friendly Societies' Bill, says "that the matter will receive the lattention of the Government." FIRE IN HER LAP. An inquest was held at West Ham on Wednesday on Mrs. Rose, the wife of a Plaistow tobaoconist, who sustained fearful injuries in a fire on Sunday. Deceased and her husband were sitting in the shop. She was rest- ing her arm on a table on which stood a lamp, when one of the legs of the table broke. The lamp was broken, and rolled into the deceased's lap. After an unsuccessful attempt by her husband to put out the fire, she rushed into the street, a" mass of flames." She died in a few hours. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. A WHITE MAN LYNCHED. A dispatch received in New York from Maysville (Kentucky) states that a mob broke into Flemingsburg gaol and hanged Thacker, a white man who committeda murder two years ago. It had been announced that Thacker, who had already been condemned once, was to be tried again, and the people feared he might in some way escape punishment.
